docs.title: How the UML render framework and resource ownership work
docs.text: For the public interfaces, generics, lifecycle contracts, and buffer integration see the API reference.

docs.title: Layer responsibilities
docs.text:
The core defines the model, skeleton, pose, scheduling, resource context, buffer, and output contracts and does not depend on Minecraft or a concrete graphics API. The host owns the frame and view entry points, the backend owns resources and drawing, the geometry adapter converts model representations, and the resource factory creates the resources of one instance. These responsibilities compose, but geometry conversion must not also manage the shared executor, frame marks, and the draw pipeline.

flowchart TD
    Host[Host frame and model pipeline] --> Scheduler[Scheduling]
    Host --> Backend[Draw backend]
    Backend --> Context[Mounted resource context]
    Context --> Factory[Per-instance resource factory]
    Factory --> Geometry[Geometry adapter]
    Context --> Buffers[CPU and GPU buffers]

Mounted resources, the host frame context, and pre-render metadata are different objects. The backend offers its services to the factory explicitly, so an adapter does not have to look the backend up by string. The context caches the resources the factory creates but does not own model instances, shared adapters, or executors.

docs.title: Prepare-then-publish
docs.text: A new mount must be prepared successfully before it is published. If a replacement fails, the unpublished new context is closed and the old mount is kept; on success the new mount is published before the old resources are released. Removal first unregisters from the registry and then closes the context; closing the whole backend tries to release every mount and aggregates the exceptions. Closing is idempotent, and a closed context cannot allocate resources again. A shared view is read-only, and changes have to go through the lifecycle entry points.

docs.title: Scheduling and sampling are separate
docs.text: Scheduling decides only strategy visibility, and the backend applies the distance and frustum gates in order. Different views have their own visibility marks and share the pose sampling cache within a frame. Physics advancement is independent of draw visibility. For the concrete frame ordering see Render Scheduling.

docs.title: Buffers and in-flight reads
docs.text:
CPU buffer indices count elements, while capacity and stride are in bytes, and the two must not be mixed up. A short update covers only the prefix and keeps the tail and the capacity; a slice borrows the original memory and must not outlive the close.

A GPU upload receives a complete snapshot, and the dirty ranges describe the changed elements. Ring slots track version and historical modifications separately and fill in the accumulated differences when the slot is used again. Storage must not be overwritten while a GPU read is in flight; a device may replace the storage and decide reclamation with a non-blocking completion query. Every draw and translucent replay records consumption, and a completion mark must not be missed even when the frame's data did not change.

The device layer owns graphics API operations and state restoration, and the ring owns the buffer/fence lifecycle. The macOS TBO orphan policy belongs to the OpenGL device implementation and has no place in the platform-independent model and scheduling layers. For the module boundaries see Rendering Backends.

docs.title: How multi-layer volumetric cloud rendering works
docs.text: For cloud field configuration, instance control, preview, and the verification entry see the API reference.

docs.title: Weather and density layers
docs.text: The sky is made of independent low, middle, and high density layers, and a weather window controls the cloud clumps, gaps, and thickness variation. The continuous density can connect and overlap across weather grid boundaries, which avoids a discrete arrangement of one cloud per cell. The low layer keeps cumulonimbus envelopes, the middle layer spreads out, and the high layer uses stretched, anisotropic shapes; a cloud tower can also span several height layers. Scene height and coverage presets are art configuration, not meteorological measurements.

docs.title: Rendering and cost
docs.text:
A cloud field is drawn with one sky-covering ray march and one compositing draw, and no fullscreen pass is created per cloud. It first intersects the ray with each layer's height interval, sorts and merges the overlapping intervals, and skips the gaps between layers outright. The sampling budget is allotted by the square root of the interval length, so a thin high cloud is not starved of budget by the lower layers and does not disappear; the densities of several cloud layers at one point are added. The total number of samples per ray is bounded by the budget, and the march ends early when transmission is very low. Weather windows and GPU textures use a cache of at most 8 entries, so travelling does not grow memory without limit.

A shared shape texture keeps the cumulonimbus tower and anvil envelopes; periodic Perlin-Worley/Worley noise generated in the background provides the body, billowing, and erosion of the continuous cloud layers. Each layer uses its own weather, noise phase, and shape scale, and thin clouds use a stretched, anisotropic shape. Quadratically spaced light intervals integrate to layer exits for soft self-shadowing. Beer–Lambert extinction accumulates premultiplied radiance and transmittance front to back, with empty-envelope skipping. Dual Henyey–Greenstein lobes control forward/backward scattering. Three approximate scattering orders progressively halve extinction and anisotropy, with decaying normalized energy; this is not a full radiative-transfer solver. A single cumulonimbus uses a cached lighting voxel atlas, usually updated every 0.25 seconds.

For the cloud field, FAST/BALANCED/HIGH use width and height resolutions of 1/3, 1/2, and 1 of the original viewport; the total budget per ray is 112/160/256 samples, with 2/4/6 light samples. The corresponding resolutions for per-cloud quality are 1/3, 1/2, and 1, with at most 48/80/128 fine steps. A low-resolution result is upscaled with conservative depth and depth-aware interpolation. Both paths truncate at the opaque scene depth and write no depth; sky clouds are not limited by the terrain far plane, and the host GL state is restored. Infinite perspective far planes are also supported.

RGBA16F stores radiance/opacity; RG32F stores extinction-weighted mean cloud distance and the scene-ray endpoint. Stable view IDs enable independent ping-pong histories. Reprojection compensates camera movement and wind, rejects incompatible depth/endpoints, boundaries, time, lighting and settings, and clamps history to the current 3×3 neighborhood. Teleports, world changes, resize and lighting discontinuities reset history. At most eight views are cached. Anonymous views or historyWeight=0 keep the independent spatial path. Mean depth approximates separated layers, so rejection is conservative; empty current rays never resurrect old silhouettes.

Composition snapshots host color and evaluates Lcloud + Tcloud * Lscene in linear light. The default explicitly decodes/encodes display sRGB; linear HDR mode does not tone-map or clamp radiance. The host owns final exposure.

Long-range views add host-sky atmospheric perspective and distance fade. Ground cloud shadows and complete weather/spectral-atmosphere simulation remain extensions; translucent objects such as water are composited with the clouds by render stage. The extra gbuffer channels of an Iris shader pack are not verified yet, so acceptance with the shader pack disabled does not imply compatibility.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• User-provided volumetric cloudscape implementation from Horizon Zero Dawn
  • Guerrilla: Nubis, original material from 2017
  • SIGGRAPH 2015: The Real-time Volumetric Cloudscapes of Horizon: Zero Dawn
  • WMO: cumulus outline, billowing top, and flat base
  • WMO: the tower and anvil of cumulonimbus
  • WMO: low, middle, and high cloud layers and their distribution across layers
  • NOAA: the ten basic cloud types and the shapes of multi-layer clouds

This implementation uses continuous density layers, procedural weather regions, and a small number of cumulonimbus shape envelopes; it does not copy the spherical-shell cloud layer or the frame-split reprojection of the original system. The hardware timings in the cited material do not represent the performance of this repository's implementation.

docs.title: World UI Input Design
docs.text:
A transparent input Screen lets players move the system cursor freely in front of world-space UI. Crosshair and free-cursor modes share the same plane-intersection and event-routing stages. For API contracts, units, integration, and acceptance commands, see the reference.

flowchart LR
    C[Crosshair: viewport center] --> P[Screen unprojection]
    S[Transparent Screen: GUI cursor] --> P
    P --> R[Render-view ray]
    R --> H[Existing ray-plane intersection]
    H --> L[Inverse UI transform: local coordinates]
    L --> N[Nearest valid rectangle]
    N --> I[Hover / button capture / keyboard focus]
    I --> G[GuiEventListener and child widgets]

docs.title: Coordinate Spaces and Render Timing
docs.text:
For cursor coordinates (x,y) and logical viewport (W,H), normalized device coordinates are nx = 2x/W - 1 and ny = 1 - 2y/H. Apply the inverse of the actual rendered projection P to (nx,ny,-1) and (nx,ny,0), performing the perspective divide. The first point is the ray origin; the normalized difference is its direction. An interior depth point supports infinite far planes, and the same construction works for orthographic cameras.

The viewpoint, screen plane, and UI plane in the reference sketch lie along this ray. The projection already contains FOV, aspect ratio, optical zoom, and render bobbing, so no estimated eye-to-screen distance or fixed cursor-offset multiplier is needed. A screen point determines a ray; a target plane or another hit constraint is required to select a unique world point.

Let M be the complete local-to-view matrix used to draw a UI. Intersect the ray and plane in view space, then apply M^-1 to obtain UI-local pixel coordinates. M includes the host model-view, camera translation, panel placement/rotation/scale. This avoids mixing a world-space ray with a plane that has already had the camera position subtracted, or subtracting half the panel size twice.

Each frame, the backend copies the projection and each interactive panel's final transform, then finishes input updates. Between frames, events use the most recently presented geometry. Clicks recompute the pointer hit before dispatch rather than relying on an earlier hover. Frame completion also updates hover and capture coordinates when the cursor is stationary but the view or panel has moved. Offscreen cameras cannot replace the main player's input snapshot.

docs.title: Canvas and Depth
docs.text:
The world plane composites one texture. Widgets, glyphs, and shadows first render into an independent RGBA+depth canvas using the ordinary orthographic GUI projection. This preserves fine separations such as 0.03 GUI-Z. Compressing the full GUI depth range into 0.1 world blocks can quantize text and shadow to the same perspective depth, producing stripes, missing fragments, and unstable borders. One unit of padding beyond the GUI depth endpoints includes the MAX_GUI_Z + 0.03 shadow layer. Every composite vertex stays at local Z=0, keeping the panel position and picking plane identical regardless of internal GUI depth.

The canvas clears to transparent black, so normal GUI blending stores premultiplied RGB. World composition uses ONE / ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA to avoid multiplying alpha twice and darkening edges. The plane tests scene depth but does not write it. Draw scopes restore framebuffer bindings, viewport, projection, blending, depth, clipping, and texture state. Removal, world changes, and shutdown release canvases; resizing replaces attachments. Panel clipping uses canvas height rather than window height.

docs.title: Input Ownership
docs.text:
Hover tracks the nearest currently hit panel. Keyboard focus tracks the last clicked panel. Each mouse button separately captures the panel that accepted its press. These can differ: when dragging from A over B, B can be hovered while A continues to receive drag and release events. Drag deltas are differences between successive projected local coordinates, not screen-pixel deltas.

Capture continues outside the rectangle by intersecting the extended panel plane. If intersection is temporarily unavailable, the last valid local coordinates are retained. Closing, removal, or focus loss still sends release to the original target. Keyboard presses also retain their target, and a focus change balances held keys with releases. Duplicate move notifications do not dispatch zero-distance drags.

The input layer does not copy or redraw the panel as a second two-dimensional Screen. Minecraft's Screen lifecycle releases/regrabs the cursor and clears gameplay keys. The transparent Screen consumes input and forwards it to the router while world simulation continues. World rendering, plane intersection, and input capture remain separate, allowing an existing occlusion or alternative hit solver to consume the same ray source later.

Normal crosshair mode has temporary keyboard ownership when the last clicked panel's nested focus chain leads to an editable text widget. A client-only KeyboardHandler HEAD hook consumes events before vanilla updates KeyMapping or handles chat/debug shortcuts; a later key notification cannot prevent those effects. Entering/leaving clears gameplay keys without changing mouse ownership or the current Screen. Escape recursively clears child focus and balances held keys. Physical keys still held at exit retain suppressed repeat/release events so they cannot become movement. Since window focus loss may skip native releases, a fresh press clears its old record and resumes gameplay.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The current implementation accepts Screens and other GuiEventListeners with explicit rectangular bounds. It uses geometric plane picking and does not synchronize server state. Callbacks for server-controlled business behavior should send packets; the server must validate permissions, distance, and business state. Panel registration belongs to the caller. Closing the input layer only clears input state.

docs.title: AnimationScope: From Business State to a Stable Image
docs.text:
An animation system answers two different questions: what state the game is in, and how that state should be displayed. Game ticks, player input, state-machine rules, and networking decide the first. Clips, poses, model placement, and render interpolation decide the second. AnimationScope joins them into one process whose results can be committed, paused, interpolated, and observed without mixing old and new state.

For content authors, the Scope defines when animation advances, which inputs belong to the same step, and when the renderer may see the result. For the renderer, it exposes completed animation results without asking the render thread to reinterpret a state machine or sample an animation source again.

docs.title: Business problems it solves
docs.text:
Business need Mechanism Visible result Block, entity, or vehicle animation follows gameplay The host submits fixed-length logical steps Animation speed does not change with client frame rate State machines, manual clips, and multi-part models stay coherent One Scope commits one generation of results The body cannot reach the next frame while a wheel group remains on the previous one Pause, resume, and seeking must not make animation race ahead One root timeline owns accumulation, pause, and discontinuity Paused time is not replayed; a seek does not interpolate across unrelated time ranges Minecraft logic advances at 20 Hz while monitors render faster Logical results and render-frame interpolation are separated Logic is stable and the image remains smooth A server owns control state while clients render it An adapter maps authoritative state into inputs or a client replica Client interpolation cannot rewrite server rules Resource reloads and model rebuilds should not restart animation Targets support rebind while the Scope retains playback state A fresh model receives subsequent writes without losing playback progress

The governing rule is simple: the logical phase produces results, and the render phase consumes them. A render frame may change interpolation phase, but it cannot advance animation time, change a revision, or execute a state machine.

docs.title: How one business event becomes animation
docs.text:
Consider a minecart entering a curve and beginning to tilt:

World state: speed, track direction, vehicle type
        -> host writes values through AnimationInputPort
        -> AnimationScope.advance(raw delta)
        -> RootTimeline emits 0..N fixed logical steps
        -> Controllers read the frozen input snapshot and read-only playback state
        -> a controller selects, switches, or stops a playback instance
        -> Playback resolves local time for each leaf clip
        -> target evaluators produce immutable target-specific results
        -> one revision is shared by the TargetPublication batch
        -> the Minecraft adapter calls ModelInstance.sample(...) for a render frame
        -> root is written first, pose second, then model update and GPU submission

Controllers answer why something plays and which playback should be selected. Playback instances answer which source time is active. Targets answer where the result is written. With those roles separated, a new trigger does not require changes to the renderer, and a new output slot does not make controllers understand a model format.

flowchart LR
    A[Game input and authoritative state] --> B[AnimationInputPort]
    B --> C[AnimationScope.advance]
    C --> D[RootTimeline fixed steps]
    D --> E[Playback local time]
    E --> F[Controller / FSM]
    F --> G[Target evaluator]
    G --> H[One revision publication batch]
    H --> I[ModelInstance.sample]
    J[partialTick] --> I
    I --> K[root → pose → model update]

docs.title: Three time domains
docs.text:
The word "time" serves three different purposes:

Time domain Business meaning Owner Must not do Host time Seconds elapsed in the current game tick MC/Proxy adapter Change a playhead or Target directly Scope logical time Fixed steps used for state advancement and results RootTimeline and AnimationScope Use a render frame or revision as seconds Render interpolation Display phase between two committed logical results RenderSampleContext.interpolationAlpha Resample an animation source, run Controllers, or create revisions

The Minecraft adapter normally uses 1/20s as the fixed step and caps catch-up. A large host delta may create several logical substeps or discard stale steps at that cap. Those are host runtime policies, not properties of an animation asset.

partialTick becomes an interpolationAlpha in [0,1] only at the adapter boundary. It lets a train already reach its next logical position while the image smoothly moves from the previous position to the current one.

docs.title: Business concepts and code responsibilities
docs.text:
Business concept Code collaborator Responsibility Animation scope AnimationScope / ManagedAnimationScope Transaction boundary for one logical step plus lifecycle entry point Root clock RootTimeline Previous/current logical time, pause, seek, and fixed-step planning Runtime input ScopeInputStore Freeze values and triggers for the step; consume triggers only after commit State rules RuntimeController Decide play, switch, stop, or other valid controls from inputs and playback views Clip arrangement PlaybackRegistry / PlaybackTimeGraph Hold playback instances and derive local time, loops, and boundaries from parent time Animation result TargetOutputEvaluator<O> Turn committed state into one immutable result for a target Output destination AnimationTarget<O> Store a publication and write one exclusive slot during a render frame Render entry ModelInstance.sample(RenderSampleContext) Sample a model at most once per frame in a fixed order

ManagedAnimationScope is the final default implementation. Integrations add Controllers, Playback, Targets, and command handlers through its builder. They do not subclass the Scope to add behavior for a block, entity, or model format.

docs.title: FSM-driven characters and blocks
docs.text: FsmPoseEvaluator wraps a StateMachine as a Controller. Each real logical substep advances the machine once, then hands the composed pose to ModelPoseTarget. Transitions, durations, variables, and triggers live in the logical phase. Bones, morphs, material frames, and IK are interpolated into the model during rendering.

docs.title: Code-controlled one-shot animation
docs.text: AnimationPlayer.play(...) creates a private Scope for a standalone player. The clip is sampled during logical substeps, and render sampling reads only committed poses. A non-looping clip naturally holds its final pose; stop() removes the playback result. follow(...) also creates a private Scope and follows an AnimationTimeline owned by another system through an observer. It does not own external time advancement, but logical sampling, publication, and render interpolation still use the same flow as standalone playback. Loop boundaries publish both end and start results so interpolation cannot cross two loop iterations.

docs.title: Vehicles and machinery made from multiple model parts
docs.text: ModelGroupScope composes a ManagedAnimationScope rather than inheriting from it. Every rigid part in the group shares the logical commit and revision. Tick-domain root and local motion are published in the same batch, while frame-domain motion updates only the render snapshot. A bogie, wheel group, and body therefore cannot observe different generations.

docs.title: Server authority with smooth client display
docs.text: In a synchronized FSM, the server remains the business-state authority and the client receives playable state through synchronization. The client presentation path still uses a Scope to produce render publications, but interpolation never writes client guesses back into server rules. Networking, authority conflicts, and connection lifecycle stay in adapters; the core Scope has no Minecraft networking types.

docs.title: Resource reloads and model rebuilds
docs.text: A reload prepares the fresh model instance and Target, then switches the binding and releases the old reference after success. Failure keeps the old binding. Rebinding a Target replaces only the write destination; it does not reset logical time, playback instances, or the latest publication.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• One successful real logical step commits one generation of results. Every Target in the batch receives the same revision.
  • revision is a commit generation, not seconds, a frame number, or a playback id. Pause, resume, and seek control commits also create revisions.
  • Inputs are frozen for the step. A Controller or internal command failure aborts the step. An expected rejection of one command can remain isolated without blocking unrelated commands.
  • A publication pass completes the whole Target batch before atomically replacing the render batch. Rendering cannot combine two revisions.
  • One model and one RenderFrameToken are sampled at most once. Targets run in stable registration order; when one model owns both root and pose, the composition root should register root before pose in the same batch.
  • A paused playback subtree freezes local time and does not replay the paused interval on resume. Seek uses SNAP semantics and does not interpolate across unrelated source times.
  • Scope close is idempotent. A closed Scope rejects advancement and releases runtime references held by registered Targets.

docs.title: Choosing an extension point
docs.text:
Desired feature Extension point "Play a hurt animation below a health threshold" RuntimeController plus typed inputs "Switch to another clip when an action finishes" Controllers, playback instances, and command handling "Arrange clip speed, loops, and windows on parent time" PlaybackBinding and the playback graph "Write bones, morphs, or material frames" TargetOutputEvaluator<PoseOutput> and a pose Target "Write placement and local motion for one rigid part" A root Target plus a model-group adapter "Read inputs from a BlockEntity, Entity, or vehicle" An MC/Proxy adapter writing through AnimationInputPort "Map MC ticks and partial frames into core time" A composition root constructing ScopeAdvance and RenderSampleContext

Two boundaries keep this extensible: Controllers do not write model slots, and Targets do not read animation sources, Controllers, or other Targets. Those restrictions make failure isolation, rebinding, and render deduplication tractable.

docs.title: Current boundaries
docs.text:
The Scope does not schedule Minecraft rendering, own world objects, load resources, or issue OpenGL/GPU uploads. Camera playback uses the private Scope in ScopedCameraPosePlayback and the kasuga:camera_pose Target; a shared timeline only produces time snapshots, while the camera layer consumes the resulting channels. See Camera Animation. FSM layers and pose composition are described in FSM, and model format and pose channels in Model Subsystems.

Implementation:

  • AnimationScope.java
  • ManagedAnimationScope.java
  • RootTimeline.java
  • TargetRegistry.java
  • ScopedPlayerPosePlayback.java
  • ScopedCameraPosePlayback.java
  • ModelInstance.java

docs.title: AnimationTarget: Writing Animation Results into Business Targets
docs.text:
Playback determines what pose or motion exists at a given time. AnimationTarget<O> determines where that result is written. One state machine may drive both a character's bones and the position of a floating effect: the pose goes to the model's pose slot, while the position goes to a property or root slot. Both share one logical commit but have different output types and write rules.

The Target is a narrow boundary between business results and render objects. It knows nothing about clips, FSMs, or playback timing. It receives an immutable result that has already been evaluated. Adding a model, output slot, or third-party adapter therefore does not make animation controllers and renderers depend on each other.

docs.title: Why result-based targets matter
docs.text:
An older pattern makes every render writer hold an animation source and resample it on the render thread. That creates three common failures:

  • Parts evaluated on the same tick may read different generations of state.
  • A logical state machine and an animation source may advance time separately, causing doubled speed, reversal, or loop misalignment.
  • Physics pre-sampling, backend sampling, and model update may write the same slot more than once.

Result-based targets divide logical processing from render sampling:

Logical phase
  Scope commit
    -> TargetOutputEvaluator<O>.evaluate(...)
    -> TargetPublication<O>
    -> Target.publish(...)

Render phase
  ModelInstance.sample(RenderSampleContext)
    -> Target.sample(publication, context)
    -> interpolate O
    -> write the Target's exclusive model or property slot

The animation source is evaluated only during logical publication. A render frame chooses the display phase between previous and current committed results.

docs.title: Stable identity
docs.text:
AnimationTargetRef
  channel: TargetChannel
  address: String

channel identifies the output contract, and address identifies an exclusive slot within the owning Scope. Built-in channels include:

channel Business output Typical destination kasuga:model_pose Composed bones, morphs, material frames, IK, and related pose channels Character, block model, robotic arm kasuga:part_root Root transform of one rigid part Vehicle wheel group, bogie, separate car part kasuga:camera_pose Position, orientation, roll, and optical zoom for one camera CameraAnimationPlayer kasuga:property Numeric value, switch, or platform property Effect strength, extension field, third-party object

Channels are extensible, but a third party must also supply an immutable output type, evaluator, continuity rule, and write adapter. One (channel, address) can be registered only once in a Scope. A configuration reload or duplicate initialization must not create two root owners for one part.

Stable identity does not mean a permanent Java object. After a resource reload, a Target can rebind to a fresh instance. The address stays stable, the destination changes, and the latest publication and playback progress survive.

docs.title: What a publication contains
docs.text:
TargetPublication<O>
  ref
  revision
  Active(previousOutput, currentOutput, continuity)
  or Cleared(reason)

A publication is the result of one logical commit for one Target. It does not expose the complete playback tree. Active lets rendering interpolate between two committed results. Cleared explicitly removes an output so stale visuals do not remain.

Continuity is selected by the target publication factory:

Situation Continuity Business behavior Ordinary logical advancement INTERPOLATE Display smoothly between two committed results Zero delta with a republished state HOLD_CURRENT Keep the current value without an artificial transition First publication, seek, or a result that declares a discontinuity SNAP Adopt the new result directly without crossing unrelated time Stop or inactive target Cleared Remove the output until a later activation

revision identifies the batch, not time. Every publication in a Target batch has the same revision. A render sample captures one complete batch, so a newer logical step being published concurrently cannot enter that sample.

docs.title: Publication and sampling
docs.text:
TargetRegistry has two phases:

publish:
  evaluate O in registration order
  create one publication for each Target
  finish the entire batch
  atomically replace the latest render batch

sample:
  capture one complete batch
  check the RenderFrameToken
  interpolate each result
  write its exclusive slot

Registration order gives deterministic publication and diagnostics. A failure while evaluating, publishing, or sampling one Target is isolated and logged; other Targets can still complete the step. A model write failure after commit does not roll back the logical revision.

Repeated sampling with the same model and RenderFrameToken is a no-op. This prevents physics pre-sampling and backend rendering from applying the same pose twice. Targets run in stable registration order; when one batch contains both root and pose, the composition root registers root first. The two slots do not clear each other.

docs.title: Current production targets
docs.text:
Target Logical result Render write Typical business use ModelPoseTarget PoseOutput ModelInstancePoseSink.applyPose(...) FSM and explicit model-pose targets ScopedPlayerPoseTarget TimedPose history ModelInstancePoseSink.applyPose(...) AnimationPlayer standalone/follow ScopedCameraPoseTarget TimedPose history Produces CameraPose for the camera layer CameraAnimationPlayer standalone/follow RigidPartBinding RigidPartOutput Root of one ModelInstance Multi-part vehicles, trains, machinery

ModelPoseTarget uses PoseOutputInterpolator for bones, morphs, discrete material frames, and clearing. RigidPartBinding captures root, local motion, and local placement during the logical phase, then composes root × local × motion for a render frame and writes only root. FSM formula tracks use the frozen query.* snapshot during each logical step, and render frames interpolate only the resulting Poses. Intermediate values of nonlinear formulas therefore use logical-step sampling as an approximation. An FSM step that crosses a clip loop boundary is marked discontinuous so the clip end is never interpolated back into its start. ScopedPlayerPoseTarget and ScopedCameraPoseTarget retain the committed samples for the current host interval and resolve them by unwrapped logical time. Both are private composition endpoints; the public entries remain AnimationPlayer and CameraAnimationPlayer. A loop boundary publishes both the end and start results.

Parent/child playback or frame-domain motion may contribute to a final value, but the Target receives only the final result. The playback graph expresses timing and sources; the Target expresses destination and write behavior. A model group also uses ModelGroupRenderPort to inject its current frame input into the committed Target batch's RenderSampleContext under one lock, so root, tick motion, and frame motion cannot come from different publication generations.

docs.title: Lifecycle and rebinding
docs.text:
• A Target establishes its address at registration. Duplicate registration of the same address fails.
  • A model rebuild prepares a fresh Target before switching the sink; failure must leave the old owner valid.
  • rebind may replace the model instance or sink, but it does not reset publication, revision, or playback progress.
  • close() is idempotent and releases model, sink, frame token, and other runtime references.
  • Closing a Scope closes only Targets it owns and has registered. Playback instances do not own Target lifecycle.

These rules turn resource reloads, chunk unloads, and visual rebuilds into endpoint replacement instead of rebuilding the whole animation state.

docs.title: When to add a Target
docs.text:
Add a Target when:

  • A result needs its own interpolation, such as position, color, weight, or camera parameter.
  • Multiple playback instances may contribute to one final value.
  • The destination is not an existing pose or root slot.
  • The destination must rebind to another platform object while preserving logical playback state.

Do not put these responsibilities in a Target:

  • Evaluating business conditions.
  • Advancing a state machine, RootTimeline, or playback instance.
  • Scanning time events and creating the next command.
  • Reading another Target and recursively driving it.
  • Resampling a source animation during render sampling.

Controllers and Scope own conditions and time. Playback owns timing and commands. Host/Proxy code owns resource lifecycle. Keeping those boundaries makes each Target stable, testable, and independently isolatable.

Implementation:

  • AnimationTarget.java
  • TargetRegistry.java
  • TargetPublication.java
  • ModelPoseTarget.java
  • ScopedPlayerPoseTarget.java
  • ScopedCameraPoseTarget.java
  • RigidPartBinding.java

docs.title: How Carriage Posture Works
docs.text: KasugaLibNext keeps a server-authoritative vertical offset on Carriage, letting the body move up and down relative to the bogeys while bogey positions, wheel speed, and track geometry stay untouched. This is a system independent of the multi-bogey feature and works for a plain two-bogey carriage as well. For usage and the switches see the guide; for the multi-bogey side see How Multi-Bogey Carriages Work.

docs.title: State model
docs.text:
• The offset is a plain float on Carriage, written by the server and the single source of truth;
  • it lives on Carriage rather than the entity because every per-dimension entity of a carriage shares the same state, and because it is saved with the train and decoupled from entity lifetimes;
  • the value is supplied by ModifyCarriagePostureEvent every tick; while enable_carriage_y_offset is off it is forced to 0;
  • the client keeps its own smoothed copy (LerpedFloat) that eases towards the synced server value.

docs.title: Per-tick update
docs.text:
CarriageMixin runs at the tail of Carriage.manageEntities (server side, once per carriage per tick):

  1. switch off: force the authoritative value to 0 and do not post the event;
  2. otherwise build ModifyCarriagePostureEvent(level, carriage) and post it on NeoForge.EVENT_BUS; listeners set the tick's offset through setYOffset(float);
  3. after the event returns, clamp to ±max_carriage_y_offset and store it as the authoritative value.

manageEntities only runs in the server-side train tick, so the event is server-side by construction; the client never posts it.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
CarriageMixin writes one float when Carriage#write returns:

KasugaYOffset: <float>
  • written only while enable_carriage_y_offset is on and the value is non-zero;
  • read restores it while the switch is on, clamped to max_carriage_y_offset;
  • only the server reads and writes this NBT; client carriages come from Train.STREAM_CODEC and receive the posture through the sync channel below.

docs.title: Client sync
docs.text:
The posture value rides on the entity's synched data instead of a dedicated channel:

  • CarriageContraptionEntity registers a SynchedEntityData float accessor in defineSynchedData;
  • the server writes the Carriage's authoritative value into that accessor at the head of tickContraption; vanilla's entity data sync sends it to tracking clients whenever it changes;
  • on the client, onSyncedDataUpdated hands the value to the client Carriage, which eases its own LerpedFloat towards it at 0.5 blocks per tick;
  • carriages themselves tick only on the server, so the easing is advanced from the client entity's tickContraption head;
  • rendering interpolates between the previous and current tick values with the partial tick, so motion stays smooth between syncs.

docs.title: Consumers
docs.text:
The authoritative value (the smoothed value on the client) flows through:

  • position and hitbox: Entity#position() adds the current offset for entities implementing CarriageContraptionEntityAccess. AbstractContraptionEntity#setPos rebuilds the hitbox from getAnchorVec() (which is position()), so the server hitbox moves with the body;
  • previous position: getPrevPositionVec() adds the same offset, so position() − getPrevPositionVec() still reflects only real movement; setServerSidePrevPosition() subtracts the current offset when capturing serverPrevPos and caches the raw position, keeping toLocalVector(..., prevAnchor) and similar consumers consistent;
  • wheel speed: the wheel-angle integration uses the real track movement with the posture offset removed — tickContraption differences position() against xo/yo/zo, and since position() carries the offset while xo/yo/zo are raw fields, the offset is removed from the difference there;
  • body rendering: OrientedContraptionEntityMixin translates the pose stack inside applyLocalTransforms' rotation chain by the interpolated offset, so the block structure and block entities move with the body;
  • vanilla bogeys: rendered by Flywheel; their visual position comes from lerp(partialTick, yOld, position()) and only contains partialTick × current offset of it, which CarriageContraptionVisualMixin removes so the bogeys stay on the rails;
  • interior bogeys: drawn directly by the entity renderer, whose outer pose never carries the offset.

docs.title: Relationship to the multi-bogey system
docs.text:
• The two systems are independent: the multi-bogey system owns the existence, sync, and curve tracking of interior bogeys; the posture system owns the body's vertical offset relative to the bogeys;
  • with both enabled, the body (and its structure) bobs while every bogey stays on the rails and wheel speed still follows real movement;
  • each system has its own common config entries and does not depend on the other.

docs.title: Switches and defaults
docs.text:
Key Effect enable_carriage_y_offset Posture switch; when off, no event is posted, the offset is 0, and every consumer is a no-op. max_carriage_y_offset Offset limit; both event results and restored save values are clamped to it.

Defaults are evaluated lazily via ModConfigSpec.Builder#define(path, Supplier<Boolean>). Other mods can override them before configs are loaded with KasugaLibCreateApi.setCarriageYOffsetDefault(boolean); an explicit value in the config file always wins.

docs.title: How Multi-Bogey Carriages Work
docs.text: KasugaLibNext extends Create's station assembly path so a single carriage can use more than two bogeys. Create's methods are not replaced; the assembly path makes three minimal interventions. The rest of the feature covers the interior bogeys' motion and orientation, curve tracking, and the derailment guard. For usage and the config switches see the guide. The carriage body's vertical posture relative to the bogeys is a separate system; see How Carriage Posture Works.

docs.title: Vanilla constraints
docs.text:
Create models a carriage as "one leading bogey + one trailing bogey", which breaks a multi-bogey structure in three places:

  1. CarriageContraption#assemble counts the captured bogeys and throws train_assembly.too_many_bogeys above two;
  2. CarriageContraption#capture only writes secondBogeyPos when the counter equals 2, so with more bogeys the caller cannot tell where the structure ends;
  3. StationBlockEntity#assemble pairs the carriage at index i with the station bogey at i + 1. For a multi-bogey group i..j, j != i + 1 triggers train_assembly.not_connected_in_order; even if that check were bypassed, every interior bogey would be assembled again as its own carriage.

docs.title: Capture phase
docs.text:
CarriageContraptionMixin does two things:

  • Defuses the count guard instead of cancelling the method. Before assemble reads bogeys for the > 2 comparison, the real count is saved to ksg$bogeys and the field is set to 2. The comparison therefore falls through and the method continues with the sideways-controls check, conductor/seat bookkeeping, and return true. Cancelling would discard those side effects, so the input is changed instead of returning early.
  • Widens capture's "second bogey" check to >= 2. capture compiles the test as != 2; clamping only the compared read to min(count, 2) makes every bogey from the second onwards pass and overwrite secondBogeyPos. The read feeding bogeys++ is untouched, so the counter stays exact.

Every secondBogeyPos = pos assignment records its position in the redundant list; the last one captured is the final trailing bogey. Capture order is BFS order, not necessarily track order, so three pieces of data are exposed:

  • isMoreThan2Bogeys(): whether this assembly really exceeded two (always false while the config switch is off);
  • getRedundantBogeys(): every position except the first and the last captured, in raw capture order;
  • the last captured position, still held in secondBogeyPos.

CarriageContraptionAccess lives outside the mixin package because Mixin forbids direct references to classes in a package owned by its config; the mixin implements it and ordinary code casts the target instance.

docs.title: Station collapse
docs.text:
StationBlockEntityMixin aligns the captured data with the station's ordered bogey list and collapses it back into the leading/trailing pair vanilla expects:

  1. Reconstruct the captured set: redundantBogeys ∪ {secondBogeyPos}.
  2. For each station index k > i, compute the expected world position (bogeyLocations, upsideDownBogeys, the two offsets, and the assembly direction) and remove the matched position from the set.
  3. Accept the group only when all of the following hold:
  4. trailing > i + 1 (at least one interior bogey);
  5. the set is fully consumed (nothing outside the group was captured);
  6. matched == trailing - i (no gaps in the range).
  7. Before overwriting the pair slot, build the CarriageBogeys from the original interior slots. Slot i + 1 may itself be an interior bogey; building after the copy would mislabel the trailing bogey as interior. Relative positions are expectedPosition(k) - contraption.anchor, the same frame as Contraption#toLocalPos.
  8. Copy the trailing bogey j's bogeyLocations, bogeyTypes, upsideDownBogeys, and two TravellingPoints into slot i + 1, and make getSecondBogeyPos() return j's expected position. Vanilla then recomputes expected(i + 1) from the copied fields, which equals the returned value, so the check passes; the constructed trailing bogey uses the trailing data and bogeySpacing becomes location[j] - location[i], the full carriage length.
  9. At the second CarriageBogey constructor call, set the loop local to trailing - 1 so the two following increments land on trailing and trailing + 1; the next iteration starts after the group and interior indices are not assembled again.
  10. When vanilla adds the new Carriage to its result list, a WrapOperation on List.add attaches the redundant bogeys; instanceof Carriage distinguishes it from the other lists sharing the erased signature.

Any failed validation returns the original secondBogeyPos, writes no state, and leaves assembly on the vanilla path.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
CarriageMixin appends a list when Carriage#write returns:

KasugaRedundantBogeys: [
  { BogeyData: { Type, Points, UpsideDown, BogeyData }, Position: [x, y, z] },
  ...
]

BogeyData stores the full CarriageBogey#write tag rather than the raw bogeyData field: rebuilding also needs the AbstractBogeyBlock type and two TravellingPoints. read restores with the same graph/dimensions as FirstBogey/SecondBogey; a tuple with an unreadable Position is skipped as a whole so both lists stay index-aligned.

Only the server writes this NBT; client carriages come from Train.STREAM_CODEC and never read it.

docs.title: Client sync
docs.text:
Train.STREAM_CODEC only carries the two real bogeys and bogeySpacing, and CarriageSyncData only carries four wheel points, so interior bogeys need a dedicated channel. CarriageExtraBogeySync sends one (trainId, carriageIndex, List<Entry>) per carriage with extras; each Entry is (carriage-local position, block registry name, upsideDown, bogeyData):

  • the block type travels as a ResourceLocation rather than AbstractBogeyBlock.STREAM_CODEC because the RPC only has a FriendlyByteBuf; the receiver resolves it through BuiltInRegistries.BLOCK;
  • assembly sends after Create broadcasts AddTrainPacket; login sends from the TAIL of playerLogin in GlobalRailwayManagerMixin. Play-phase payloads on one connection arrive in write order, so the client already knows the Train;
  • the client handler replaces both lists, making repeated or late syncs idempotent; unknown block types are skipped together with their positions;
  • client-side bogeys use the three-argument constructor, so their TravellingPoints are empty.

docs.title: Interior bogeys: motion, orientation, and curve tracking
docs.text:
Client-side interior bogeys have no track points, so calling CarriageBogey#updateAngles directly would always hit the derailed fallback. CarriageContraptionEntityMixin runs after the second updateAngles call and computes:

Wheel angle: the same integration as Create, new = (old - 360 · d / (2π · r)) % 360, where d is the entity's real movement along the track this tick.

Orientation (yaw/pitch): starting from the carriage's leading wheel point, walk along the graph towards the trailing bogey by half leading wheel spacing + along ± half this bogey's wheel spacing, sampling the bogey's two wheel contact points, then apply vanilla updateAngles' formula (Δ = front contact − rear contact, yaw = −(deg(atan2(Δz, Δx)) + 90), pitch = deg(atan2(Δy, horizontal length))).

  • the walk uses TravellingPoint#travel: curved edges map distance onto the Bezier parameter through TrackEdge#incrementT → BezierConnection, and at nodes follow(trailing point) picks the branch, so across an S-bend the sample is the real curve tangent at that spot;
  • each stride is at most 5 blocks so the distance-to-Bezier-parameter mapping stays accurate;
  • along is the relative position projected onto the assembly direction — the bogey's distance from the leading bogey;
  • when the client has no track graph yet, the train is derailed, the walk is blocked, or the sampled direction degenerates, it falls back to interpolating the end bogeys' angles.

Curve offset: the body is the chord between the two real bogeys while the track is curved, so interior bogeys need a lateral shift towards the outside of the turn to keep their wheels on the rails. Using the end bogeys' yaw difference θ, the arc is:

L = bogeySpacing
R = L / (2 · sin(|θ|/2))
u = (t − 0.5) · L
offset(t) = −sign(θ) · (sqrt(R² − u²) − R · cos(|θ|/2))

The height peaks at the chord midpoint and is 0 at the ends; positive is to the right of the leading-to-trailing chord, and the arc bulges to the outside of the turn. The result is clamped to max_bogey_offset, stored per bogey in a LerpedFloat, and interpolated with the partial tick when rendering.

Rendering: CarriageContraptionEntityRendererMixin passes the same along projection to CarriageContraptionEntityRenderer#translateBogey as the chord position, and applies the lateral offset as a world-space horizontal translation before translateBogey — the local +X axis of translateBogey's carriage frame maps to world (sin viewYRot, 0, cos viewYRot). The Flywheel visualization only knows carriage.bogeys, so the renderer mixin draws the extra bogeys directly.

docs.title: Derailment guard
docs.text:
CarriageMixin also runs a check at the tail of Carriage.manageEntities (server, once per carriage per tick):

  • preconditions: multi-bogey on, derailed_on_bogey_offset_overflow on, the carriage has interior bogeys, the train is not derailed, and the graph plus the four track points of the end bogeys are valid;
  • the end headings are derived from the real track points (the server does not maintain the client-side yaw LerpedFloats), using the same formula as updateAngles;
  • the arc height peaks at the chord midpoint, so the midpoint value R · (1 − cos(|θ|/2)) is used; it is at least as large as what any interior bogey needs, covering every position;
  • above max_bogey_offset, the train derails through Create's own high-stress procedure: speed = 0, cancel navigation, runtime.tick, derailed = true, status.highStress(). Already-derailed trains skip the check.

docs.title: Switches
docs.text:
The multi-bogey-related common configs in CreateConfig:

Key Effect enable_multi_bogey_carriage Master switch; when off, capture, assembly, persistence, sync, rendering, and angle computation all return to the vanilla path. max_bogey_offset Interior-bogey curve offset limit and the derailment threshold. derailed_on_bogey_offset_overflow Whether the required curve offset exceeding max_bogey_offset derails the train.

With enable_multi_bogey_carriage off:

  • capture no longer clamps the counter → vanilla too_many_bogeys;
  • station collapse returns the original secondBogeyPos;
  • NBT is neither written nor read;
  • the client drops incoming payloads and skips rendering and angle updates.

Defaults are evaluated lazily via ModConfigSpec.Builder#define(path, Supplier<Boolean>). Other mods can override them before configs are loaded with KasugaLibCreateApi.setMultiBogeyCarriageDefault and setDerailedOnBogeyOffsetDefault; an explicit value in the config file always wins.

docs.title: KasugaLib Data-Driven System
docs.text:
This directory documents the data-driven implementation in the current working tree. Its contents are organized from modules/data-driven, the registration framework in modules/core, and the FSM reload integration in modules/modelling (verified 2026-11-13, and cross-checked against current sources), without relying on reserved capabilities from older design drafts.

The data-driven system solves three problems:

  1. Converting blocks, items, block entities, and property groups declared in JSON into the existing Reg registration tree;
  2. Writing state machine definitions and animation clips that can change during resource reload into separate reload buckets;
  3. Allowing a host to organize multiple fixed resource roots into a single startup build with priority ordering, validation, and declared registry claims.

Production wiring in v2 has three layers: core's ResourceSource/ResourceSnapshot first fixes the actual bytes and source identity; data-driven's ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(...) projects the specified root into a registration view; and DataDrivenBuildPipeline then performs index discovery, strict JSON decoding, definition selection, claim preflight, and apply. The registration phase and reload phase share the data/<namespace>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/ syntax, but the registration phase reads host-approved fixed roots whereas the reload phase reads the active Minecraft pack stack. Adding or removing Minecraft registry entries at runtime is outside the scope of this framework.

docs.title: Two Registration Entry Points
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Registration event arrives for a mod"] --> B{"Is a provider installed for this mod?"}
    B -- No --> C["JsonTreeBuilder.buildForMod"]
    C --> D["Scan indexes and mod JAR in the mod file"]
    D --> E["Legacy single-source parse and apply"]
    B -- Yes --> F["DataDrivenRegistrationProvider.build"]
    F --> G["Host builds ContentSource from fixed ResourceSnapshot"]
    G --> H["DataDrivenBuildPipeline.prepare"]
    H --> I{"STRICT and blocking diagnostics present?"}
    I -- Yes --> J["REJECTED, do not apply"]
    I -- No --> K["DataDrivenBuildPipeline.build"]
    K --> L["Apply by phase and parent dependencies"]
    L --> M["Run finalizers"]
    M --> N["Return JsonRegistryGroup"]

During registration dispatch, JsonTreeIntegration checks DataDrivenRegistrationProviders first. When a provider is found, the legacy JAR scan does not run, and the root group returned by the provider is attached directly to that mod's registration tree. When no provider is installed, JsonTreeBuilder.buildForMod(modId) is called, preserving the compatibility entry point for existing mods. If the provider returns null, it signals that the host has taken over and attaches no root group in this cycle, without falling back to the legacy scan.

New hosts typically use DataDrivenBuildPipeline, because it handles multiple sources simultaneously, declares source ownership, preflights cross-source references, checks final registry claims, and rejects an entire unsafe batch before apply. Small compatibility scenarios can still use the legacy entry point directly.

docs.title: Four Data Domains
docs.text:
Domain Source Effective Timing Current Use Registration (REGISTRATION) Host-approved fixed ResourceSnapshot exposed via ContentSource Mod construction, before registration dispatch registry_groups, blocks, items, embedded block entities Reload data (RELOAD_DATA) Active resource pack stack Initial Manager attach and every /reload state_machines, animation_clips Reload assets (RELOAD_ASSETS) Active resource pack stack Resource reload Models, textures, language files, and other ordinary assets Config (CONFIG) Game directory or host config Decided by host Startup switches, pack ordering, and other host configuration

Diagnostics.Domain reserves address space for these four source categories. Today the reload orchestrator actively writes to RELOAD_DATA, while the legacy registration entry point writes to a separate per-mod compatibility error bucket keyed by mod id. The REGISTRATION enum value does not replace that legacy bucket, and ordinary assets and config are handled by their respective hosts. The structured BuildDiagnostic results from the new DataDrivenBuildPipeline form a separate reporting model and are not automatically written into Diagnostics.

docs.title: Key Invariants
docs.text:
• A ContentSource's logical file list is fixed when opened and sorted by slash-separated logical path. In v2, SnapshotContentSource reads bytes already captured in a ResourceSnapshot and does not track subsequent changes in the original directory or archive.
  • ResourceSourceDescriptor's rank is non-negative; each source/root in a prepare call must have a unique rank. Explicit platform ranks determine sourceOrder instead of ad-hoc reordering by caller list position.
  • Across multiple sources, larger sourceOrder values take higher priority; non-registration definitions pick a winner by priority (unless a handler declares OVERLAY). In STRICT mode, registration definitions retain all candidates and verify final (registry, id) claims.
  • Strict registration definitions declare every final Minecraft registry key before apply. Multiple claims targeting the same (registry, id) reject the entire batch.
  • parse, resolveIdentity, validate, claims, and parentDefinition must have no registration side effects; only apply on selected definitions may mutate the registration context.
  • STRICT mode uses strict UTF-8 decoding and StrictResourceJson for manifests, registration content, and reload preflight; duplicate keys, comments, trailing commas, non-object roots, and overly deep or large JSON documents block the build. LEGACY continues to use Gson's tolerant parsing.
  • The legacy JsonTreeBuilder and pipeline LEGACY mode map an explicit minecraft:foo to <hostModId>:foo, whereas v2 STRICT preserves minecraft:foo. The pipeline selects the identity rule via BuildOptions, and DefinitionKey, claims, and apply all use that same mode.
  • TypeHandler phase takes precedence over handler registration order. Built-in content runs in the order: registry groups, blocks/items, embedded block entities.
  • Both TypeHandlerRegistry and ReloadHandlerRegistry are meant to be populated during startup only; reload handler insertion order determines type traversal and registration order, while deduplication within a single handler still depends on file/entry candidate order.
  • Reload buckets clear only resource-sourced entries on initial Manager attach and at the start of each reload cycle. Script- or code-registered entries of the same name take precedence over resource entries.
  • Once registration completes, Minecraft registry entries cannot be added or removed via /reload. Changing such entries requires restarting and rebuilding both client and server registries.
  • RegistryGroup.dispatchWhen evaluates its predicate on each dispatch; when the predicate returns false, that group and its entire subtree are skipped.
  • BuildResult.Status is APPLIED, REJECTED, or FAILED; FAILED may have already executed partial apply calls or finalizers, and there is no automatic rollback.

docs.title: Current Boundaries
docs.text:
The framework turns registration-phase JSON into Reg nodes and lets those Reg nodes enter Minecraft registries during the final registry events. It does not generate models, language files, textures, or loot tables; those assets still need to be supplied using standard mod, resource pack, or data pack layouts. A platform can project both the registration layer and the MC resource layer from the same ResourceSnapshot, while the host remains responsible for creating roots, assigning unique ranks, configuring consumer routing, and controlling publication timing.

StateProperty, FSM state machine semantics, animation clip codecs, and concrete factory parameters are defined by each extension type. This directory covers wiring and lifecycle; for field-level details, see Block-State Properties, FSM Reference, and the concrete factory sources.

Strict mode proves only what it can inspect. Extension authors and hosts must actively verify whether a custom factory also creates a block item, whether a custom handler omits any claims, and whether all existing host registrations have been included in the reserved snapshot. Built-in block and item DefinitionKeys and claims share a single mode-aware final-ID rule, preserving explicit minecraft: in STRICT mode; see Troubleshooting and Migration. The framework does not implement concrete pack discovery, world save compatibility, or cross-startup pack history; those policies belong to the host. ApprovedResourcePacks and MappedPackResources already provide the infrastructure to project MC pack layers from fixed sources/roots, and registration providers must not publish those layers before strict preflight and dependency closure succeed.

docs.title: Concepts and Lifecycle
docs.text: The data-driven system separates content capture, build policy, and actual registration. core's ResourceSource captures and fixes the bytes of a source/root, ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(...) projects the snapshot into a registration view, TypeHandler interprets each type, DataDrivenBuildPipeline determines which definitions enter the build, and the Reg tree completes Minecraft registration during the existing registration phase.

docs.title: Registration Phase vs. Reload Phase
docs.text:
The registration phase runs during mod construction and before registry events. Once content enters BuiltInRegistries or the corresponding deferred registry, it stays fixed for the lifetime of the process. The registration phase is suited for:

  • Block, Item, and BlockEntityType;
  • Registry groups that govern object construction;
  • Java types, codecs, or behavior selection;
  • Startup configuration requiring cross-definition preflight.

The reload phase runs when ResourceManager first attaches and whenever the resource stack is rebuilt afterward. Resource/data packs can override content at the same path, so the reload phase is suited for data that does not alter Java registry shape:

  • FSM state machine definitions;
  • Animation clips;
  • Other replaceable buckets managed by custom ReloadHandler implementations.

The same content file must not be listed in both on_register and on_reload. That conflict fails closed in both domains, and neither domain consumes the file.

Although the registration phase and reload phase share the index directory, manifest fields, and logical path constraints, they read from different sources:

Phase Actual Input Interpreter Result Registration Host-approved fixed ResourceSnapshot exposed via ContentSource; falls back to legacy mod JAR scan only when no provider is installed TypeHandler JsonRegistryGroup for this startup Reload Active pack stack selected by ResourceManager ReloadHandler Resource buckets that can be cleared and rebuilt

DataDrivenBuildPipeline.prepare can preflight on_reload files during the registration build, but it only invokes the decoder and does not run clearBucket or register. Actual reload registration is still performed by ReloadOrchestrator.

docs.title: Core Terms
docs.text:
Term Meaning source An independently addressable content root within a prepare call; in v2, typically projected from a concrete ResourceSource/ResourceSnapshot ResourceSourceDescriptor Platform identity: ownerId, sourceId, rootId, non-negative rank, and origin SourceDescriptor Registration-view metadata augmenting platform identity with allowed namespaces and a diagnostic label scene index The set of entry indexes chosen by the host for the current registration scenario; expressed in Java by ContentSource.indexes() LogicalPath A slash-separated path relative to a source root; disallows absolute paths, ., .., and backslashes index manifest An index file under data/<ns>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/*.json that lists content file paths only content path A path in a manifest relative to data/<ns>/, required to end with .json owner Ownership unit of a content source; cross-owner references must declare direct dependencies explicitly handler An extension type that interprets one top-level JSON field definition The result of a handler's parse identity Logical identity within one handler type, used for overrides and deduplication claim A final Minecraft registry key a definition intends to occupy provider The entry point where a host takes over building a mod's JSON root group finalizer A host hook executed once after all selected definitions have been applied dispatch group A RegistryGroup subtree that may carry a runtime predicate

sourceOrder, declarationOrder, logicalPath, and jsonPointer establish a reproducible build order and diagnostic location. For shared platform sources, sourceOrder comes from the explicit rank; every source/root rank must be unique within a session. Handlers must not rely on undefined map iteration orders.

docs.title: Fixed Roots and main/parcel
docs.text:
The platform assigns no business meaning to rootId, requiring only that it match [A-Za-z0-9_-][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127} (and not . or ..). Train-pack hosts commonly use:

  • main: the pack root content, with the lowest rank;
  • parcel-*: a separate root for each parcel in the manifest, assigned increasing ranks in the frozen manifest order.

These roots share the same ownerId and sourceId, while (sourceId, rootId) must be unique. Business parcel IDs may contain a resource namespace colon, whereas platform rootIds cannot; the host should maintain a stable, collision-free, loggable mapping. Registration, resource discovery, and reload must read from the same startup snapshot rather than using a snapshot on one side and reopening the install directory on the other.

docs.title: Startup Registration Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Mod as Host mod
    participant Registry as RegisterContextRegistry
    participant Integration as JsonTreeIntegration
    participant Provider as Registration provider
    participant Pipeline as BuildPipeline
    participant Tree as Reg tree
    participant MC as Minecraft registry events

    Mod->>Registry: Create mod root
    Registry->>Integration: Registration-phase callback
    Integration->>Provider: find(hostModId)
    Provider->>Pipeline: prepare(sources, options, dependencies)
    Pipeline-->>Provider: PreparedContent
    Provider->>Pipeline: build(prepared)
    Pipeline->>Tree: Create JsonRegistryGroup
    Pipeline->>Tree: Apply definitions by phase/parent
    Pipeline->>Pipeline: Run finalizers
    Pipeline-->>Provider: BuildResult
    Provider-->>Integration: rootGroup or null
    Integration->>Registry: root.addChild(rootGroup)
    MC->>Tree: dispatchRegister

The host provider must be installed before the registration callback runs. JsonTreeIntegration looks up the provider by mod id inside the callback; installing too late does not execute retroactively, so installation must happen before the registry events fire.

Returning null from a provider indicates that the mod has no JSON registration tree for this round. Runtime exceptions thrown by a provider are not swallowed by the legacy entry point's catch; the host should convert expected failures into BuildResult and diagnostics inside the provider.

docs.title: What prepare Does
docs.text:
DataDrivenBuildPipeline.prepare completes every step that requires no registration side effects:

  1. Reads explicit rank from shared platform sources and stably sorts by it; only legacy SourceDescriptors receive sourceOrder by input list position;
  2. Checks for duplicate (sourceId, rootId) pairs and verifies that all source/root ranks are unique;
  3. Checks whether owner dependency declarations point to known sources;
  4. Scans each source's indexes and aggregates on_register and on_reload paths;
  5. Reads and parses on_register content files;
  6. Extracts embedded types;
  7. Calls resolveIdentity on each definition;
  8. Decodes on_reload files for preflight inspection only, without registering them into reload buckets;
  9. In STRICT mode, verifies handler capabilities (STRICT_PREFLIGHT, strictValidationImplemented(), and a single identity role);
  10. Selects definitions according to BuildOptions;
  11. In STRICT mode, calls validate to check references, resources, factories, and strict properties;
  12. Checks selected parentDefinition references for cycles;
  13. Calls claims on selected definitions and checks reserved keys and duplicate claims.

prepare never calls apply. It does invoke parse, resolveIdentity(...), capabilities, strictValidationImplemented, validate, parentDefinition, claims, and reload decoders, so all of those methods must be side-effect-free. The pipeline selects LEGACY or STRICT identity rules for DefinitionKey via BuildOptions. Throwing from a custom apply causes build to return FAILED, whereas built-in registration handlers catch per-entry apply exceptions and continue as warnings when running in a non-strict context. Before entering the logic above, STRICT mode decodes every manifest, registration content file, and reload file with StrictResourceJson: the root must be a single object, and duplicate keys, comments, trailing commas, invalid UTF-8, depth exceeding 64, or more than 100,000 nodes produce blocking diagnostics.

If processing a source throws an uncaught RuntimeException, the pipeline records SOURCE_READ_FAILED and continues with the remaining sources, without rolling back files or definitions already parsed from that source. STRICT rejects the build due to the blocking diagnostic; LEGACY may still proceed with partial results.

docs.title: What build Does
docs.text:
build creates a fresh JsonRegistryGroup and RegBuildContext from an immutable PreparedContent, then:

  1. Returns REJECTED if STRICT mode is active and any ERROR diagnostic is present;
  2. Creates the root group and configures the default namespace mapping;
  3. Sorts selected definitions by TypeHandler.getPhase(), handler registration order, source order, logical path, JSON pointer, declaration order, and parentDefinition dependencies;
  4. Invokes apply on each definition inside BuildContext.withCurrentDefinition;
  5. Runs finalizers after all definitions finish;
  6. Returns APPLIED, FAILED, or REJECTED.
Status Meaning Did apply run? REJECTED STRICT preflight found blocking diagnostics No; rootGroup() is null APPLIED All selected apply calls and finalizers succeeded Yes FAILED Context creation, sorting, apply, or a finalizer threw a runtime exception Partial apply calls may have run; typically retains an incomplete rootGroup

Both BuildResult.successful() and BuildResult.applied() return true only when the status is APPLIED (both return false on FAILED and REJECTED). Callers inspecting FAILED should check status() and cause(), and avoid mounting an incomplete rootGroup unless partial side effects are known to be safe.

Note that prepared.hasBlockingDiagnostics() checks only Severity.ERROR. LEGACY builds do not consult this predicate to block apply, so a LEGACY result can be APPLIED while still carrying error diagnostics. successful() indicates that the apply pass completed, not that the inputs were error-free.

docs.title: How the Same Data Enters Different Phases
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S["ContentSource"] --> I["manifest"]
    I --> R["on_register"]
    I --> L["on_reload"]
    R --> P["parse + identity + validate + claims"]
    P --> A["apply Reg tree"]
    L --> D["preflight decode only in build pipeline"]
    I --> O["ReloadOrchestrator on attach or /reload"]
    O --> B["reload buckets"]

In DataDrivenBuildPipeline, preflight for on_reload verifies only that the manifest-listed files are readable, that their top-level types are registered, and that the decoders report no errors. It uses the process-wide ReloadHandlerRegistry rather than the TypeHandler list passed to the pipeline constructor, and it does not perform globDirectories() discovery. Actual reload registration is executed by ReloadOrchestrator on initial Manager attach and on every resource reload.

docs.title: Source Provenance from BuildContext
docs.text:
The BuildContext passed to apply temporarily binds the active definition via withCurrentDefinition and exposes:

  • getHostModId() / getModId(): the mod owning the build root;
  • getRootGroup(): the JsonRegistryGroup of this build;
  • getCurrentDefinition(): the full LocatedDefinition;
  • getSourceId(): the current source id;
  • getOwnerId(): the current content owner;
  • getNamespaces(): the namespaces accessible to that source;
  • getCurrentHandlerType(): the current handler's type field name;
  • getCurrentLogicalPath(): the current content file path;
  • getCurrentJsonPointer(): the current definition's location within the file;
  • isStrict(): the active build policy;
  • putMeta / getMeta: temporary cross-type data scoped to this build.

getModId() is a historical alias returning the same host id as getHostModId(). Content namespaces and owners must be read from source provenance rather than treating the host id as the namespace for every definition.

docs.title: Concurrency and Resource Lifecycle
docs.text:
Registration builds are deterministic startup operations. The provider table uses a process-wide ConcurrentHashMap, and the source list and PreparedContent are copied on construction; this does not mean handlers, Reg subclasses, or host resources may be mutated concurrently across arbitrary threads.

Callers own ContentSource instances and any streams opened from them; the pipeline never closes sources. SnapshotContentSource owns and closes its wrapped ResourceSnapshot; once closed, existing streams/leases may finish reading, while new reads fail. Once prepare finishes, standard handlers have already copied parsed results into definitions, so sources can normally be closed immediately. If a custom definition retains a ContentSource, path, or deferred-read logic, it must define and manage that extra lifecycle itself.

FixedResourceSource holds a process-level baseline snapshot. Every capture() creates an independent snapshot via ResourceSnapshot.Builder.copy, allowing separate consumers to retire their own snapshots without causing STALE_REFERENCE for one another; closing a fixed source retires only its baseline. The original directory, ZIP, or union filesystem is no longer read after pinning.

The commit order for a registration provider should be: complete strict prepare, pack rejection / dependency closure, and claims checks, succeed in build and update the host's registered set, and only then publish the corresponding MC resource layers. Publishing in the reverse order exposes rejected source/roots to ResourceManager.

TypeHandlerRegistry, ReloadHandlerRegistry, FactoryRegistry, and DataDrivenRegistrationProviders are process-wide state. The current API assumes handlers, factories, and providers are registered before the first prepare or registration dispatch and does not guarantee safety under concurrent mutation during active builds or reloads.

docs.title: Runtime Dispatch
docs.text:
The JsonRegistryGroup returned by a data build is a standard Reg subtree. When Minecraft registry events arrive, the existing RegisterContextRegistry calls dispatchRegister on the root, registering child nodes recursively.

RegistryGroup.dispatchWhen(BooleanSupplier) lets a host decide at dispatch time whether an entire subtree is enabled—for example, to gate code registrations owned by a pack set. RegistryClaimSnapshot.collect skips groups whose predicate returns false along with their subtrees; JSON builds and resource availability remain controlled separately by the host.

docs.title: Index and JSON Format
docs.text: This page describes the current registration handlers, reload handlers, and resource layout. Complete codec fields inside objects remain defined by each handler, while the three-layer grammar stays consistent: manifests select files, top-level keys in content files select handlers, and array elements are parsed by handlers. The v2 registration path also requires source bytes to be fixed up front rather than feeding a live, mutating installation directory directly into a build.

docs.title: Standard Directory Layout
docs.text:
Relative to one source root:

data/
  example/
    kasuga_lib/
      data_driven/
        index.json
    kasuga_content/
      groups.json
      blocks.json
      state_machines/
        panel.json
assets/
  example/
    blockstates/
    models/
    textures/
    lang/
pack.mcmeta

The index directory is fixed at:

data/<namespace>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/

The spellings kasuga_lib and data_driven are part of the protocol. ContentSource.indexes() recognizes only namespaces declared in the descriptor, and the directory hierarchy must be exact: data/<ns>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/<file>.json. Only direct child .json files in this directory are collected; deeper subdirectories are not traversed recursively.

Paths listed in a manifest are relative to data/<namespace>/:

kasuga_content/blocks.json
state_machines/panel.json

Content files may originate from an ordinary mod JAR, external directory, or ZIP, though production paths should first capture and pin them into a ResourceSnapshot via ResourceSources. Whether a source root includes pack.mcmeta affects only MC resource projection, not whether SnapshotContentSource can read registration JSON.

docs.title: Roots and Scene Indexing
docs.text:
In platform identity, rootId identifies a concrete resource root. In these pages, "scene indexing" refers to the composition of which roots the current registration scene reads from and which entry manifests each root exposes—it is not a separate JSON schema or Java type, and is implemented by combining:

ResourceSnapshot snapshot = fixedRoot.capture();
ContentSource source = ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(
        snapshot,
        descriptor,
        namespaces,
        label,
        declaredIndexes
);
  • By default, ContentSource.indexes() discovers only direct .json children under data/<declared-namespace>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/.
  • ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(..., declaredIndexes) restricts the entry set to the exact logical paths declared by the caller; pass null to restore default discovery.
  • Passing an empty collection declares that the root has no manifests, which is valid for an assets/data-only root that still contributes resources through the platform's MC projection.
  • declaredIndexes filters only manifests; it does not prune files from the snapshot. Content in the same root referenced by a manifest can still be opened via open(path), and the host is responsible for verifying that declared indexes exist and match allowed layouts.
  • Each index is resolved within its own (sourceId, rootId). Distinct roots retain separate definition provenance and independent claims even if they share manifest names, namespaces, or logical paths.

Typical train-pack layouts map the pack root to main and each parcel listed in the manifest order to parcel-*. main can auto-discover pack-root indexes, whereas parcel roots should expose only the entry paths declared in parcel.json.indexes. Business IDs such as <namespace>:<parcel> cannot serve directly as platform rootId values because colons are disallowed in platform IDs; the host should maintain a stable mapping. These names are host conventions, not semantics enforced by KasugaLib.

Every active (sourceId, rootId) must have a unique, non-negative global rank. Ranks must be allocated sequentially—or at least distinctly—across all main and parcel roots of every pack, never restarting from 0 per pack. DataDrivenBuildPipeline rejects duplicate ranks; LEGACY may still continue to apply, but a result carrying errors should not be treated as healthy.

docs.title: Index Manifest
docs.text:
A manifest is a JSON object permitting only two top-level fields:

{
  "on_register": [
    "kasuga_content/groups.json",
    "kasuga_content/blocks.json"
  ],
  "on_reload": [
    "animation_clips/wheels.json"
  ]
}
Field Type Purpose Empty Array on_register string[] Parsed at startup to build Reg nodes Valid; marks the domain as declared with no registration files on_reload string[] Parsed from the pack stack on initial Manager attach and every /reload Valid; marks the domain as declared with no reload files
