Both fields are individually optional, but they cannot both be omitted. A pack declaring only on_reload is a valid reload-only source.

Every path must be:

  • Non-empty;
  • Relative (must not start with /);
  • Separated by /;
  • Free of backslashes, Windows drive prefixes, empty segments, ., .., NUL, or other ISO control characters;
  • Suffixed with .json;
  • Resolved exclusively under data/<namespace>/ by relative concatenation.

When the same path appears in both on_register and on_reload, manifest diagnostics record MANIFEST_INVALID and neither domain consumes the file. DataDrivenBuildPipeline silently deduplicates paths repeated within the same domain, and the legacy registration entry point uses parsedSources to avoid parsing the same registration file twice. Runtime reload manifest reading currently does not deduplicate repeated entries within on_reload, so each path should appear only once.

The legacy field sources has been removed. Using it yields MANIFEST_INVALID and it is not treated as an alias for on_register.

A single source may contain multiple manifests. Their declarations are aggregated per namespace; the new pipeline checks cross-domain conflicts first, then sorts on_register paths by full logical path before parsing.

Both the multi-source pipeline and runtime reload ultimately construct ResourceLocation values from on_reload paths. Path casing and characters must match [a-z0-9/._-]; however, DataDrivenBuildPipeline's reload preflight checks only LogicalPath validity and source existence without constructing ResourceLocation, so passing strict preflight does not substitute for runtime ResourceLocation validation during reload.

Under STRICT mode, "JSON object" is enforced by StrictResourceJson:

  • Input must be valid UTF-8 and the entire file must be a single JSON object;
  • reader.setLenient(false) rejects comments, single-quoted fields, trailing commas, and non-standard JSON;
  • Duplicate keys in any object fail immediately instead of silently keeping the last value;
  • Default limits are depth 64, 100,000 nodes, and 8 MiB of text;
  • Unknown manifest fields, omitting both domains, non-array fields, non-string entries, and cross-domain path conflicts are all blocking diagnostics.

LEGACY mode uses Gson's lenient parsing. Even if LEGACY reports manifest schema errors, it may still proceed to apply, so startup success does not prove schema health.

docs.title: Registration-Phase Top-Level Fields
docs.text:
A content file is a JSON object whose top-level keys name handler types and whose values are arrays of objects:

{
  "registry_groups": [],
  "blocks": [],
  "items": []
}

Built-in top-level handlers:

Field Handler Phase Occupies Registry? registry_groups RegistryGroupHandler PHASE_GROUPS = 0 No blocks BlockTypeHandler PHASE_CONTENT = 1 Yes items ItemTypeHandler PHASE_CONTENT = 1 Yes Embedded block_entity BlockEntityTypeHandler PHASE_EMBEDDED = 2 Yes

block_entities is BlockEntityTypeHandler.getTypeName(), but that handler's getParentTypeName() is blocks and getEmbeddedKeyName() is block_entity. It may appear only under the block_entity key of a block entry and cannot be written as a top-level field.

A content file may declare multiple top-level fields. Unknown top-level fields are warnings in LEGACY and errors in STRICT. When a known field is not an array, an array element is not an object, or parse throws, an error is always recorded: LEGACY continues applying parseable sibling entries, while STRICT rejects the entire batch before apply.

Whether unknown keys inside a handler's entry object fail depends on the handler. Built-in Gson definitions generally ignore undeclared fields; top-level file fields are checked uniformly by the pipeline.

docs.title: registry_groups
docs.text:
Registry groups provide parent-to-child property inheritance for blocks and items.

{
  "registry_groups": [
    {
      "id": "example:base",
      "properties": {
        "strength": [2.0, 6.0]
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "example:panels",
      "parent": "example:base",
      "item_properties": {
        "tab": "example:main",
        "stacks_to": 16
      }
    }
  ]
}
Field Type Required Meaning id string Yes Group lookup key, matched by exact raw string parent string No Parent group id; attaches to the JSON root group when omitted properties object No Block property modifiers item_properties object No Item property modifiers; tab is also stored as the group's default creative tab

Group IDs do not undergo EffectiveId normalization: panels and example:panels are distinct groups. A block or item's registry_group must match the group's raw id string verbatim.

Parent groups are applied before child groups. STRICT verifies that the parent group exists and is visible to the current owner, and rejects parent cycles.

docs.title: blocks
docs.text:
{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "example:control_panel",
      "type": "data_driven_block",
      "registry_group": "example:panels",
      "properties": {
        "destroy_time": 2.0,
        "requires_correct_tool": true
      },
      "state_properties": {
        "active": {
          "type": "boolean",
          "default": false
        }
      },
      "item_properties": {
        "tab": "example:main",
        "stacks_to": 64
      },
      "params": {
        "factory_specific": true
      },
      "block_entity": {
        "type": "example_be",
        "params": {
          "model": "example:models/block/control_panel"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Field Type Required Purpose id string Yes Block id type string Yes Block factory type in FactoryRegistry registry_group string No Registry group id properties object No BlockBehaviour.Properties modifiers item_properties object No Property modifiers and creative tab for the same-id block item state_properties object No Real BlockState property set params object No Open parameters passed verbatim to the factory state_machine JSON primitive No Forwarded to params.state_machine on the embedded BE when block_entity is present block_entity object No Embedded block entity definition

STRICT mode requires id to be an explicit valid namespace:path, whereas the legacy JsonTreeBuilder entry point permits bare IDs. The two EffectiveId rules handle explicit minecraft: differently:

Identity Rule panel minecraft:panel example:panel EffectiveId.ofLegacy <hostModId>:panel <hostModId>:panel example:panel EffectiveId.of <hostModId>:panel (rejected later by STRICT validate) minecraft:panel example:panel

As a result, STRICT genuinely claims an explicit minecraft: key; the host must explicitly permit such overrides and include vanilla entries in reserved checks if desired. The legacy entry point's rewriting is compatibility behavior, not the v2 pack protocol.

DataDrivenBuildPipeline selects the strict branch of the three-argument resolveIdentity via BuildOptions: LEGACY uses the historical table above, while STRICT preserves explicit namespaces. The legacy JAR entry point remains JsonTreeBuilder.buildForMod. Train packs and external packs should use BuildOptions.STRICT.

type must match a registered factory. When state_properties is declared, the factory must also implement StatefulBlockFactory.

Supported keys in properties and item_properties are listed below. During apply, the built-in parsers (parseBlockProperties / parseItemProperties) log a warning and skip unknown keys or malformed values. In STRICT mode, however, the built-in handlers invoke JsonPropertyParser.validateStrict and JsonItemParser.validateStrict, turning unknown keys and invalid built-in property values into blocking CONTENT_INVALID errors (custom keys can be registered for strict validation via registerStrictCompiler / registerStrictParser).

docs.title: Block Properties (properties)
docs.text: Key Value no_occlusion boolean no_collision / no_collission boolean (both spellings accepted) requires_correct_tool boolean replaceable boolean dynamic_shape boolean random_ticks boolean no_loot_table boolean ignited_by_lava boolean liquid boolean force_solid_on boolean air boolean no_terrain_particles boolean light_emission integer (0–15 in STRICT) friction number speed_factor number jump_factor number destroy_time number explosion_resistance number strength number or [destroyTime, explosionResistance] map_color DyeColor name sound_type Supported SoundType name

docs.title: Item Properties
docs.text:
Blocks use item_properties; standalone items use properties.

Key Value Notes stacks_to integer Maximum stack size (1–99 in STRICT) rarity string common, uncommon, rare, epic (case-insensitive) fire_resistant boolean Fire resistance durability integer Maximum durability (positive integer in STRICT) no_repair boolean Disables repairing tab string Creative tab ResourceLocation, consumed separately by the loader

Properties are applied parent-first along the registry_group parent chain. Child definitions or more specific block/item properties override matching settings from parent groups.

docs.title: items
docs.text:
{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "example:manual",
      "type": "simple_item",
      "registry_group": "example:common_items",
      "properties": {
        "tab": "example:main",
        "stacks_to": 1
      },
      "params": {
        "factory_specific": "value"
      }
    }
  ]
}
Field Type Required Purpose id string Yes Item id type string Yes Item factory type registry_group string No Registry group id properties object No Item properties and creative tab params object No Passed to the item factory

Standalone items claim only minecraft:item. Block items are derived from the block factory's createsBlockItem capability; see Factories, Registry Groups, and Host Integration.

docs.title: Embedded block_entity
docs.text:
Block entities have no independent JSON id. The loader uses the host block's effective id as the definition identity and derives a block entity type id, typically <blockPath>_be.

{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "example:machine",
      "type": "example_block",
      "state_machine": "example:machine_fsm",
      "block_entity": {
        "type": "example_be",
        "params": {
          "model": "example:models/block/machine"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

BlockEntityTypeHandler.extractEmbedded performs the following steps:

  • Deep-copies block_entity;
  • Injects the host block's id as _parent_block;
  • If the host block carries a JSON primitive state_machine, writes it into params.state_machine;
  • Hands the resulting object to BlockEntityTypeHandler.parse.

The public fields of the embedded object are type and params. _parent_block is injected internally and should not be written by content authors.

If block_entities is written as a top-level field, STRICT rejects the entire batch as an unknown top-level field; LEGACY records an error and continues processing valid blocks in the same file, including a diagnostic hint naming the parent field and embedded key.

docs.title: Block-State Properties
docs.text:
state_properties creates Java Property instances and BlockState combinations, taking effect only during the registration phase.

type Required / Optional Fields Notes boolean Optional default Creates a new BooleanProperty integer min, max; optional default Bounded non-negative integer range enum values; optional default String value set backed by StringStateProperty vanilla property; optional default References a vanilla BlockStateProperties field

Property names and enum values must match [a-z0-9_]+. For integer, min and max are required; the range must be non-negative, have max > min, contain 2 to 64 values, and have max < Integer.MAX_VALUE (2147483647). boolean defaults to false. vanilla.property must be an uppercase public static field name on BlockStateProperties, and the vanilla property's own name must match the JSON key. A single block definition may declare at most 4096 state combinations. A vanilla property key does not automatically substitute for a newly created boolean property of the same name.

Modifying block-state properties changes the state encoding persisted in worlds. Adding, removing, or reordering properties after release can cause saved data to fall back or reset; the framework provides no automatic migration. See Block-State Properties for full rules and the Java API.

docs.title: Reload Content
docs.text: Top-level keys in reload content must be claimed by a registered ReloadHandler.

docs.title: state_machines
docs.text:
{
  "state_machines": [
    {
      "id": "example:panel",
      "layers": [
        {
          "id": "base",
          "initial_state": "idle",
          "states": [
            {
              "id": "idle",
              "duration_ticks": 20
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

state_machines/ is currently the only reload type with a directory glob. .json files placed under data/<ns>/state_machines/ can be discovered even without a manifest (for unmanaged legacy packs); files already listed in on_reload are not read a second time via the glob. The directory governs discovery only—files are still routed by their top-level keys.

docs.title: animation_clips
docs.text:
{
  "animation_clips": [
    {
      "id": "example:wheel_spin",
      "duration_seconds": 2.5,
      "bones": []
    }
  ]
}

Animation clips are currently discovered only through on_reload. There is no animation_clips/ directory glob, so files omitted from manifests are not read.

A single reload file may include multiple known top-level types, with each handler contributing entries independently; unknown top-level keys emit diagnostics while known types still contribute.

An empty registration content file {} is structurally valid and yields zero definitions. Whether an empty reload content file is valid depends on the decoder; the current FSM decoders report an error because their target top-level key is missing.

docs.title: File Ordering
docs.text:
The deterministic order of the v2 build pipeline is:

  1. Shared platform sources sorted ascending by explicit rank; only legacy SourceDescriptors receive zero-based order by input position;
  2. Within each source, manifests are aggregated and repeated paths within the same domain are deduplicated;
  3. on_register content paths are sorted lexicographically by full logical path;
  4. Within a single content file, top-level handlers run in the order passed to the pipeline constructor;
  5. Array elements for a single handler preserve file order;
  6. Embedded types follow their parent array element order.

For non-registration definitions sharing an identity, later sources, later files, and later array elements win. The legacy JsonTreeBuilder scans in index-filename order and manifest-array order; when migrating to the multi-source pipeline, do not assume both entry points visit duplicated paths in identical file order. STRICT registration types retain all candidates, and final applicability is governed by (registry, id) claims rather than simple last-wins.

on_register paths are deduplicated at the manifest layer and then sorted by full logical path by the new pipeline; the order of top-level keys inside a JSON file does not drive sorting. Array elements retain file order, while final apply ordering remains constrained by phase, handler order, source order, and parentDefinition.

docs.title: Minimal Registration Pack
docs.text:
data/example/kasuga_lib/data_driven/index.json
data/example/kasuga_content/groups.json
data/example/kasuga_content/items.json
assets/example/lang/en_us.json
pack.mcmeta

index.json:

{
  "on_register": [
    "kasuga_content/groups.json",
    "kasuga_content/items.json"
  ]
}

groups.json:

{
  "registry_groups": [
    {
      "id": "example:items",
      "item_properties": {
        "tab": "example:main"
      }
    }
  ]
}

items.json:

{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "example:token",
      "type": "simple_item",
      "registry_group": "example:items",
      "properties": {
        "stacks_to": 16
      }
    }
  ]
}

This handles Java registration only. You still need assets/example/models/item/token.json, textures, and language entries; to participate in resource/data pack overrides, also provide a valid pack.mcmeta.

The example assumes the host has registered a simple_item factory. Released packs should replace example types with their own stably registered factories rather than contentTesting types.

docs.title: TypeHandler and Preflight
docs.text:
TypeHandler<T> is the extension point for registration-phase content types. A handler owns one top-level field or one embedded field, parses JSON into a typed definition, and applies it to RegBuildContext.

public interface TypeHandler<T> {
    String getTypeName();
    int getPhase();
    T parse(JsonObject json);
    void apply(T definition, BuildContext context);

    default Set<HandlerCapability> capabilities() { return Set.of(); }
    default boolean strictValidationImplemented() { return false; }
    default void validate(T definition, ValidationContext context) {}
    default List<RegistryClaim> claims(T definition, ValidationContext context) {
        return List.of();
    }
    default DefinitionKey parentDefinition(T definition) { return null; }
    default String getParentTypeName() { return null; }
    default String getEmbeddedKeyName() { return null; }
    default List<JsonObject> extractEmbedded(JsonObject parentJson) { return null; }
    default String resolveIdentity(String modId, T definition) { return null; }
    default String resolveIdentity(String modId, T definition, boolean strict) {
        return resolveIdentity(modId, definition);
    }
}

Source: TypeHandler.java.

docs.title: Handler Registration
docs.text:
The new pipeline does not auto-discover handlers. The host passes a list of handler instances to DataDrivenBuildPipeline:

DataDrivenBuildPipeline pipeline = new DataDrivenBuildPipeline(
        "example",
        List.of(new RegistryGroupHandler(), new BlockTypeHandler(), new ItemTypeHandler()),
        finalizers
);

The legacy JsonTreeBuilder uses the process-wide TypeHandlerRegistry. On the first call to buildForMod or parseContentBody, ensureHandlersRegistered() registers the four built-in handlers:

JsonTreeBuilder.ensureHandlersRegistered();
Collection<TypeHandler<?>> handlers = TypeHandlerRegistry.all();

To reuse the legacy registry in the new pipeline, copy its contents into a normal collection before passing it to the pipeline constructor. all() returns a read-only view, while the registry itself remains a global static map where registering the same name overwrites the previous handler.

DataDrivenBuildPipeline neither auto-discovers handlers nor fills in built-in handlers automatically. If a host wants to reuse the built-in set, it must call JsonTreeBuilder.ensureHandlersRegistered() before constructing the pipeline and copy TypeHandlerRegistry.all(). Because the registry is not synchronized for concurrent mutation, additions should happen only before the first build.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as BuildPipeline
    participant H as TypeHandler
    participant V as ValidationContext
    participant C as BuildContext

    P->>H: parse(json)
    P->>H: resolveIdentity(hostModId, definition, strict)
    P->>H: capabilities() & strictValidationImplemented()
    Note over P: identity selection
    P->>H: validate(definition, V) only in STRICT
    P->>H: parentDefinition(definition) for cycle checks
    P->>H: claims(definition, V) for selected REGISTRY_CLAIMS
    P->>H: apply(definition, C)

Method contracts:

Method Must Be Side-Effect-Free Primary Responsibility capabilities / strictValidationImplemented Yes Declare STRICT readiness and identity role parse Yes Convert JSON into a definition object without registering anything resolveIdentity(..., strict) Yes Derive a stable logical id in the handler's namespace, respecting LEGACY/STRICT rules validate Yes Validate references, resources, factories, and field semantics parentDefinition Yes Return the parent definition that must be applied first claims Yes List all final Minecraft registry keys apply May mutate registration tree Create Reg nodes, attach to groups, and configure properties/factory params

parentDefinition is called during prepare for cycle detection and again during build for topological ordering. Both calls must return identical results and must not depend on changing iteration order.

More precisely, parse and resolveIdentity run for every successfully parsed definition, including candidates that are later overridden; validate runs only on selected definitions and only in STRICT mode; claims runs only on selected definitions whose handler declares REGISTRY_CLAIMS. LEGACY still collects claims and records conflicts, but does not block apply. apply runs only on selected definitions.

docs.title: From JSON Tree to Reg Tree
docs.text:
The "JSON tree" is not a Minecraft registry itself, but a tree of Reg registration intentions built per build call:

flowchart TD
    R["JsonRegistryGroup: example:json_root"] --> G0["registry_groups/example:base"]
    R --> G1["registry_groups/example:panels"]
    G0 --> G1
    R --> B["BlockReg example:panel"]
    G1 --> B
    B --> BI["ItemReg example:panel"]
    B --> BE["BlockEntityReg example:panel_be"]
    R --> I["ItemReg example:standalone"]

A handler's apply turns a definition into tree nodes:

  • RegistryGroupHandler creates a JsonRegistryGroup and stores it in RegBuildContext.registryGroups;
  • RegTypeHandler invokes the factory to create a block or item Reg, attaches it to its target group, and stores it in regStore;
  • BlockEntityTypeHandler obtains a BE Reg from its factory and attaches it as a child node of the host block;
  • Reg.setParent establishes both the parent/child link and the property inheritance chain;
  • withProperty stores deferred property modifiers on the node;
  • configure attaches registration-phase modifiers (such as creative tab bindings);
  • JsonRegistryGroup is attached as a child of the mod's Registry root.

RegBuildContext.getRegistryGroup(id) and getReg(typeName, rawId) are scoped to a single apply pass. They allow later phases to look up earlier objects—for example, a block entity resolving its host block via _parent_block—and are not persisted as global singletons.

Actual writes into Minecraft registries happen when dispatchRegister calls MinecraftDeferRegistryReg.register. prepare and build only construct registration intentions; if a host discards the root after a successful build, un-dispatched entries never enter Minecraft registries.

Reg.applyProperties evaluates property modifiers parent-first during object construction, so registry group ordering determines not only hierarchy, but also the final BlockBehaviour.Properties, Item.Properties, and creative tab mappings.

docs.title: parse
docs.text:
parse receives only the definition JsonObject—not the mod id, source descriptor, or validation context. When required fields are missing or cannot be decoded, it should throw a RuntimeException with a clear message; the pipeline records it as PARSE_FAILED along with the logical path and JSON Pointer.

Before parse runs in STRICT mode, StrictResourceJson has already decoded the entire file and verified that the manifest or content root is a single JSON object. Malformed UTF-8, duplicate keys, comments, trailing commas, trailing documents, or documents exceeding depth/node limits never reach the handler. LEGACY mode delegates to Gson's tolerant rules for backward compatibility.

Even if a definition later loses in last-wins selection, parse has already run. Never register objects, mutate global caches, or alter other definitions inside parse.

docs.title: Identity and EffectiveId
docs.text:
resolveIdentity(hostModId, definition) returns the identity within that handler's type domain. Here hostModId is the pipeline's registration host, not the definition's source owner. A DefinitionKey consists of:

(handler.getTypeName(), identity)

Different handler types can safely reuse the same string id because their type domains differ.

Returning null indicates an anonymous definition:

  • LEGACY permits anonymous definitions and applies all of them;
  • STRICT records MISSING_IDENTITY and rejects the entire build.

DataDrivenBuildPipeline passes options.isStrict() to the three-argument resolveIdentity(hostModId, definition, strict). The legacy JsonTreeBuilder still calls the two-argument overload. For built-in blocks, items, and embedded block entities, the two rules behave as follows:

Raw id STRICT effective id LEGACY effective id panel <hostModId>:panel, then rejected by validate with INVALID_IDENTITY <hostModId>:panel minecraft:panel minecraft:panel <hostModId>:panel example:panel example:panel example:panel

In the legacy entry point, a bare id and an explicit minecraft: id collide as a historical compatibility quirk. Three-argument STRICT requires an explicit namespace and preserves explicit minecraft: namespaces as-is. DataDrivenBuildPipeline in LEGACY mode uses the historical rule for DefinitionKey, while STRICT mode preserves explicit namespaces. Embedded block entities use their host block's effective id under the active rule. registry_groups uses the raw group id string verbatim because other definitions reference groups by raw string.

In STRICT mode, BlockTypeHandler and ItemTypeHandler reject bare IDs; only explicit, valid namespace:path IDs pass validation. RegTypeHandler.apply in STRICT attaches the ResourceLocation mapping for any explicit namespace, so minecraft:path is no longer rewritten to the host namespace. LEGACY retains the old minecraft: rewrite compatibility rule.

Logical configuration identity and registry identity are distinct concepts:

  • Identity governs configuration overrides, deduplication, and DefinitionKey;
  • RegistryClaim governs final Minecraft registry keys.

Custom handlers must keep the relationship between identity and claims consistent. If one definition occupies multiple keys, list all of them in claims; if the identity names configuration rather than a registry entry, declare NON_REGISTRATION.

docs.title: Phase
docs.text:
getPhase() governs the coarse apply stages:

Constant Value Typical Content PHASE_GROUPS 0 registry_groups PHASE_CONTENT 1 blocks, items PHASE_EMBEDDED 2 Embedded block_entity

Phase takes higher priority than handler list order. Even if handlers are passed in reverse order, phase 0 still runs before phase 1. Pipeline handler order breaks ties only within the same phase.

Full deterministic apply order:

  1. Phase (getPhase());
  2. First occurrence index of the handler in the pipeline list;
  3. sourceOrder;
  4. logicalPath;
  5. jsonPointer;
  6. declarationOrder;
  7. Topological constraints formed by parentDefinition.

When a parent edge exists, the parent definition always applies before its child, overriding the base comparator if necessary.

docs.title: Parent and Cycles
docs.text:
parentDefinition accepts only a DefinitionKey. Returning a missing parent does not raise an error automatically; handlers should verify it in validate via requireDefinition.

During prepare, the pipeline traces parent chains across selected definitions. When a cycle is detected:

  • Every member on the cycle receives GROUP_CYCLE;
  • Under STRICT, this is a blocking error;
  • Under LEGACY, it is logged as a warning and still enters apply ordering.

If apply ordering encounters a cycle it cannot resolve topologically, it appends the remaining nodes sorted by the comparator so build never loops infinitely.

docs.title: Embedded Types
docs.text:
An embedded handler is described by four methods on TypeHandler:

String getTypeName();        // internal type name, e.g. "block_entities"
String getParentTypeName();  // "blocks"
String getEmbeddedKeyName(); // "block_entity"
List<JsonObject> extractEmbedded(JsonObject parentJson);

Returning null from extractEmbedded indicates the parent entry has no embedded child of this type; returning a list passes each object to the embedded handler's parse. A parent type can technically host multiple embedded handlers as long as their type names and JSON keys do not collide.

Embedded types cannot appear as top-level fields. The new pipeline dispatches top-level arrays only to handlers where getParentTypeName() == null; the legacy entry point emits a diagnostic with location guidance if block_entities is written at the top level.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
STRICT mode accepts only used handlers that satisfy all of the following:

STRICT_PREFLIGHT
and strictValidationImplemented() == true
and exactly one of (
    NON_REGISTRATION
    REGISTRY_CLAIMS
)

Even if a type has no content, the pipeline checks for duplicate typeName() values across the handler list and emits HANDLER_NOT_STRICT_READY if any type name appears more than once. "Used" means prepare parsed at least one definition for that type; an empty array does not trigger capability checks for that handler.

Capability Meaning STRICT_PREFLIGHT validate is side-effect-free and catches build-blocking problems before apply NON_REGISTRATION Definitions are startup configuration and occupy no Minecraft registry entries REGISTRY_CLAIMS Definitions may occupy Minecraft registry entries and must report all claims OVERLAY Retains all candidates sharing an identity instead of dropping lower-priority ones

A typical NON_REGISTRATION handler is RegistryGroupHandler. Without OVERLAY, configuration definitions select only the highest-priority candidate even in STRICT mode, because configuration follows override semantics.

Registration types with REGISTRY_CLAIMS retain all candidates for the same DefinitionKey in STRICT mode. Claim checking then inspects each final registry key; if multiple definitions compete for the same key, the entire batch is rejected. This prevents sources from bypassing conflict detection by using different definition IDs that resolve to the same block id.

If a handler declares REGISTRY_CLAIMS yet returns an empty list, the framework cannot observe the keys it actually registers, and strict mode may miss a conflict—maintaining accurate claim reporting is the extension's responsibility.

docs.title: ValidationContext
docs.text:
ValidationContext provides a read-only view over the prepared session:

Method Purpose hostModId() Current registration host source() / sourceOrder() Provenance of the current definition currentDefinition() Current LocatedDefinition directDependencies() Direct dependencies declared by the current owner find(key) Returns the visible candidate for key if and only if exactly one candidate is visible to the current owner findAllVisible(key) All candidates for key owned by the current owner or its direct dependencies findAll(key) All parsed candidates for key across all owners, including invisible ones findAll(typeDomain) All parsed definitions of one handler type in declaration order canReference(key) Whether at least one candidate exists and is owned by the current owner or a direct dependency requireDefinition(key, pointer) Emits MISSING_REFERENCE, REFERENCE_NOT_DECLARED, or REFERENCE_AMBIGUOUS when invalid; returns whether the reference is valid and unambiguous resourceExists(domain, location) Checks logical resources under assets/ or data/ across visible sources (plus sharedAssetOwners for ASSETS) factoryAvailable(type, id) Checks whether a factory is registered factorySupports(type, id, class) Checks whether the registered factory implements a capability interface isReserved(symbol) / reservedSymbols() Queries host-reserved configuration symbols claim(registry, id) / claimAt(registry, id, pointer) Creates a claim carrying the current source provenance error(...) / warning(...) Records a VALIDATION diagnostic

find(key) delegates to findAllVisible(key), so it enforces owner visibility and returns Optional.empty() when zero or more than one visible candidate exists. For cross-owner references with clear diagnostics, prefer requireDefinition(key, pointer), or inspect findAllVisible(key) directly when custom resolution across multiple visible candidates is needed.

Dependencies are direct only: if A depends on B and B depends on C, A cannot reference C's definitions or resources unless C is explicitly listed in A's dependencies.

resourceExists searches only sources owned by the current owner or its direct dependencies (and sharedAssetOwners when domain == ASSETS) whose descriptor permits the target namespace:

assets/<namespace>/<path>
data/<namespace>/<path>

It checks the source's logical file list; it does not register resource packs or guarantee which file the Minecraft client's runtime pack stack will select.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
claims returns every final registry key produced by the definition:

@Override
public List<RegistryClaim> claims(PanelDef definition, ValidationContext context) {
    ResourceLocation id = ResourceLocation.parse(definition.id());
    return List.of(context.claim("minecraft:block", id));
}

context.claim automatically attaches the current source, sourceOrder, definitionKey, logical path, and JSON Pointer. Registry strings follow built-in conventions such as minecraft:block, minecraft:item, and minecraft:block_entity_type.

Every claim requires a non-null definition identity. In STRICT mode, missing identities fail earlier during PARSE; in LEGACY mode, calling context.claim on an anonymous definition throws IllegalStateException and records CLAIM_FAILED.

STRICT mode checks:

  • Whether any claim conflicts with the host's reserved snapshot;
  • Whether distinct definitions claim the same (registry, id);
  • Whether a handler omits any key remains the handler's responsibility.

Claims are collected before apply. Built-in handlers derive ResourceLocation values using the same identity rules as apply; custom handlers must do the same so preflight and the registration tree never diverge.

Built-in handlers keep DefinitionKey, claims, and apply aligned on the same identity mode: explicit minecraft: retains its namespace in STRICT, while LEGACY uses the historical host mapping. Custom handlers must ensure the same consistency themselves.

LEGACY still collects claims. Normal claim conflicts are recorded as warnings; conflicts with reserved host keys are always recorded as errors, though LEGACY builds still proceed. Neither conflict should be ignored in production.

docs.title: Minimal Custom Handler
docs.text:
The handler below registers a configuration symbol without occupying a Minecraft registry entry:

public record PanelMode(String id, String mode) {}

public final class PanelModeHandler implements TypeHandler<PanelMode> {
    @Override
    public String getTypeName() {
        return "panel_modes";
    }

    @Override
    public int getPhase() {
        return PHASE_CONTENT;
    }

    @Override
    public Set<HandlerCapability> capabilities() {
        return Set.of(
                HandlerCapability.STRICT_PREFLIGHT,
                HandlerCapability.NON_REGISTRATION
        );
    }

    @Override
    public boolean strictValidationImplemented() {
        return true;
    }

    @Override
    public PanelMode parse(JsonObject json) {
        return new PanelMode(
                json.get("id").getAsString(),
                json.get("mode").getAsString()
        );
    }

    @Override
    public String resolveIdentity(String hostModId, PanelMode definition) {
        return definition.id();
    }

    @Override
    public void validate(PanelMode definition, ValidationContext context) {
        if (!Set.of("idle", "running").contains(definition.mode())) {
            context.error(
                    BuildDiagnostic.Code.CONTENT_INVALID,
                    "/mode",
                    "Unknown panel mode " + definition.mode(),
                    "Use idle or running."
            );
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void apply(PanelMode definition, BuildContext context) {
        context.putMeta("panel_modes", definition.id(), definition.mode());
    }
}

If another handler reads that configuration, ensure its phase or apply order runs after metaStore is populated, or move cross-type assembly into a finalizer. metaStore is scoped strictly to the current build's RegBuildContext.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Top-level field names are unique within the pipeline's handler list.
  • parse, identity resolution, validate, claims, and parentDefinition have no side effects.
  • Three-argument resolveIdentity handles STRICT and LEGACY explicitly without leaking the minecraft: compatibility rewrite into v2 STRICT.
  • STRICT handlers declare STRICT_PREFLIGHT, return true from strictValidationImplemented(), and declare exactly one identity role (NON_REGISTRATION or REGISTRY_CLAIMS).
  • Every Minecraft registry output is listed in claims.
  • Types requiring a parent to exist first use both getPhase() and parentDefinition.
  • Cross-owner references call requireDefinition or canReference.
  • Factories, resources, and registry group references are checked inside validate.
  • Embedded types extract only from parent objects and never claim top-level fields.
  • Priority and selection semantics for duplicate identities match either configuration override or strict registration rules.

docs.title: ReloadHandler and Resource Reload
docs.text:
Reload data comes from the active Minecraft ResourceManager pack stack rather than the registration provider's ResourceSnapshot. Resource/data packs can override content at the same namespace and path, so definitions in this domain must be reconstructible on every resource reload.

ReloadOrchestrator owns the complete cycle: clearing buckets, discovery, decoding, deduplication, registration, and post-reload cross-type checks. It extends types via ReloadHandlerRegistry without hard-coding state_machines or animation_clips. Because ScopedResourceManager.addListener triggers onReloaded immediately on registration, loading runs both when the Manager first attaches and on every subsequent /reload.

docs.title: ReloadHandler
docs.text:
public interface ReloadHandler<T> {
    String typeName();
    default String describeFile() { return "reload-domain file"; }
    default Set<String> globDirectories() { return Set.of(); }
    void clearBucket();
    Decoded<T> decode(JsonObject root);
    void register(T payload);
    default void afterReload(List<Reloaded<T>> registered) {}
}

Source: ReloadHandler.java.

docs.title: Callback Responsibilities
docs.text:
Callback Timing Contract typeName() Registration and routing Top-level JSON key and deduplication namespace for this type describeFile() Diagnostics Human-readable file noun for decode messages globDirectories() Discovery Extra data/<ns>/.../*.json directories to scan; default empty = index-only clearBucket() Before each cycle's discovery Clears resource-sourced entries only; preserves script/code entries decode(root) On each matched file Pure decode; must not perform I/O or throw on malformed content register(payload) After all discovery and deduplication Writes into the handler's bucket; may throw on failure afterReload(list) After all handlers finish register Runs cross-type or bucket-wide post-load validation

decode receives the entire file already parsed into a JsonObject. Because a single file may carry multiple top-level keys, each decoder should inspect only its own key.

Decoded.Entry(id, payload) binds a payload to its deduplication identity. The identity should be a stable, namespace-qualified string. The orchestrator accepts whatever string the decoder returns; null opts the entry out of deduplication without prepending a namespace automatically. FSM decoders guarantee non-empty, stringified definition IDs themselves.

docs.title: Handler Registration
docs.text:
@Context
public final class MyReloadHandlers {
    @PostConstruct
    void init() {
        ReloadHandlerRegistry.register(new MyDefinitionsReloadHandler(MyBuckets.DEFINITIONS));
    }
}

ReloadHandlerRegistry behavior:

  • Indexed by typeName();
  • Re-registering the same typeName() replaces the instance in place while keeping its original iteration position;
  • all() returns a read-only view in registration order;
  • clearForTest() is reserved strictly for isolating in-JVM tests.

Registration order determines top-level routing order and the order in which candidates are organized before register. Cross-type afterReload checks should rely on the guarantee that all handlers have finished register, not on another handler's afterReload running first.

The registry itself is not a thread-safe container. Handlers should be installed before server or client ResourceManager reloads start, never added or removed concurrently during reload callbacks.

The built-in modelling handlers are registered at @Context startup by FsmReloadHandlerRegistrar in the following order:

  1. state_machines;
  2. animation_clips.

ReloadHandlerRegistry lives in data-driven, while the concrete FSM handlers remain in modelling, preserving the modelling -> data-driven dependency direction. Third-party extensions should similarly place handlers that depend on their own or Minecraft types in downstream modules rather than introducing reverse imports into data-driven.

docs.title: One Reload Cycle
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Manager first attach or ResourceManager reload"] --> B["Build HandlerCycle list in registry order"]
    B --> C["Clear RELOAD_DATA diagnostics"]
    C --> D["Call clearBucket per handler"]
    D --> E["Sort namespaces alphabetically"]
    E --> F["Read namespace manifests on_reload"]
    F --> G["Discover handler glob files, skipping index-listed paths"]
    G --> H["Read files listed in on_reload"]
    H --> I["Deduplicate last-wins and register per handler"]
    I --> J["Run afterReload per handler"]

Cycle rules:

  • Diagnostics.Domain.RELOAD_DATA is cleared at the start of every cycle so diagnostics do not accumulate across reloads.
  • clearBucket() is called once per registered handler regardless of whether any files exist in that cycle.
  • Namespaces are processed in ascending alphabetical order.
  • For each namespace, manifests under kasuga_lib/data_driven/ are read first to collect on_reload paths; directory globs then scan unlisted files (skipping managed sources covered by ManagedReloadAllowlist); finally, index-listed files are read.
  • Within a handler, glob candidates precede index candidates, so for the same id an index entry wins.
  • A file matched by both glob and index is read once through the index path.
  • register begins only after all discovery and decode calls across all handlers have completed; each handler deduplicates its candidates first and then registers winners.
  • afterReload runs only after every handler's register phase has completed.

Keep these three distinct "completion" points separate:

  1. Every file has been read and decoded, and candidates have been appended to each handler's glob/index lists;
  2. DuplicateIdResolver has selected the winners for each handler and called register in order;
  3. Finally, afterReload is called across all handlers.

Consequently, state machine reference validation sees animation clips registered during the same cycle, while individual decode calls must never assume other types are already registered.

docs.title: Paths and Overrides
docs.text:
The actual resource path for reload indexes is:

data/<namespace>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/<index>.json

Content paths remain relative to data/<namespace>/. They are resolved via:

resourceManager.getResourceStack(ResourceLocation.fromNamespaceAndPath(namespace, path))

For legacy (unmanaged) packs, ReloadOrchestrator selects the top resource in the stack (findFirst()), allowing higher-priority data packs to override matching files. For managed sources registered via ManagedReloadAllowlist, readReloadPaths and collectIndex filter to allowlisted managed layers ordered by ManagedReloadAllowlist.priority, and collectGlob skips managed sources so managed roots load only manifest-authorized reload files. When identities include namespaces, equal IDs across different namespaces never collide.

Registration-phase ContentSource reads from the host-selected sources, whereas reload reads from the game's currently active pack stack. Hosts that want registration schemas and data pack schemas to agree must validate both sides separately rather than assuming registration-time ZIP contents match runtime reload contents.

For main/parcel train packs, registration should read all active roots from frozen FixedResourceSource instances and publish those same roots as Approved pack layers into the Minecraft stack. Runtime reload still selects files along the active MC pack stack (with ManagedReloadAllowlist enforcing index/content authorization for managed packs) rather than re-capturing the registration provider's snapshot. When a user changes pack ordering or enabled state, the registered set and reloadable set must go through a consistent host startup flow instead of mutating registries during /reload.

docs.title: File Routing
docs.text:
Each known top-level key is decoded independently by its matching handler:

{
  "state_machines": [],
  "animation_clips": []
}

The file above contributes to both types. Unknown top-level keys emit diagnostics while known keys still decode and contribute. Non-object files are rejected as a whole; a JSON parse failure does not abort other files.

ContentStructure handles shared file-shape checks and unknown-key detection. Each decoder is responsible for verifying:

  • Whether its own top-level key is present;
  • Whether its value is a JSON array;
  • Whether every array element is a JSON object;
  • Whether the codec decodes each payload cleanly.

File-level vs. element-level rejection is governed by each decoder. The built-in FSM decoders reject malformed wrapper shapes while skipping invalid elements and retaining valid siblings.

docs.title: Deduplication and Failure Isolation
docs.text:
The orchestrator applies DuplicateIdResolver to each handler's candidate list:

  • Identity is Decoded.Entry.id();
  • Duplicates sharing (typeName, id) follow last-wins;
  • Losing payloads never reach register;
  • Each conflict logs a WARN and records an entry in Diagnostics.Domain.RELOAD_DATA;
  • Conflict entries are attributed to the namespace of the losing file.

Failures are isolated across boundaries:

  • A clearBucket() failure on one handler does not stop other handlers;
  • A read or decode failure on one file does not stop other files;
  • A discovery failure in one namespace does not stop subsequent namespaces;
  • A register() failure on one winner does not stop other winners;
  • An afterReload() failure on one handler does not stop subsequent handlers;
  • An outer fallback guard prevents runtime exceptions from escaping the reload listener.

Failure isolation guarantees that the cycle finishes, not transactional rollback. Errors after clearBucket can leave empty or partially populated buckets, and diagnostics record what failed to load in that round.

Diagnostics are split across two outlets:

  • File reads, unknown top-level keys, decode, register, and after-phase failures are written by the orchestrator into Diagnostics.Domain.RELOAD_DATA;
  • Runtime manifest parsing delegates to JsonTreeBuilder.parseIndexManifest and resolveIndexManifests to share the registration-side schema rules, so manifest schema errors land in the legacy per-mod/namespace error bucket, which is not cleared at the start of each reload cycle.

/kasuga_data errors <namespace> prints both outlets, so visibility in that command does not imply both entries live in RELOAD_DATA.

docs.title: state_machines
docs.text:
FsmReloadHandler:

  • typeName() returns state_machines;
  • Declares glob directory state_machines;
  • clearBucket() calls FsmDefinitions.clearResource();
  • decode delegates to StateMachineDefinitionLoader.decodeFile;
  • register writes to the RESOURCE half of FsmDefinitions;
  • afterReload verifies whether states[].clip entries exist in the clip bucket.

Script- or code-registered definitions survive clearResource(). When a script entry and a resource entry share an id, the script entry stays active and afterReload skips the resource definition because it is no longer the live entry in the bucket.

Dangling clip references:

  • Log a WARN;
  • Record an entry in RELOAD_DATA diagnostics;
  • Do not block state machine registration;
  • Degrade affected runtime states to an available static pose.

Because Diagnostics source buckets do not store severity, dangling clip references still count toward the error total shown by /kasuga_data errors even though they are logged as WARN.

docs.title: animation_clips
docs.text:
FsmClipsReloadHandler:

  • Index-only via on_reload, with no directory glob;
  • clearBucket() calls FsmAnimationClips.clearResource();
  • decode delegates to AnimationClipLoader.decodeFile;
  • register delegates to AnimationClipLoader.register.

animation_clips/*.json files omitted from manifests are not loaded. Placing them under state_machines/ does not automatically turn them into clips via the glob either; files are always routed by top-level key, and the directory affects discovery only.

docs.title: Reload Content in STRICT Preflight
docs.text:
DataDrivenBuildPipeline.prepare reads on_reload files listed in source manifests and runs each top-level key through the corresponding decoder in ReloadHandlerRegistry:

  • Unregistered top-level key: blocking error in STRICT;
  • Decoder errors: blocking error in STRICT;
  • Decoder throws an exception: converted to CONTENT_INVALID;
  • Neither clearBucket nor register is called.

This lets third-party external packs catch reload schema mistakes before startup completes. Preflight does not run globDirectories() discovery, so state_machines/ files omitted from manifests skip this preflight and are discovered only at runtime by ReloadOrchestrator.

Preflight queries the process-wide ReloadHandlerRegistry rather than the TypeHandler list passed to DataDrivenBuildPipeline. The host must install reload handlers before running a STRICT prepare intended to validate reload schemas. Preflight also does not construct ResourceLocation instances, so uppercase letters or invalid resource-path characters may be rejected only at runtime. Note that STRICT preflight uses StrictResourceJson, whereas runtime ReloadOrchestrator reads via Minecraft Resource and Gson JsonParser, so runtime parsing is more permissive toward inputs like duplicate keys than preflight.

docs.title: Custom ReloadHandler Example
docs.text:
public record DisplayRule(ResourceLocation id, String template) {}

public final class DisplayRulesReloadHandler
        implements ReloadHandler<DisplayRule> {

    private final DisplayRuleBucket bucket;

    public DisplayRulesReloadHandler(DisplayRuleBucket bucket) {
        this.bucket = bucket;
    }

    @Override
    public String typeName() {
        return "display_rules";
    }

    @Override
    public String describeFile() {
        return "display rule file";
    }

    @Override
    public Set<String> globDirectories() {
        return Set.of("display_rules");
    }

    @Override
    public void clearBucket() {
        bucket.clearResource();
    }

    @Override
    public Decoded<DisplayRule> decode(JsonObject root) {
        JsonElement value = root.get(typeName());
        if (value == null || !value.isJsonArray()) {
            return new Decoded<>(
                    List.of(),
                    List.of("display_rules must be an array")
            );
        }

        List<Decoded.Entry<DisplayRule>> entries = new ArrayList<>();
        List<String> errors = new ArrayList<>();
        for (JsonElement element : value.getAsJsonArray()) {
            if (!element.isJsonObject()) {
                errors.add("each display rule must be an object");
                continue;
            }
            JsonObject object = element.getAsJsonObject();
            JsonElement idValue = object.get("id");
            if (idValue == null || !idValue.isJsonPrimitive()
                    || !idValue.getAsJsonPrimitive().isString()) {
                errors.add("display rule id must be a string");
                continue;
            }
            ResourceLocation id = ResourceLocation.tryParse(idValue.getAsString());
            if (id == null) {
                errors.add("display rule id is invalid");
                continue;
            }
            JsonElement templateValue = object.get("template");
            if (templateValue == null || !templateValue.isJsonPrimitive()
                    || !templateValue.getAsJsonPrimitive().isString()) {
                errors.add("display rule template must be a string");
                continue;
            }
            entries.add(new Decoded.Entry<>(
                    id.toString(),
                    new DisplayRule(id, templateValue.getAsString())
            ));
        }
        return new Decoded<>(entries, errors);
    }

    @Override
    public void register(DisplayRule payload) {
        bucket.registerResource(payload.id(), payload);
    }
}

This example illustrates responsibility boundaries; DisplayRuleBucket is fictional. Production buckets should distinguish RESOURCE and SCRIPT sources like the FSM buckets so clearBucket clears only resource-sourced entries.

docs.title: Testing Recommendations
docs.text:
• Pure decode: construct JsonObject instances directly and assert entries and errors;
  • Registry ordering: register two handlers and verify in-place replacement preserves order and type names;
  • Mixed-file routing: put two known top-level keys in one file;
  • Unknown keys: verify diagnostics are recorded while known keys still contribute;
  • Last-wins: test glob and index candidates sharing the same (typeName, id);
  • Clear isolation: throw from one handler's clearBucket and verify other handlers still run;
  • afterReload: verify it runs after all register calls and can observe other handlers' buckets;
  • Resource overrides: use a ResourceManager test fixture to verify higher-priority pack selection.

Existing tests live under modules/modelling/src/test/java/lib/kasuga/rendering/models/mc/dynamic/fsm/, covering mixed files, file order, exception boundaries, script-wins, and cross-type references.

docs.title: Content Sources, Snapshots, and Security
docs.text:
In v2, registration sources have two layers:

  1. core's ResourceSource captures a physical source and returns an immutable ResourceSnapshot;
  2. data-driven's ContentSource exposes a concrete root as a manifest and JSON read view.

Production wiring should follow ResourceSource -> ResourceSnapshot -> ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(...) -> DataDrivenBuildPipeline. ContentSourceFactory.directory, zip, modJar, and open—which open directories or ZIPs directly—remain available for legacy entry points and test compatibility, and no longer represent the v2 fixed-startup-snapshot model.

ResourceSourceDescriptor descriptor = new ResourceSourceDescriptor(
        "example",
        "example-pack",
        "main",
        17,
        ResourceSourceDescriptor.Origin.EXTERNAL
);

try (ResourceSource fixed = ResourceSources.fixed(
             descriptor,
             ResourceSources.mod(descriptor, modRoot, InputPolicy.DEFAULT),
             InputPolicy.DEFAULT);
     ContentSource source = ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(
             fixed.capture(),
             descriptor,
             Set.of("example"),
             "example pack root main"
     )) {
    PreparedContent prepared = pipeline.prepare(
            List.of(source),
            BuildOptions.STRICT
    );
}

docs.title: Platform Identity
docs.text:
ResourceSourceDescriptor(ownerId, sourceId, rootId, rank, origin) is the single provider identity in core:

Field Constraints Purpose ownerId Matches platform ID rule ([A-Za-z0-9_-][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}, not . or ..) Defines ownership, dependency visibility, and access grants sourceId Matches the same rule One logical host source, typically one pack rootId Matches the same rule Concrete root within the source rank Non-negative integer Global resource layer order; higher values take higher priority origin EXTERNAL, MC_MANAGED, DERIVED Source category and projection restrictions

Colons are disallowed in platform IDs. A business parcel ID such as example_railway:m1 cannot be used directly as a rootId; the host must maintain a stable mapping such as parcel-m1.

data-driven's SourceDescriptor retains both the four-argument legacy constructor and the platform-descriptor constructor. When created via SourceDescriptor.of(ResourceSourceDescriptor, namespaces, label):

  • sourceId() and ownerId() match the platform descriptor;
  • rootId(), rank(), and origin() delegate directly to the platform descriptor;
  • resource() returns the underlying platform descriptor;
  • namespaces is the allowed set of namespaces for registration reads, required to be non-empty and stably sorted;
  • diagnosticLabel is used for human-readable diagnostic reporting only.

For the legacy four-argument SourceDescriptor.of(sourceId, ownerId, namespaces), resource() is null. Only for such legacy compatibility sources does the pipeline assign sourceOrder by input list position; platform sources always use their explicit rank.

docs.title: The ContentSource Interface
docs.text:
public interface ContentSource extends AutoCloseable {
    SourceDescriptor descriptor();
    Optional<InputStream> open(LogicalPath path) throws IOException;
    boolean exists(LogicalPath path);
    List<LocatedFile> files();
    default List<LocatedFile> indexes();
    default InputStream requireOpen(LogicalPath path) throws IOException;
}

files() returns the immutable file list fixed when the view was opened, sorted by logical path. LocatedFile holds the descriptor, LogicalPath, size, and—when backed by a platform snapshot—the ResourceUri, SHA-256 revision, and tags.

By default, indexes() matches only files under declared namespaces at:

data/<namespace>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/<name>.json

Only direct children of data_driven/ are matched, without recursion. The namespace segment in data/<namespace> must appear in SourceDescriptor.namespaces.

ContentSource is a read protocol, not a sandbox. While path traversal and archive layout are constrained by the implementations, handlers, JSON codecs, and factories still execute inside the host JVM; untrusted packs still require host-side restrictions on dependencies, resource budgets, and side effects.

docs.title: Scene Indexing, main, and parcel Roots
docs.text:
In these pages, "scene indexing" refers to selecting which roots participate in the current registration scene and which entry manifests each root exposes. It is a composition convention, not a separate Java or JSON type.

At the platform level, a pack typically maps as:

pack owner/source
├─ main       (lower rank; uses default indexes() or host-declared pack root entries)
├─ parcel-m1  (higher rank; exposes only parcel.json.indexes)
├─ parcel-m2  (even higher rank; exposes only parcel.json.indexes)
└─ shared     (host-defined shared root, still with its own unique rank and index set)

main, parcel-*, and shared are host conventions. KasugaLib requires only that:

  • Each (sourceId, rootId) is unique within a single prepare call;
  • Each root's rank is non-negative and unique across all roots in that prepare call;
  • rootId contains no colons;
  • Registration, MC resource discovery, and reload consumers reference the same frozen root;
  • Disabled roots are omitted from both the ContentSource list and MC ApprovedResourcePacks registration.

Ranks must be allocated in global order across all packs. Restarting from 0 for each pack causes ROUTING_CONFLICT on shared paths and duplicate-rank errors in the pipeline. Dependency topology governs preparation and reference visibility, and must never reorder ranks.

docs.title: ResourceSnapshot
docs.text:
The output of ResourceSnapshot.capture() is an immutable byte collection:

  • Each file retains its captured bytes, size, detected type/subtype, SHA-256 revision, and logical path;
  • Files up to InputPolicy.memoryThresholdBytes are kept in memory;
  • Larger files are written to randomly named private temporary spool files;
  • Per-JSON, per-file, total-byte, and file-count budgets are enforced byte-by-byte during capture;
  • A snapshot forbids duplicate ResourceUris, duplicate logical paths, and file/directory prefix conflicts.

A LocatedResourceFile is identified by its concrete provider URI:

ksg://<source>/roots/<root>/<path>[#<child>]

When a childKey is present, the file descriptor's origin becomes DERIVED while rank, owner, source, and root inherit from the parent provider; parentUri() returns the URI without the child key. Runtime derived outputs therefore preserve provenance without impersonating a new external source.

readBytes() reads the full file contents once. open() acquires a temporary read lease, and open(existingLease) increments the snapshot reference count until the returned stream is closed.

Calling ResourceSnapshot.close() retires the snapshot:

  • No new leases can be acquired afterward;
  • Existing valid leases and open streams can still finish reading;
  • Memory buffers are cleared and private spool files are deleted only when the final reference releases;
  • close() is idempotent.

ResourceSnapshot.Builder.copy(file) preserves the original URI, logical path, type, subtype, and tags while re-capturing bytes and computing the revision. It accepts only files with the exact same ownerId, sourceId, and rootId, preventing foreign provider content from being re-attributed under another identity.

docs.title: FixedResourceSource
docs.text:
ResourceSources.fixed(descriptor, liveSource, policy) immediately executes liveSource.capture() on creation and then closes liveSource. The returned FixedResourceSource retains this baseline snapshot.

On every subsequent fixed.capture():

  1. A new ResourceSnapshot.Builder is created under the same descriptor;
  2. Builder.copy copies every file from the baseline;
  3. An independent, closeable snapshot is returned.

Consequently:

  • Modifying the original directory or archive after pinning does not affect later reads;
  • Closing one consumer's snapshot never causes STALE_REFERENCE in another consumer;
  • Closing the FixedResourceSource itself causes future capture() calls to fail;
  • Closing the fixed source retires the baseline, while snapshots already handed out keep independent reference counts and remain readable.

If the baseline contains files from a different ownerId, sourceId, or rootId, capture fails rather than re-labeling a foreign provider.

Every discovery pass in ApprovedResourcePacks and every prepare cycle calls capture(). Passing a fixed source ensures all consumers read the startup bytes; passing a live ResourceSources.directory or archive source instead re-reads the install location.

docs.title: SnapshotContentSource
docs.text:
ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(...) projects a ResourceSnapshot into a registration view and transfers ownership of that snapshot to the returned SnapshotContentSource:

ContentSource source = ContentSourceFactory.snapshot(
        snapshot,
        resourceDescriptor,
        namespaces,
        diagnosticLabel,
        declaredIndexes // optional
);

Construction checks that:

  • Every file in the snapshot belongs to the supplied ownerId, sourceId, and rootId;
  • No logical path is duplicated;
  • Files are sorted by path and expose URI, revision, tags, and size;
  • The descriptor is built via SourceDescriptor.of(resourceDescriptor, namespaces, label).

declaredIndexes has narrow semantics: it replaces the candidate set returned by indexes(), keeping those listed paths that exist in the snapshot sorted by path. It does not:

  • Delete undeclared files from the snapshot;
  • Restrict content paths opened later by open();
  • Automatically verify that declared indexes sit inside the standard directory;
  • Automatically emit diagnostics for missing declared index paths.

Passing an empty collection declares "explicitly zero indexes", suited for roots providing ordinary assets/data only; passing null restores standard index-directory discovery.

Train-pack hosts should verify before building that every parcel index exists in its root snapshot; host components such as a pack resource snapshotter typically perform this check during slicing.

Closing SnapshotContentSource closes the snapshot it owns. Callers must not pass the same snapshot instance to a second owner to close; capture separate snapshots from the FixedResourceSource when multiple consumers need independent lifetimes.

docs.title: Directory
docs.text:
ResourceSource live = ResourceSources.directory(
        descriptor,
        directory,
        InputPolicy.DEFAULT
);

directory inspects the root and the entire tree:

  • Neither the root nor any descendant may be a symbolic link;
  • Only directories and regular files are permitted;
  • Entry count is capped;
  • Each capture() enumerates/reads twice and compares file descriptors and revisions to detect mutations mid-capture.

It reads through DirectoryVfs. Constructing that VFS may scan or hash the existing tree up front, so budget checks cannot undo that initial I/O cost; pin immutable startup inputs early with ResourceSources.fixed(...).

docs.title: Read-Only Non-Default NIO Roots
docs.text:
ResourceSource source = ResourceSources.readOnlyDirectory(
        descriptor,
        unionFilesystemRoot,
        InputPolicy.DEFAULT
);

This adapter handles read-only filesystem providers that do not support directory creation or LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS on stream open, such as NeoForge's union filesystem for expanded mods. It still rejects symbolic links and special files and performs the two-pass capture consistency check.

docs.title: Mod Root
docs.text:
ResourceSource source = ResourceSources.mod(
        descriptor,
        pathFromFindResource,
        InputPolicy.DEFAULT
);

Dispatch rules:

  • Non-directory regular files use archive;
  • Default-filesystem directories use directory;
  • Non-default-filesystem directories use readOnlyDirectory.

Expanded mods, ordinary JARs, and union filesystems therefore work without requiring the host to guess the backend from the path string.

docs.title: Archive
docs.text:
ResourceSource source = ResourceSources.archive(
        descriptor,
        zipOrJar,
        InputPolicy.DEFAULT
);

The v2 archive entry copies the archive within size limits, validates the raw central directory, and inflates each entry while counting actual bytes. It rejects:

  • Non-regular files, symlinks, encrypted archives, and split archives;
  • ZIP64 archives;
  • Duplicate raw paths or logical paths;
  • File/directory path conflicts;
  • Special Unix entries such as symlinks, devices, or FIFOs;
  • Exceeding JSON, single-file, total-byte, or file-count budgets;
  • Entry size or CRC mismatches.

The archive is captured twice and descriptors/revisions are compared so a package modified mid-capture is never accepted silently.

docs.title: VFS
docs.text: ResourceSources.vfs(descriptor, files, owned, sourcePrefix, logicalPrefix, policy) captures a bounded snapshot from a host's existing VirtualFileSystem. sourcePrefix is the path inside the VFS root for the URI, while logicalPrefix is the path prefix exposed in the registration view; keep the two separate. Unless the VFS itself already performs strict archive/link validation, wrapping a generic VFS does not synthesize those guarantees.

docs.title: InputPolicy and Limits
docs.text:
InputPolicy.DEFAULT:

Limit Default Single JSON file (maxJsonBytes) 8 MiB Single regular file (maxFileBytes) 256 MiB Total per snapshot/root (maxTotalBytes) 1 GiB File count (maxFiles) 50,000 JSON nesting depth (maxJsonDepth) 64 Memory-to-spool threshold (memoryThresholdBytes) 1 MiB

Construction requires positive counts/sizes, maxJsonBytes <= maxFileBytes <= maxTotalBytes, depth between 1 and 256, and a spool threshold up to Integer.MAX_VALUE.

Budgets apply per ResourceSnapshot.Builder—that is, per concrete root. If a host splits a pack across main, parcel, and shared roots, it should enforce pack-wide budgets explicitly, because separate valid roots do not share a single 1 GiB cap.

StrictResourceJson also enforces an 8 MiB text limit and a 100,000-node limit; inputs should still be bounded by InputPolicy before reaching that parser so unbounded reads cannot happen first.

docs.title: Streams, Leases, and Closing
docs.text:
try (InputStream input = source.requireOpen(path);
     Reader reader = new InputStreamReader(input, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
    // read while the source is open
}
  • open returns Optional.empty() for missing paths;
  • requireOpen throws SourceAccessException(NOT_FOUND) for missing paths;
  • Once a SnapshotContentSource is closed, open, exists, and files throw IllegalStateException;
  • The pipeline never closes ContentSource instances;
  • Standard definitions copy their parsed data during prepare, so ContentSource instances can usually be closed before build;
  • Custom definitions that defer file reads must acquire and close their own streams/leases.

docs.title: Strict JSON
docs.text:
In STRICT mode, DataDrivenBuildPipeline decodes bytes with a strict UTF-8 decoder first and then calls StrictResourceJson.parse:

  • Rejects malformed UTF-8;
  • Disables Gson lenient mode, rejecting comments, single quotes, and trailing commas;
  • Requires the file to contain exactly one JSON object;
  • Rejects duplicate keys;
  • Enforces default limits of 64 nesting levels and 100,000 nodes;
  • Applies this path uniformly to manifests, registration content, and reload preflight.

LEGACY mode uses JsonParser.parseString for tolerant compatibility. Note that runtime ReloadOrchestrator reads from Minecraft's ResourceManager using Gson's JsonParser rather than inheriting the provider's STRICT byte snapshot; pipeline reload preflight validates schema in the frozen sources, whereas runtime /reload reads whichever packs MC selects.

docs.title: Legacy ContentSource Adapters
docs.text:
The following APIs remain in the codebase:

ContentSourceFactory.directory(path, descriptor);
ContentSourceFactory.zip(path, descriptor);
ContentSourceFactory.modJar(IModFile, descriptor);
ContentSourceFactory.open(path, descriptor);
  • DirectoryContentSource fixes the file list on open, but reads live file bytes when streams are opened;
  • ZipContentSource supports ordinary archives and ZIP64 central-directory metadata bounded by SourceLimits.maxFiles, keeping the ZipFile handle open until closed;
  • ModJarContentSource reads modFile.getSecureJar().getRootPath() without closing the shared secure JAR filesystem.

These adapters are suitable for legacy entry points, import tools, or compatibility tests. New registration providers that must guarantee registration, initial resource discovery, and reload never observe a changing install directory should use core's ResourceSources, ResourceSnapshot, and FixedResourceSource.

docs.title: Source Priority and Dependencies
docs.text:
Shared platform sources are processed in ascending ResourceSourceDescriptor.rank order:

main rank 10
parcel-m1 rank 11
parcel-m2 rank 12
next-pack main rank 13

Larger values have higher priority. Non-registration definitions select a winner by priority (unless using OVERLAY), while STRICT registration definitions retain all candidates and check final claims. Dependencies and priority are orthogonal dimensions:

  • rank determines override order and deterministic traversal order;
  • dependencies determines whether one owner can reference definitions and resources owned by another owner;
  • Dependency topology never reorders ranks or promotes a source.

docs.title: Relationship to MC Resource Projection
docs.text:
The same ResourceSnapshot can feed both the registration view and MC pack layers:

  • Registration side: SnapshotContentSource;
  • MC side: ApprovedResourcePacks discovery via MappedPackResources, where each (sourceId, rootId) becomes a separate pack layer.

MappedPackResources holds snapshot leases for its files and exposes only host-routed assets/, data/, pack.mcmeta, and pack.png paths. When pack.mcmeta is absent, the projection layer synthesizes runtime metadata for the current PackType without altering the author's snapshot.

Approved pack discovery is an independent consumer path that may invoke capture() repeatedly. Only a FixedResourceSource guarantees that every discovery uses startup bytes. Registration providers should update the single approved-root set only after strict preflight, dependency closure, and build succeed, before resource discovery publishes those roots.

Source priority does not set Minecraft's resource pack order automatically, so both the root list, order, and ranks should derive from the same frozen snapshot selection. When using MappedPackResources, avoid materializing a second authoritative directory copy on disk to re-scan as a plain path pack.

docs.title: SourceAccessException
docs.text:
Legacy ContentSource adapters report failures via SourceAccessException.Reason:

Reason Meaning NOT_FOUND Source or logical file does not exist ACCESS_DENIED Filesystem denied access OUT_OF_BOUNDS Reserved error reason for out-of-bounds paths SYMLINK_REJECTED Root, tree node, or archive entry is a symbolic link DUPLICATE_ENTRY Duplicate raw or logical entry INVALID_ENTRY Special file, malformed directory entry, invalid name, etc. LIMIT_EXCEEDED File count or byte budget exceeded CORRUPT_ARCHIVE Invalid ZIP structure or inflate failure SOURCE_CLOSED open called after close() IO_ERROR Other I/O failure

core's ResourceSources throws IOException with stable message prefixes such as SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, UNSAFE_PATH, DUPLICATE_ENTRY, LIMIT_EXCEEDED, and INVALID_ARCHIVE. Host error reporting should preserve the original message and source/root context rather than collapsing them into a generic "file not found".

docs.title: Multi-Source Build Pipeline
docs.text:
DataDrivenBuildPipeline organizes discovery, parsing, policy selection, preflight validation, and apply across multiple ContentSource instances into an immutable two-phase prepare/build workflow. Each ContentSource should come from an already-frozen ResourceSnapshot, ensuring prepare, initial MC discovery, and subsequent consumers never read different snapshots of an install directory.

PreparedContent prepared =
        pipeline.prepare(sources, BuildOptions.STRICT, dependencies);

BuildResult result = pipeline.build(prepared);

Source: DataDrivenBuildPipeline.java.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
Core constructor:

new DataDrivenBuildPipeline(
        String hostModId,
        Collection<? extends TypeHandler<?>> handlers,
        Collection<? extends BuildFinalizer> finalizers
)

Extended constructors allow customizing RegistrationTarget, reserved symbols, and reserved registry keys (a 5-argument overload omitting reservedRegistryClaims is also available):

new DataDrivenBuildPipeline(
        hostModId,
        handlers,
        finalizers,
        RegistrationTarget.standard(),
        reservedSymbols,
        reservedRegistryClaims
);

Constructor arguments are copied defensively. Handler list order participates in deterministic tie-breaking within each phase. Handler type names must be non-blank, and STRICT prepare rejects duplicate type names.

RegistrationTarget.standard() constructs:

new RegBuildContext(hostModId, rootGroup, options.isStrict())

A custom target lets the host supply its own RegBuildContext subclass. The contract expects the returned context to bind the supplied host and root group; build does not inspect internal context fields via reflection to enforce this.

docs.title: prepare Inputs
docs.text:
prepare(sources, options, dependencies) (and the four-argument overload prepare(sources, options, dependencies, sharedAssetOwners)) takes:

Collection<? extends ContentSource> sources
BuildOptions options
Map<String, ? extends Collection<String>> dependencies

Source priority comes from the source descriptor:

  • Sources backed by ResourceSourceDescriptor use their explicit, non-negative rank; the pipeline sorts by rank first, breaking ties by input position while reporting duplicate ranks as errors;
  • Only legacy four-argument SourceDescriptors with resource() == null receive a zero-based sourceOrder from their iteration position in the input collection;
  • (sourceId, rootId) is the unique key for a platform source root. A single sourceId may contain main, parcel, and shared roots.

ValidationContext.sourceOrder() and LocatedDefinition.sourceOrder() store the effective order used during the session. Explicit platform rank is the source of truth for that order, not the caller's list ordering.

dependencies maps each ownerId to the other owners it is allowed to reference directly:

Map.of(
        "example_addon", Set.of("example_core"),
        "example_theme", Set.of("example_core", "example_addon")
)

Every owner present in sources is automatically assigned an empty dependency set if omitted. Declaring a dependency on an owner absent from sources logs UNKNOWN_DEPENDENCY as an error in STRICT and a warning in LEGACY.

docs.title: Deterministic Ordering in prepare
docs.text:
Sort sources by explicit rank
  → Aggregate manifests per source
  → Deduplicate register / reload paths
  → Sort register paths by logicalPath
  → Process top-level content keys in pipeline handler list order
  → Preserve file order within each handler array

Pass sequence:

  1. Check (sourceId, rootId) uniqueness and global rank uniqueness;
  2. Normalize and validate owner dependencies;
  3. Read manifests per source, locate register/reload paths, and parse registration content;
  4. Read reload files and run ReloadHandler.decode for preflight checks;
  5. Check STRICT handler capabilities and strictValidationImplemented();
  6. Select effective definitions by identity and priority;
  7. Run validate (STRICT only);
  8. Check parentDefinition references for cycles;
  9. Collect claims and check registry conflicts;
  10. Produce an immutable PreparedContent.

Source processing is isolated per source. If enumerating or reading a source throws a RuntimeException, the pipeline records SOURCE_READ_FAILED and continues with the next source, without rolling back paths or definitions already collected from the failing source. STRICT then rejects the build due to the blocking diagnostic, while LEGACY may apply partial results.

Each source's effective manifest set comes from ContentSource.indexes(). Standard ContentSource implementations discover direct children under data/<ns>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/; SnapshotContentSource with declaredIndexes exposes only the paths named by the host. This entry selection is what these pages call scene indexing. It does not strip content files from the snapshot, so manifests can still open content from the same fixed root.

PreparedContent holds:
