docs.title: Installation and Deployment
docs.text: This page is for server owners, modpack authors, and release packagers. It explains how to build deployable artifacts from source, install the right JARs into mods/, handle optional mods and native libraries, and configure dedicated servers and clients.

docs.title: 1. Pre-Flight Checklist
docs.text:
Item Requirement Minecraft 1.21.1 Mod Loader NeoForge 21.1.268 or newer ([21.1.268,)) Runtime Java Java 21 Core Artifact kasuga-library-1.0.0-all.jar (the -all Shadow JAR) Companion Mods (Aggregate JAR) Create 6.0.11-346 + Flywheel 1.0.7 + Ponder 1.0.92+mc1.21.1 + Registrate MC1.21-1.3.0+67 (see Section 3)

Never deploy the unshaded thin JAR or split sub-module JARs

  • Do not install kasuga-library-1.0.0.jar (~44 KB); it omits relocated Micronaut/Caliko/jgltf/ZXing classes and embedded sub-modules.
  • Do not install individual sub-module JARs (such as kasuga-core-*.jar or kasuga-modelling-*.jar) alongside kasuga_lib; FML/JPMS module resolution will fail on split packages or duplicate mod IDs.

docs.title: 2. Building Deployable Artifacts from Source
docs.text:
The repository currently defines only local file-system publishing (file://${project.projectDir}/repo). From the repository root (with JDK 21), build the aggregate mod JAR with:

./gradlew :modules:library:assemble

Copy the resulting shaded artifact into your client or server mods/ directory:

  • modules/library/build/libs/kasuga-library-1.0.0-all.jar

To run the full compile, JVM unit test, Javadoc, and plugin verification suite (without launching a real Minecraft world):

./gradlew renderingReleaseCheck

See Build and Verification Entries for the scope of each Gradle verification task.

docs.title: 3.1 Create and Its Dependencies
docs.text:
Although KasugaLibNext gates its Create DI beans behind @CreateModBeans (IfCreateModLoaded), the :modules:library META-INF/neoforge.mods.toml currently registers all three Mixin configs:

  • kasuga_lib.mixins.json
  • kasuga_lib_iris.mixins.json (required: false)
  • kasuga_lib_create.mixins.json (required: true, plugin CreateMixinPlugin)

CreateMixinPlugin inspects com/simibubi/create/content/trains/track/BezierConnection.class when applying track Mixins and throws IllegalStateException("Create BezierConnection is missing") if absent. When deploying the full kasuga-library-*-all.jar, install a compatible 1.21.1 Create build (6.0.11-346 and its dependencies Ponder, Flywheel, and Registrate) in mods/.

docs.title: 3.2 Javet JavaScript Engine (kasuga_lib_javet)
docs.text:
Install kasuga_lib_javet (external/slp/javet) only if your modpack, datapack, or dependent mods load script packages (package.toml) targeting the javascript engine.

Packaging caveat: Unlike modules/library/build.gradle, external/slp/javet/build.gradle currently leaves shadowJar on the default runtimeClasspath configuration. As a result, :external:slp:javet:shadowJar produces a ~116 MB kasuga-javet-1.0.0-all.jar that bundles net.minecraft.* and kasuga_lib classes and must not be dropped into a production mods/ folder as-is. Meanwhile, the thin kasuga-javet-1.0.0.jar omits com.caoccao.javet:javet:5.0.1 and org.apache.httpcomponents:httpclient:4.5.13. Before shipping in a modpack, package only javet and httpclient with the Javet adapter classes without bundling Minecraft or kasuga_lib.

Offline / air-gapped V8 native deployment:

  1. At runtime JavetDownloader looks under <gameDir>/native-libraries/javet/ for the host's V8 native library (libjavet-v8-<os>-<arch>.*).
  2. If absent, first startup attempts to download javet-<runtime>-<os>-<arch>-5.0.1.jar from maven.aliyun.com or repo1.maven.org and extract the native binary.
  3. For offline servers, pre-extract the matching native library from com.caoccao.javet:javet-v8-<os>-<arch>:5.0.1 into <gameDir>/native-libraries/javet/.
  4. Dedicated-server escape hatch: if a server must boot without kasuga_lib_javet while scripts declare javascript, set ignore_scripting_errors = true in config/kasuga_lib-server.toml (logs a WARN instead of throwing).

docs.title: 3.3 Optional Client / Companion Mods
docs.text: Mod Side Behavior Iris (1.8.14-beta.1) & Sodium (0.8.14-beta.2) Client-only kasuga_lib_iris.mixins.json is non-required; IrisCameraMixinPlugin and IrisCompat probe Iris/Sodium ABIs at startup and cleanly fall back to native rendering when absent or incompatible Voxy Client-only VoxyCompat checks ModList.get().isLoaded("voxy") automatically Sable Both (optional) Enables Sable scene hosts and enable_sable_weather_filter only when Sable is installed LDLib2 (2.2.44) / ModernUI Optional Required only when installing the matching external/uip/* companion integration mod

docs.title: 4. Box3D Native Library and Cross-Platform Packaging
docs.text:
Ragdoll and rigid-body physics (PMX and glTF Ragdoll Configuration) run on the vendored Box3D C17 engine via the kasuga_box3d JNI library. NativeBox3D extracts /native/<os>-<arch>/<mappedName> from the JAR:

  • Building locally with ./gradlew :modules:library:assemble compiles only the build host's OS/architecture when cmake is on PATH (for example native/macos-aarch64/libkasuga_box3d.dylib on Apple Silicon).
  • If cmake is missing on PATH, Gradle logs a warning and omits the native binary; at runtime NativeBox3D.availableOrWarn() disables Box3D physics gracefully while all non-physics modelling and rendering features keep working.
  • Cross-platform release JARs: To support Linux x86_64, Windows x86_64, and macOS ARM64 from a single JAR, follow the package-universal workflow in .github/workflows/build.yml (compile buildBox3D on each OS and pass -PkasugaBox3DNativeResources=<dir> or merge all native/<os>-<arch>/ directories at the top level of the JAR).

docs.title: 5. Server/Client Configuration and Headless Launches
docs.text:
Via @Configurable, KasugaLibNext registers NeoForge ModConfigSpec files under config/:

Config File Key Settings and Defaults Notes config/kasuga_lib-server.toml ignore_scripting_errors = false Controls whether missing script engines on a dedicated server log a warning instead of throwing (ScriptingServerApplication) config/kasuga_lib-common.toml enable_multi_bogey_carriage = falseenable_carriage_y_offset = falsemax_bogey_offset = 1.0max_carriage_y_offset = 0.5derailed_on_bogey_offset_overflow = falseenable_contraption_lod = trueenable_contraption_weather_filter = trueenable_sable_weather_filter = true Create train, multi-bogey carriage, contraption LOD, and indoor weather-filter toggles (CreateConfig, registered when Create is loaded) config/kasuga_lib-client.toml ignore_block_entity_renderer = falseenable_weather_filter = trueincluded_entity_types = []excluded_entity_types = [] Client BER registration guard (ClientRenderingRegistry) and 3D indoor weather filter (WeatherFilterConfig)

For the full option catalog, see Configuration Options and PBR.

docs.title: Dedicated Servers and Headless Clients
docs.text:
• Dedicated servers (DEDICATED_SERVER): No OpenGL context or display server is needed. KasugaLibMixinPlugin and IrisCameraMixinPlugin skip all client mixins, and @BeanOnlyIn.Client beans are not instantiated.
  • Headless / CI preview clients: When running a client without a visible window (runClientHeadless), NeoForge's early splash window must be disabled beforehand (earlyWindowControl = false in config/fml.toml), and -Dkasuga.headless=hidden (desktop hidden window) or -Dkasuga.headless=egl (Linux EGL pbuffer) must be set. See Offscreen Output and Multi-Camera Rendering.

docs.title: 6. Modpack Reloading and Diagnostic Commands
docs.text:
Keep the two phases distinct when maintaining modpacks (see Data-driven getting started):

  • Registration phase (requires restart): on_register entries under data/<namespace>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/*.json are read from mod JARs only at startup; edits require restarting both server and client.
  • Reload phase and client assets (hot-reloadable): on_reload entries (state_machines/, animation_clips/) come from the pack stack and update on /reload; client assets/<namespace>/models/model_proxy.json and model/texture packs reload on F3 + T.

Built-in diagnostic commands (/kasuga_data requires permission level 2):

  • /kasuga_data errors / /kasuga_data errors <mod> — inspect registration and reload error buckets.
  • /kasuga_proxy list — list registered proxy_model / proxy_model_be entries.
  • /kasuga_effects / /kasuga_pbr status — inspect client effect pipelines and PMX→PBR state.

docs.title: Minimal Example Project
docs.text:
This page walks through a complete, runnable NeoForge 1.21.1 minimal downstream mod project wired to KasugaLibNext via a Gradle composite build. It demonstrates Registry, BlockReg, ItemReg, and CreativeTabReg, plus notes on optional Micronaut DI and data-driven integration.

See Dependencies and Runtime Environment for prerequisite versions. The setup below assumes your mod directory sits next to KasugaLibNext (../KasugaLibNext).

docs.title: 1. Directory Layout
docs.text:
examplemod/
├── settings.gradle
├── build.gradle
├── gradle.properties
└── src/
    └── main/
        ├── java/com/example/examplemod/
        │   └── ExampleMod.java
        ├── resources/assets/examplemod/
        │   └── lang/en_us.json
        └── templates/META-INF/
            └── neoforge.mods.toml

docs.title: build.gradle
docs.text:
Because the aggregate kasuga-library-*-all.jar currently declares kasuga_lib_create.mixins.json, dev runs (runClient / runServer) also provide Create, Ponder, Flywheel, and Registrate (matching modules/library/build.gradle and KuaYue/modules/core/build.gradle):

plugins {
    id 'java-library'
    id 'net.neoforged.moddev' version '2.0.107'
}

version = mod_version
group = mod_group_id

java.toolchain.languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    maven { url = 'https://maven.createmod.net' }
    maven { url = 'https://maven.ithundxr.dev/snapshots' }
}

neoForge {
    version = project.neo_version

    parchment {
        mappingsVersion = project.parchment_mappings_version
        minecraftVersion = project.parchment_minecraft_version
    }

    runs {
        client {
            client()
        }
        server {
            server()
            programArgument '--nogui'
        }
    }

    mods {
        "${mod_id}" {
            sourceSet(sourceSets.main)
        }
    }
}

dependencies {
    implementation('lib.kasuga:kasuga_lib:1.0.0') {
        attributes {
            attribute(Bundling.BUNDLING_ATTRIBUTE, objects.named(Bundling, Bundling.SHADOWED))
        }
        transitive = false
    }

    // Companion mods expected at runtime by kasuga_lib_create.mixins.json
    implementation("com.simibubi.create:create-${minecraft_version}:${create_version}") { transitive = false }
    implementation("net.createmod.ponder:ponder-neoforge:${ponder_version}+mc${minecraft_version}")
    compileOnly("dev.engine-room.flywheel:flywheel-neoforge-api-${minecraft_version}:${flywheel_version}")
    runtimeOnly("dev.engine-room.flywheel:flywheel-neoforge-${minecraft_version}:${flywheel_version}")
    implementation("com.tterrag.registrate:Registrate:${registrate_version}")
}

def generateModMetadata = tasks.register('generateModMetadata', ProcessResources) {
    def replaceProperties = [
            minecraft_version       : minecraft_version,
            minecraft_version_range : minecraft_version_range,
            neo_version             : neo_version,
            loader_version_range    : loader_version_range,
            kasuga_lib_version_range: kasuga_lib_version_range,
            mod_id                  : mod_id,
            mod_name                : mod_name,
            mod_license             : mod_license,
            mod_version             : mod_version,
            mod_authors             : mod_authors,
            mod_description         : mod_description
    ]
    inputs.properties replaceProperties
    expand replaceProperties
    from 'src/main/templates'
    into 'build/generated/sources/modMetadata'
}
sourceSets.main.resources.srcDir generateModMetadata
neoForge.ideSyncTask generateModMetadata

tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach {
    options.encoding = 'UTF-8'
}

docs.title: 4. Minimal Java Entry Point ExampleMod.java
docs.text:
When using only KasugaLibRegistry and the Reg builders, your downstream mod does not need Micronaut or annotation processing: Registry.register(modEventBus) delegates via KasugaLib.afterRunning (KasugaLibStartupEvent) to KasugaLib's own ApplicationContext and dispatches registration stages as well as JsonTreeIntegration (automatically loading data/examplemod/kasuga_lib/data_driven/*.json if present).

package com.example.examplemod;

import lib.kasuga.KasugaLibRegistry;
import lib.kasuga.registration.Registry;
import lib.kasuga.registration.core.CreativeTabModifiers;
import lib.kasuga.registration.minecraft.block.BlockReg;
import lib.kasuga.registration.minecraft.creative_tab.CreativeTabReg;
import lib.kasuga.registration.minecraft.item.ItemReg;
import net.minecraft.network.chat.Component;
import net.minecraft.world.item.Item;
import net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.Block;
import net.neoforged.api.distmarker.Dist;
import net.neoforged.bus.api.IEventBus;
import net.neoforged.fml.ModContainer;
import net.neoforged.fml.common.Mod;
import net.neoforged.fml.loading.FMLEnvironment;

@Mod(ExampleMod.MODID)
public class ExampleMod {
    public static final String MODID = "examplemod";

    public static final Registry REGISTRY = KasugaLibRegistry.getRegistryOf(MODID);

    public static final CreativeTabReg EXAMPLE_TAB = new CreativeTabReg("example_tab")
            .title(Component.translatable("itemGroup.examplemod.example_tab"))
            .icon(() -> new ItemStack(ExampleMod.EXAMPLE_ITEM.getEntry()))
            .setParent(REGISTRY);

    public static final ItemReg<Item> EXAMPLE_ITEM = ItemReg.of("example_item", Item::new)
            .stacksTo(64)
            .tabTo(EXAMPLE_TAB)
            .setParent(REGISTRY);

    public static final BlockReg<Block> EXAMPLE_BLOCK = BlockReg.of("example_block", Block::new)
            .strength(2.0f, 3.0f)
            .requiresCorrectToolForDrops()
            .withDefaultBlockItem("example_block")
            .configure(CreativeTabModifiers.set(EXAMPLE_TAB::getResourceLocation))
            .setParent(REGISTRY);

    public ExampleMod(IEventBus modEventBus, ModContainer modContainer) {
        REGISTRY.register(modEventBus);
        if (FMLEnvironment.dist == Dist.CLIENT) {
            REGISTRY.registerClient(modEventBus);
        }
    }
}

Key behaviors (from modules/core):

  • KasugaLibRegistry.getRegistryOf(MODID) creates the root Registry and attaches ResourceLocationModifiers.withNamespace(MODID), so child entries resolve under examplemod:<name>.
  • BlockReg.withDefaultBlockItem("example_block") attaches a child ItemReg<BlockItem>; configuring CreativeTabModifiers.set(EXAMPLE_TAB::getResourceLocation) on the BlockReg (or a parent RegistryGroup) propagates down to that child BlockItem.
  • Call EXAMPLE_ITEM.getEntry() / EXAMPLE_BLOCK.getEntry() only after RegisterEvent has run (e.g., inside Supplier callbacks or gameplay code), never during static field initialization.
  • REGISTRY.registerClient(modEventBus) is annotated @OnlyIn(Dist.CLIENT) and handles client-only stages (menu screens, model baking completion, fluid client extensions), so guard it behind FMLEnvironment.dist == Dist.CLIENT or a @BeanOnlyIn.Client bean.

Add a minimal language file at src/main/resources/assets/examplemod/lang/en_us.json:

{
  "itemGroup.examplemod.example_tab": "Example Mod",
  "item.examplemod.example_item": "Example Item",
  "block.examplemod.example_block": "Example Block"
}

docs.title: 5. Build and Run
docs.text:
From examplemod/:

./gradlew build
./gradlew runClient
./gradlew runServer

The startup log prints KasugaLibApplication initialized., and in-game you will find the Example Mod creative tab containing Example Item and Example Block.

docs.title: 6. Next Steps: Micronaut DI and Data-Driven Content
docs.text:
For larger mods that want modular dependency injection or @Configurable NeoForge configs, mirror the KasugaLib / KuaYue pattern:

  1. Add lib.kasuga:inject and Micronaut 4.9.10 (plus annotationProcessor 'io.micronaut:micronaut-inject-java:4.9.10') as shown in Dependencies and Runtime Environment.
  2. Initialize your mod's ApplicationContext inside your @Mod constructor:
public static final ApplicationContext context = ModApplicationContext.create(ExampleMod.class);

public ExampleMod(IEventBus modEventBus, ModContainer modContainer) {
    ModApplicationContext.init(context, modEventBus, modContainer);
}
  1. Dispatch REGISTRY.register(modEventBus) from a @Context bean and REGISTRY.registerClient(modEventBus) from a @Context + @BeanOnlyIn.Client bean.

Continue exploring:

  • Data-driven getting started: from an empty directory to a moving block: register blocks, state machines, and clips with JSON
  • Integrating Content With the Proxy Kernel and Modelling Module: attach .bbmodel, .gltf, and .mmd.zip models to block entities
  • Lifecycle and Initialization Order and Sidedness Model: registration stages and client/server isolation rules

docs.title: Content Integration: Block and Item Model Resources
docs.text:
This page answers one question: when a block or item is drawn by this project's render pipeline, how should blockstate and the vanilla models/item/*.json be written?

API signatures live in ItemModelRenderers; binding a world block to a state machine/model is covered by FSM and Integrating Content With the Proxy Kernel.

docs.title: 1. Pick the path first
docs.text:
Content World rendering Item rendering Block (project pipeline) Block entity rendering (RenderShape.ENTITYBLOCK_ANIMATED) ItemModelRenderer (BEWLR) Item (project pipeline) — same as above Vanilla static block / item Vanilla baked model Vanilla baked model

Only the first case needs a blockstate; both project-pipeline cases need the item model line below.

docs.title: 2. What blockstate is for
docs.text:
// assets/<ns>/blockstates/<block_path>.json
{
  "variants": {
    "running=false": {"model": "<ns>:block/<placeholder>"},
    "running=true":  {"model": "<ns>:block/<placeholder>"}
  }
}

Rules:

  1. The file name equals the block's registry path, independent of Java class names.
  2. Variant keys must cover every property combination. A block without properties uses ""; n boolean properties need 2^n keys. Missing keys log Unable to load variant and fall back to a missing model.
  3. Under ENTITYBLOCK_ANIMATED it does not participate in world drawing, but it still decides:
  4. the break/hit particle texture (taken from the referenced model's particle);
  5. resource bake validation (a missing variant/model logs an error);
  6. the world appearance if getRenderShape is ever switched back to MODEL.
  7. The referenced model must be a vanilla-bakery-compatible JSON (parent/elements/textures). .bbmodel, .geo.json, .glb and .mmd.zip are read by this project's own loaders and cannot be referenced here.

Recommended: give the block a minimal dedicated placeholder (a plate or a cube) whose particle points at the real texture instead of borrowing an unrelated block's model.

docs.title: 3. Two ways to write the item model
4. Three steps for item rendering
docs.text:
// 1) declare which model the item uses (any time before the client extension event)
ItemModelRenderers.register(item, MODEL_ID, null);   // third is MMD entry; four-argument overload sets a GUI scale

// 2) write builtin/entity in the item model JSON (above)

// 3) register the client extension for that item
@EventBusSubscriber(modid = "your_mod", value = Dist.CLIENT)
final class ClientSetup {
    @SubscribeEvent
    static void onClientExtensions(RegisterClientExtensionsEvent event) {
        event.registerItem(ItemModelRenderers.clientExtensions(), item);
    }
}

The library registers no items automatically: item ids belong to the content.

docs.title: 5. Who owns the display transform
docs.text:
A vanilla block item's isometric look comes from the display section of models/block/block.json. builtin/entity receives ItemTransforms.NO_TRANSFORMS, so those transforms do not apply automatically; ItemModelRenderer ships the same table:

context rotation (X,Y,Z) translation scale GUI 30, 225, 0 0 0.625 GROUND 0 0, 3, 0 0.25 FIXED 0 0 0.5 THIRD_PERSON_* 75, 45, 0 0, 2.5, 0 0.375 FIRST_PERSON_* 0, 45, 0 0 0.4 HEAD / NONE no transform

Two details:

  • ItemRenderer already applied translate(-0.5) for the vanilla [0,1] model space. This project's models are origin-centred, so the BEWLR cancels it with translate(0.5) before applying the table.
  • The GUI PoseStack is flipped with scale(16, -16, 16), so screen-down is -Y. ItemModelRenderer.GUI_DOWN_SHIFT is the per-item GUI vertical nudge.

A custom BEWLR needs both steps, otherwise the icon renders unrotated and at full size.

docs.title: 6. World path and item path are separate
docs.text:
World Item Driver ProxyInstance.tick → FsmAnimatedModel / McModelHandle ItemModelRenderer.renderByItem Instance identity ProxyIdentity (dimension+pos / UUID / external id) kasuga_lib:item/<ns>/<path>, one per item Scheduling world pass (ALWAYS / VANILLA_RENDERER) VANILLA_RENDERER only, widened for the draw State machine yes (server-authoritative + sync) no: items have no tick channel, static preview only

So an item icon shows the model's default pose; it does not follow the block's FSM state. Showing a specific state on the item requires applying fixed parameters to the ModelInstance at draw time (out of scope here).

docs.title: 7. Common failures
docs.text: Symptom Cause Checkerboard block/icon the placeholder model's texture is missing (textures/block/...) Item invisible item model is builtin/entity but no IClientItemExtensions registered Icon too large / facing the camera a custom BEWLR skipped the display table or the -0.5 cancellation A model appears at the world origin the item instance was not scheduled as VANILLA_RENDERER and the world pass drew it Wrong break particles the placeholder model's particle texture is wrong Block turns checkerboard after adding a property the blockstate does not cover the new property combination

docs.title: 8. Reference implementation
docs.text:
The two fan blocks in contentTesting are the complete sample:

File Role FanBlock.java RenderShape.ENTITYBLOCK_ANIMATED, the RUNNING property, ProxyTickers FanBlockEntity.java ProxyHost + Proxies.install; machine/model come from constructor arguments FanItemClientExtensions.java ItemModelRenderers.register + registerItem for both items blockstates/example_fan*.json two running variants, placeholder model models/item/example_fan*.json builtin/entity

docs.title: Nebula Warp Flight Demo
docs.text: Nebula is a full rendering demo in contentTesting: an OBJ starship flies through a volumetric nebula, passing through charging, jump, warp, and exit stages while the camera gradually pulls back from a close-up to a wide shot. It demonstrates how Kasuga's post-processing graph, managed MRT, OBJ/MTL loading, GPU resources, shader parameters, and a shared animation clock work together. It is not shipped in the release library JAR.

docs.title: Running and Recording
docs.text:
Requires JDK 21; recording additionally requires Python, nbtlib==2.0.4, and ffmpeg / ffprobe on PATH.

python3 -m venv build/nebula-venv
build/nebula-venv/bin/pip install nbtlib==2.0.4
build/nebula-venv/bin/python scripts/nebula-sim.py --world /absolute/path/to/test-world

The script copies the source save into an isolated client directory, defaulting to build/nebula-sim/client/saves/nebula-sim. When --world is omitted, it uses modules/modelling/run/client/saves/New World, so you must prepare a test save before the first run. The demo only starts in a private singleplayer integrated server (not opened to LAN). The player is temporarily moved high above The End and restored to their original position, dimension, view orientation, game mode, flight state, and HUD state when stopping normally or exiting the world.

Input / Command Behavior /kasuga_nebula Start or restart the showcase /kasuga_nebula warp / Space Enter warp charging during cruise phases that allow manual trigger Hold right mouse button + drag Adjust the follow camera's orbit orientation /kasuga_nebula stop / Esc Stop and restore player state F3+T Rebuild shaders, models, and textures through the resource reload chain

The demo draws no top-left control panel and keeps the lightning discharge frequency at 0.25 Hz by default. The camera pulls back between 10.5 and 15 seconds; the wide shot uses scene time and does not wrap with the 15-second warp cycle.

Full client verification and 15-second offline 4K60 export:

build/nebula-venv/bin/python scripts/nebula-sim.py --test --record-seconds 15 \
  --width 3840 --height 2160 --fps 60 --allow-slow-render \
  --timeout-seconds 1800 --output build/nebula-kasuga-migration-4k60

The CLI prints NEBULA_RENDER_PROGRESS 0%..100% and outputs nebula-sim.mp4, PNG frames, and report.json. All 900 frames use the same simulation clock, advancing 1/60 second per frame; 60 FPS is the video timebase. --allow-slow-render only disables the dev-machine GPU duration gate; frame, timing, and lifecycle checks still run.

docs.title: Code and Resource Entry Points
docs.text:
The Java demo lives in modules/modelling/src/contentTesting/java/test/kasuga/modelling/demo/nebula/, and its unit tests live in modules/modelling/src/test/java/test/kasuga/modelling/demo/nebula/.

Class Responsibility NebulaDemo Registers the shader/graph and manages the player session, per-frame input, and resource generation NebulaPipeline Declares the targets, passes, and read/write dependencies used at runtime; topology tests call the same factory method NebulaStarshipRenderer Uses the library's OBJ loader and GPU objects to submit geometry to the passed-in graph target NebulaTextures Generates noise atlases and uploads dynamic scene data to TBOBuffer NebulaSimulation / NebulaWarpSequence Unified timeline, lightning simulation, manual trigger, and warp FSM NebulaFlight Starship trajectory, wake, local coordinates, and camera curves NebulaClientSmokeTest Real-GPU pixel checks, reload, cleanup, and fixed-step capture acceptance

Resources are under modules/modelling/src/contentTesting/resources/assets/kasuga_demo/: models/constitution_starship.obj with matching MTL/PNGs, shaders/core/nebula_starship.{vert,frag}, nebula_volume.{json,vsh,fsh}, and shaders/include/. The OBJ, MTL, textures, and geometry shaders are all loaded via Minecraft's ResourceManager, supporting resource pack overrides.

docs.title: Render Pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  A[starship_geometry_pass] --> B[starship_gbuffer: 3 × RGBA16F + depth24]
  B --> C[nebula_march: hull lighting + volume integration]
  D[TBOBuffer + noise atlases] --> C
  C --> E[nebula_volume_target: RGBA8]
  E --> F[nebula_present: Kasuga copyColor]
  F --> G[MAIN]

PostProcessTargetDescriptor.colorAttachments(...) declares three half-float attachments; useDepth(true) provides sampleable depth. The target pool adapts the library's FrameBuffer through MultiAttachmentRenderTarget, allocating at the actual output dimensions. The geometry renderer owns neither its own FBO nor a second target pool.

G-buffer Slot Contents color 0 Linear base color RGB and surface mask color 1 World normal XYZ and validity flag color 2 metallic / roughness / AO / emission depth 24-bit depth; the volume pass reconstructs the hull hit distance and truncates foreground integration

The geometry pass declares writes(GBUFFER); the volume pass declares reads(GBUFFER).writes(VOLUME) and samples via colorSampler(name, context.read(GBUFFER), index) and depthSampler. Finally, context.copyColor(VOLUME, MAIN, false) presents to the main target, reusing the library copy instead of creating another present shader.

Low-level resources are managed by GlslProgram, VertexArrayObject, VBOBuffer, TBOBuffer, GpuTexture2D, and the target pool. The demo layer retains only the GL calls needed for draw state, timing, and diagnostics; generic allocation, binding restoration, and release are handled in the library. After a resource reload, the shader handle's generation triggers OBJ/PBR/noise reconstruction; on stop, the current targets are released via the graph's physical target IDs and reallocated on demand on restart. Deletion checks run immediately after release to avoid false positives from GL name reuse.

docs.title: Model and Materials
docs.text:
KsgObjLoader.loadFlatMesh reuses the existing OBJ/MTL processors and outputs a triangulated vertex stream for custom geometry shaders. Negative indices, groups/objects, and usemtl follow the shared parsing chain; missing normals fall back to generated face normals, and missing UVs default to zero. The current asset has 6,564 triangles with a 16-float vertex layout: position (3), normal (3), UV (2), baseColor/opacity (4), and emissionStrength/roughness/materialKind/padding (4). Metallic values are supplied by a data texture.

MTL Directive Nebula Usage map_Kd Imagegen base color, decoded as sRGB map_Bump Tangent-space normal data map map_Pr Demo-specific packed metallic / roughness / AO data map map_Ke Emissive data map Ke / Pr Material emissive color / scalar roughness

In this demo, map_Pr carries a packed data texture; that channel layout is a Nebula shader convention and does not imply that other OBJ renderers interpret it the same way. Texture names come from the MTL. The base color generation prompt is in imagegen-material-prompt.txt, and the remaining data textures are generated by the asset script.

nebula_starship.frag only outputs surface data; nebula_hull_lighting.glsl evaluates GGX/Schlick direct lighting and indirect light from the cloud field; nebula_warp_medium.glsl supplies non-emissive dust/smoke density. Indirect light samples cloud density and the lit field across a hemisphere while accounting for AO as a bounded-probe GI approximation. The wake alters the medium through evacuation, compression, and twin-vortex domain distortion, which is then extinguished, scattered, and composited together with the nebula.

docs.title: Dynamic Data and Parameters
docs.text:
Dynamic data uses samplerBuffer DataSampler, bound after shader apply via FullscreenPassBuilder.bufferSampler. The TBO is pinned to texture unit 7, leaving other 2D sampler units free; shared sampler JSON entries must not be treated as ordinary getUniform() uniforms.

The layout spans 384 vec4 entries (64 × 6 × 16 = 6144 bytes), uploaded in full every frame. The logical row layout is only for packing clarity; the shader reads entries with texelFetch(DataSampler, y * 64 + x) (y as row, x as column).

Range (vec4 index) Contents 0–23 / 24–25 Stern wake history positions / lightning point lights; 26–63 zero-padded 64–127 / 128–191 Lightning segment start + energy / end + width 192–223 / 224–255 Culled stars / near-camera dust motes, zero-padded 256–319 / 320–383 Twin-engine particle heads + brightness / tails + radius

RenderShaderDescriptor's ShaderParameterSchema / ShaderParameterBlock manages seven scalar parameters: InteractionStrength, IndirectStrength, SmokeStrength, CoreStrength, DetailStrength, GlobalFlash, and ShipScale. Time, matrices, and per-frame counts are still set via uniforms; they are scene inputs rather than persisted user parameters.

docs.title: Camera, FSM, and Clock
docs.text:
Only AnimationTimeline advances scene time: interactive mode is driven by 20 Hz ticks, while recording mode disables tick advance and drives it per frame via captureFrame(fps). Cloud motion, starship trajectory, wake, lightning, and camera all read the same clock.

StateMachine<DoubleSupplier> guards read the warp cycle time directly to handle CRUISE, CHARGING, JUMP, WARP, EXIT, READY, and cross-phase seeks; the FSM does not own a second playback clock. Manual triggering only adjusts the warp offset without resetting the flight trajectory or the ending camera pull-back.

Phase-driven camera motion uses CameraAnimationClip.Track, Keyframe, and the shared Easing.quinticHermite, sharing knot velocities and accelerations. The ending lens reveal uses a CameraAnimationPlayer following the scene timeline to widen the baseline 66° FOV to 74°; sampling never advances the clock. This custom Hermite easing is constructed in Java and currently has no matching custom-parameter JSON codec.

The camera retains procedural tracking and warp-specific offsets, producing a WorldCameraView. Both the geometry and volume passes share its forward, inverseView, and projection matrices so yaw/pitch/roll, FOV, and local coordinates match without rendering a second copy of the Minecraft world.

docs.title: Verification and Boundaries
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:compileContentTestingJava \
  :modules:modelling:modelUnitTest \
  --tests 'test.kasuga.modelling.demo.nebula.*' \
  --tests 'lib.kasuga.rendering.effect.post.*' \
  --tests 'lib.kasuga.rendering.models.uml.dynamic.math.EasingTest' \
  --tests 'lib.kasuga.rendering.output.camera.*'
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderGlTest

JVM tests cover the real graph declaration, MRT formats, OBJ/MTL loading, envelope bounds, timing, FSM transitions, and camera curves. The client smoke test verifies sampler bindings, pixel luminance, hull mask coverage, core/GI/texture/smoke A/B checks, near-to-wide camera motion, resize, reload generation, repeated start/stop, disconnect, and player state restoration.

Migration acceptance records are in the example README. Current GPU evidence comes from Apple M3 Max, Java 21, Minecraft 1.21.1, and NeoForge 21.1.203 with Iris/Sodium installed and no external shader pack enabled; other GPUs and enabled external shader packs require separate verification.

docs.title: Offscreen Output and Multi-Camera Rendering
docs.text:
This page maintains the interface, startup and operation reference; for isolation, data flow and synchronization principles see the explanation page. The Player, Free and Fixed categories and their creation entry points are in the camera API. The configuration of the standalone-world camera views below applies to Free/Fixed; Player shares the vanilla final main frame and the player's current configuration. The performance and client acceptance sections below keep the historical records from that time; they do not mean this documentation migration re-ran the corresponding tests.

This page corresponds to Minecraft 1.21.1 / NeoForge 21.1.203; the compatibility path actually verified Sodium 0.6.13 and Iris 1.8.12. All camera views render in order inside one client process and the main OpenGL context; multi-window uses auxiliary contexts with a shared texture to display finished frames. Camera views each own world caches, a terrain renderer, camera, projection, color/depth targets and an Iris pipeline, while the main view still takes the vanilla rendering path.

Offscreen output delivers a GPU FBO and the game tick keeps running. The headless startup entry points support a hidden desktop context and an EGL pbuffer context on Linux without X11/Wayland. A full Minecraft client and an OpenGL driver are still required; there is currently no fixed-timestep offline video exporter and no built-in video encoder, so a caller can send frames to its own compositing, encoding and transport modules.

docs.title: Dual-Camera DEBUG Startup
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaDebugDualCamera=true

# Optional: enter an existing singleplayer world; omit it to enter normally from the menu.
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaDebugDualCamera=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

The equivalent JVM switch is -Dkasuga.debugDualCamera=true. It is off by default and creates no DEBUG camera view or preview target. On entering a world it creates debug:first-person and debug:third-person, with first person on the left and third person on the right, and the window title states the left-right order. The two have separate sessions, FOV follows the user setting, size follows the window, render distance 8 chunks, Fancy, shader pack off. Third person sits 4 blocks back along the view direction and checks for wall occlusion; first person hides the player's own entity.

The DEBUG preview is the world image and contains no first-person hand or HUD. Opening a menu/inventory pauses the side-by-side compositing and displays the original screen normally. Leaving the world releases the camera views and they are rebuilt automatically the next time you enter. The main view still runs, and DEBUG compositing happens before the final screen output; while it is active, subscribing to the main view also captures the side-by-side image.

The automated check is for an isolated world copy only:

./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaDebugDualCamera=true \
  -PkasugaDebugDualCameraCaptureFrames=180 \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

After previewing 180 frames it writes debug/dual-camera.png, prints DUAL_CAMERA_DEBUG_PASS and closes the client. The plain DEBUG switch keeps running and does not exit automatically.

docs.title: Multi-Window
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaDebugMultiWindow=true

After entering a world, first and third person each get their own window and the MC main window keeps displaying. It works with kasugaQuickPlayWorld / kasugaClientDirectory; for testing, -PkasugaDebugDualCameraCaptureFrames=120 prints MULTI_WINDOW_DEBUG_PASS and exits after both paths have presented 120 frames. Off by default. DEBUG temporarily disables pause-on-lost-focus and restores the previous setting afterwards; an ordinary API caller can set mc.options.pauseOnLostFocus itself.

import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.gl.FramePreviewWindow;
import lib.kasuga.rendering.output.mc.MinecraftFrameWindows;

// Owns both the camera and the window: closing either this view's native window releases the camera.
var windowCamera = MinecraftFrameWindows.createCamera("monitor:wide", () ->
        new WorldCameraView(100, 80, 100, 0, 20, 0, 70, 640, 360), settings,
        new FramePreviewWindow.Options("Wide camera", 640, 360));
windowCamera.pause();
windowCamera.resume();
windowCamera.resize(1280, 720);
windowCamera.close();

// Owns only the window and a subscription: closing this window does not close the existing camera.
var mirror = MinecraftFrameWindows.open("capture:wide",
        new FramePreviewWindow.Options("Existing camera", 640, 360));
var mainMonitor = MinecraftFrameWindows.open(MinecraftFrameOutputs.MAIN_VIEW,
        new FramePreviewWindow.Options("Final MC + GUI", 640, 360));
mirror.close();
mainMonitor.close();

All operations are called on the MC render thread. The camera size follows the window framebuffer/DPI; while minimized the last valid size is kept. Close events are handled every frame, and a paused camera view can also be closed. A window that only subscribed keeps the last frame after the source camera view stops publishing, and the caller is responsible for closing it. Exiting MC releases the windows together and only then releases the main context.

An auxiliary window uses a GL context with a shared texture, its own read FBO and a bidirectional GPU fence. Presenting only copies the finished frame and adds no world rendering; a camera view captures once per frame and multiple subscribers share the read-only output FBO. Each auxiliary window still has its own context-local read FBO, which is only the read entry point onto the shared texture and does not allocate a separate output color texture. The main context may overwrite the next frame only after the texture read completes; no CPU glFinish is used. Every present restores MC's current context / GL capabilities. Standalone windows can be stretched, and the image keeps its aspect ratio with black bars. GLFW initialization, the global error callback and termination are still managed by MC.

This is not multiple clients: player input, ticks and the main window event loop still belong to one MC. Linux Null/EGL mode provides no native window, and calling the multi-window API reports an explicit error.

docs.title: Headless MC Launcher
docs.text:
The repository provides scripts/run-headless-client.sh and the Gradle runClientHeadless entry point. By default it uses the standalone modules/modelling/run/headless-client directory and does not reuse the everyday client. A single-player Quick Play world must already exist under that directory's saves/; an existing directory can also be specified:

./scripts/run-headless-client.sh \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/headless-client \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaHeadlessFps=60

# Or connect straight to a server; the client session's authentication requirements still apply.
./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaHeadlessServer=localhost:25565

# Gradle direct entry point for a desktop machine.
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless -PkasugaHeadlessBackend=hidden \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

This is the startup entry point for this repository's NeoForge development client; it keeps the Gradle mod/classpath configuration and does not handle account login or video encoding. Without a world/server specified it starts into an offscreen menu for a caller's client extension to control; it does not create a new world automatically.

Mode GL context Display service hidden, default on macOS/Windows a GLFW window hidden from creation needs a desktop display environment egl, default on Linux GLFW Null platform + EGL pbuffer needs no X11/Wayland/Xvfb

Before startup, prepareHeadlessClient sets earlyWindowControl = false in the chosen client directory's config/fml.toml, so that NeoForge does not display a splash before the game mixins take effect. This setting is kept in that directory. MC does not go fullscreen, the context is not displayed, vsync is not enabled and pause-on-lost-focus is disabled; the render frame rate is controlled separately by kasugaHeadlessFps (default 60). The first-time accessibility introduction screen is skipped, while game ticks, world loading, resource packs and the regular loading screens still run.

Linux needs Java 21, a C compiler, CMake, patch, curl and an EGL driver that supports desktop OpenGL. For example, a Debian/Ubuntu Mesa environment can install libegl1, libgl1-mesa-dri, build-essential, cmake, patch, curl. On first launch the script automatically downloads the pinned GLFW 3.4 source, verifies its SHA-256, applies a small in-repository pbuffer patch and compiles a shared library with X11/Wayland disabled. The build output lands in modules/modelling/build/headless-glfw/cmake/src/libglfw.so and is reused on later launches.

# Linux: the script unsets DISPLAY / WAYLAND_DISPLAY and defaults EGL_PLATFORM=surfaceless.
./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

# Pre-build separately, or deploy a precompiled library for the same architecture.
./scripts/build-headless-glfw.sh
KASUGA_HEADLESS_GLFW_LIBRARY=/opt/kasuga/libglfw.so \
  ./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaHeadlessServer=localhost:25565

# Force software rendering; only for functional verification on a machine with no GPU.
LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 ALSOFT_DRIVERS=null \
  ./scripts/run-headless-client.sh -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

The upstream GLFW 3.4 plain EGL path only selects a window surface; the patch selects a pbuffer config and calls eglCreatePbufferSurface on the Null platform only. Substituting the upstream GLFW library for this one is not equivalent. If you start Gradle's egl mode directly, you must unset the display environment variables yourself, set EGL_PLATFORM=surfaceless and pass -PkasugaHeadlessGlfwLibrary=/absolute/libglfw.so. The JVM equivalents are -Dkasuga.headless=egl and -Dorg.lwjgl.glfw.libname=..., and NeoForge's early window configuration must still be turned off before startup.

No display service still means a GL driver is required. Hardware EGL depends on driver support and render node permissions; multi-camera shader packs and large resource packs still consume the corresponding CPU/GPU memory. A hidden window or a pbuffer does not eliminate world rendering cost, and software rendering does not stand for production hardware performance.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The real client uses a world copy and an isolated directory to check shader/shadow sessions, pixel content of different material atlases, chunks and entities beyond 1024 blocks, restoration of metadata defaults, main RGB consistency, fog and state restoration, resize, pause/resume, callback closure and failure release.

./gradlew :modules:modelling:modelUnitTest :modules:modelling:renderGlTest
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaTestWorldViews=true -PkasugaTestCameraIris=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

# The path with Iris/Sodium not installed.
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaRendererMods=false -PkasugaTestWorldViews=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/vanilla-test-client

The client artifacts are debug/world-views/report.json and PNGs, with the success marker WORLD_VIEWS_SMOKE_PASS. The standalone GL regression covers final blit RGB/orientation/alpha, resize, abnormal state recovery and resource release, and needs no full MC launch.

docs.title: JFR Testing and Performance Optimization
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaTestCameraPerformance=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/performance-test-client
python3 scripts/analyze-camera-jfr.py \
  /path/to/cameras-4.jfr --output /path/to/analysis.json

The real MC runs 0, 1, 2 and 4 additional camera views in turn, then re-measures 0 at the end; each group warms up for 8 seconds and JFR profile records for 12 seconds. The additional camera views are 1280×720, 4 chunks, Fancy, no shader pack, and the main view uses the test shader pack, vsync is off and an empty consumer measures delivery. The test exits by itself; the results are the per-group JFR files and report.json in debug/camera-performance/; do not enable DEBUG or another benchmark at the same time. Each run overwrites that directory, so copy the records before comparing.

2026-10-02, Apple M3 Max, main window 1708×960, first round of comparison in the real client:

Metric for 4 additional camera views Before optimization After optimization Host frame mean CPU render 2.913 ms 2.953 ms Host frame P95 3.305 ms 3.278 ms Host frame P99 3.870 ms 3.500 ms Sum of mean camera pass durations 1.262 ms 0.945 ms Render thread allocation rate 207.31 MB/s 156.70 MB/s Cloud path allocation samples 131 12

Two optimizations were implemented from the JFR data:

  1. The Iris/Sodium hadShadersOn flag used to be global, so with the main view's shader pack on and the camera views' off it flipped back and forth, which repeatedly invalidated the cloud geometry cache. It is now kept per CloudRenderer instance and switched/restored during drawing; real-client tests covered the actual Mixin path.
  2. Gaussian sampling for fog/sky color produced a temporary Vec3 on every loop iteration. The camera views use the same kernel, sampling and addition order, accumulate in scalars and create the final Vec3 at the end. Comparing 200 fixed random positive/negative and fractional coordinates against vanilla, the double bits of all three components are identical, and the sampling order of 216 samples matches too. The main view keeps the vanilla path.

The observed allocation rate dropped by about 24% and the sum of mean camera pass durations by about 25%, while the whole-frame mean stayed flat, so there are no grounds for claiming an FPS increase. The first 0-camera-view mean was 2.900 ms and the closing re-measurement 1.601 ms, which shows clear warm-up/world activity/environment variance. The two rounds are not a statistical A/B with the world state locked, and they cover neither complex commercial shader packs, large entity scenes nor other GPUs.

Host frame timing uses RenderFrameEvent.Pre/Post and does not wait for the GPU to finish, so it does not represent full swap/present, encoding or end-to-end latency. kasuga.CameraRenderPass records world + Iris final composition and excludes the output blit/consumers; kasuga.CameraChunkSnapshot records server snapshot build/encoding. The allocation rate uses the jdk.ThreadAllocationStatistics delta divided by time; do not accumulate ObjectAllocationSample.weight, because the first sample may carry allocations from before recording started. The number of allocation samples is a pointer for locating hotspots, not an exact byte count.

The raw records are in ../modules/modelling/build/camera-performance-baseline and modules/modelling/build/camera-performance-optimized/, and are local build artifacts. The remaining hotspots are mostly biome/noise reads, terrain/entity frustum filtering and entity vertex building. Later work should re-measure in complex scenes; the full entity state sent every 5 ticks could be deduplicated further by value, but the sync semantics for returning to default values must be preserved.

docs.title: Player Motion Synchronization Fix
docs.text:
A camera view subscription sends entity state every 5 ticks, whereas the vanilla teleport handler interpolates over 3 ticks, which produces a two-tick stutter. Distant camera view entities were changed to interpolate over 5 ticks. For entities the main client already tracks, the camera view copies their position, previous-tick position, rotation and limb animation history into their own copy before each render; a player's client-side predicted movement no longer takes a round trip through the server subscription. The separate Entity/ClientLevel is kept, and FOV/render resource isolation is unaffected.

A real-client regression has the player move/turn/change walking animation continuously, and at partial tick 0, 0.25, 0.75 and 1 of 120 output frames checks that the copy's position interpolation, rotation history and animation phase agree:

./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaTestCameraMotion=true \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/test-client

This test deliberately modifies the player position inside the isolated world and restores it at the end. The success marker is CAMERA_MOTION_SMOKE_PASS, and the report is debug/camera-motion.json.

docs.title: Final Code Re-Measurement
docs.text:
After the player motion fix, vanilla distant terrain positioning and the RGBA readback interface were added, the same JFR scenario was run again (empty consumer, excluding the synchronous CPU readback cost):

Additional camera views Mean CPU render P95 P99 0, first 2.198 ms 4.053 ms 5.440 ms 1 2.033 ms 2.543 ms 2.852 ms 2 2.125 ms 2.534 ms 2.952 ms 4 2.846 ms 3.267 ms 3.878 ms 0, closing re-measurement 1.253 ms 1.479 ms 1.657 ms

With 4 camera views the render thread allocation rate is 138.14 MB/s, the sum of mean camera pass durations is 1.040 ms and the cloud path allocation samples are 14. Against the original 207.31 MB/s record, the observed allocation rate dropped by about 33%, while whole-frame time is still at a similar level; the warm-up and unlocked-world limitations above still apply. "1 camera view being faster than the first 0-camera-view run" must not be read as additional camera views speeding anything up. The records and analysis are kept in ../modules/modelling/build/camera-performance-final.

Verification summary: 625 JVM cases, 0 failures/errors, 1 skipped; 9 standalone GL check groups passed, including RGBA orientation, alpha and PBO/pack state restoration; the vanilla and Iris client multi-camera checks, the dual-camera DEBUG actual output, the 120-frame player motion regression and the final JFR test passed. The integrated server's chunk/entity subscription path was actually run; a standalone dedicated server and arbitrary third-party shader pack/resource pack combinations are outside this verification's coverage.

docs.title: Verification of Multi-Window and Headless Startup, and Additional Optimizations
docs.text:
After the new features were completed, renderingReleaseCheck passed; the JVM checks are 627 cases, 0 failures/errors, 1 skipped. The standalone GL regression is 10 groups, adding shared window texture presenting, bidirectional fences, current context/capabilities restoration, resize and independent window closing, plus Sodium-type RGBA native blit keeping RGB and forcing output alpha=1.

Actual check Result macOS MC + Iris/Sodium, multi-camera windows and mirroring an existing camera view passed; closing a paused camera view, DPI resize, other camera views continuing after one window closes Multi-window first/third person DEBUG startup MULTI_WINDOW_DEBUG_PASS macOS run-headless-client.sh hidden mode HEADLESS_CLIENT_SMOKE_PASS, main frame plus two camera view PNGs Debian 12 aarch64, no DISPLAY / WAYLAND_DISPLAY, GLFW Null + EGL HEADLESS_CLIENT_SMOKE_PASS, main frame plus two camera view PNGs

The Linux verification used Mesa 22.3.6's llvmpipe / OpenGL 4.5 and did not start Xvfb. It checked that the native window was never visible, that the context came back to its place, that there was no GL error, and that RGBA was non-empty with an opaque alpha. The main frame PNG includes the hand/HUD, and the camera view PNGs are their respective world views; JFR also recorded 80 render passes per camera view. What ran was the JVM / classpath exported from that NeoForge client configuration; the whole Gradle project was not rebuilt inside the VM. This proves that the client rendering path can run without a display service; it does not prove NVIDIA/AMD hardware EGL, Windows or all third-party shader pack combinations.

The test VM temporarily used 12 GiB of memory and a 6.5 GiB Java heap and loaded this machine's large test models, including three 16384×8192 atlases; this is not a minimum runtime memory requirement. The artifacts are kept in the ignored modules/modelling/build/headless-linux-smoke/debug and headless-linux-jfr.

Two startup/background performance issues were fixed as well:

  • GLFW Null's glfwWaitEventsTimeout is an empty function, so MC's frame limiting loop busy-waits. EGL mode was changed to LockSupport.parkNanos, and early wake-ups are still handled by the original frame deadline loop. For the same 60 FPS offscreen menu, 4 seconds of JFR each: before the optimization, 26 of 74 render thread execution samples were in limitDisplayFPS; after, 0 of 50. This is short-duration CPU sampling evidence and cannot be taken as a world rendering FPS gain or an exact CPU percentage.
  • The PBR cache key used to allocate a whole-image int[] and an equally large byte buffer for scratch, adding 8 × width × height bytes of scratch. It now chunks by 4096 pixels with 32 KiB of scratch, and the SHA-256 descriptor, size and big-endian ARGB order are unchanged. Tests cover chunk boundaries, different raster formats and subimages, and old on-disk caches stay valid. The actual memory demand of the source image, the bake result and the GPU atlas is still there.

The earlier 0/1/2/4 camera view JFR tables do not include the new window presenting cost or the synchronous CPU readback cost, so their durations cannot be applied directly to multi-window or software EGL deployments.

This is the hands-on page for the offscreen and multi-camera topic. For the output and camera contracts see multi-camera output contracts, and for the principles see offscreen output and multi-camera principles.

docs.title: Integrating Content With the Proxy Kernel
docs.text:
This guide is for mod authors who need block entities, Create devices, or external hosts to drive model animation. The target is one ProxyDefinition, one ProxySession, and one ManagedAnimationScope per element instance, with typed ports separating host, logic, and visual concerns.

Read Proxy system principles first, especially the session lifecycle, tick/frame boundary, and port definitions.

docs.title: Choose the Host Integration
docs.text:
Host condition Recommended integration A normal BlockEntity or BlockEntityType is available BlockEntityProxyDefinitions + ProxyTickers The block already has a ticker that must keep running ProxyTickers.forBlockEntity(type, existing) Client-only visuals with no authoritative machine state ProxyTickers.forClientBlockEntity(type) No Minecraft block-entity lifecycle, such as a Create train visual Direct ProxyRuntime.register / attach plus external lifecycle forwarding

Prefer the type catalog for normal blocks. Do not create a model, scope, or second tick from a block-entity constructor.

docs.title: 1. Define Immutable Input, Output, Command, and Frame Types
docs.text:
These four types are the stable contract between the host adapter and the kernel. Records or other immutable value objects are good choices.

public record MyInput(float speed, boolean powered) {
}

public record MyOutput(int committedStep) {
}

public enum MyCommand {
    TOGGLE
}

public record MyFrame(float rootAngle) {
}

Do not put StateMachine<?>, Level, ModelInstance, or a renderer in these types. They belong inside a composition or visual, not in a public port value.

docs.title: 2. Implement Ports and Assemble a Composition
docs.text:
Create a composition for each element instance. The skeleton below uses a no-op controller and no targets; replace them with the real FSM and TargetBindings when animation is required.

public static ProxyComposition<MyBlockEntity, MyInput, MyOutput, MyCommand, MyFrame>
create(MyBlockEntity element) {
    ProxyInputPort<MyBlockEntity, MyInput> input =
            host -> new MyInput(host.speed(), host.isPowered());

    ProxyControllerPort<MyInput, MyOutput> controller =
            new ProxyControllerPort<>() {
                private MyOutput output;

                @Override
                public void prepare(MyInput input) {
                    // Prepare this step's input only. Do not advance an FSM or another scope.
                }

                @Override
                public RuntimeController<Void> controller() {
                    return RuntimeController.none();
                }

                @Override
                public MyOutput output() {
                    return output;
                }
            };

    return ProxyComposition.of(
            LogicalStepPolicy.fixed(1.0 / 20.0, 5),
            input,
            controller,
            (host, value) -> {
                // Write to the host only after the scope commits successfully.
            },
            ProxyCommandPort.none(),
            ProxyVisualPort.none(),
            List.of() // Add TargetBindings when the visual needs animation.
    );
}

When a visual needs to replace models, reuse RigidPartVisualStage or DeferredModelPoseTarget; do not create another ManagedAnimationScope.

When a playback graph is needed, use the extended ProxyComposition.of(...) overload and pass initial ProxyPlaybackRoots, TargetBindings, and a PlaybackCommandApplierFactory:

return ProxyComposition.of(
        policy, input, controller, writeback,
        ProxyCommandPort.none(), visual,
        List.of(poseBinding),
        List.of(new ProxyPlaybackRoot("idle", idleBinding)),
        ScopedPlaybackCommandApplier.factory(
                Map.of("idle", idleBinding, "active", activeBinding))
);

The controller emits Play, Stop, Pause, Resume, Seek, SetSpeed, SetBoundaryPolicy, or Replace via ControlFrame.commands(). After the scope is created, the factory binds its PlaybackControlPort; ScopedPlaybackCommandApplier stages the playback registry per logical step and restores it on failure. Definition IDs and clip content belong to the caller's presentation configuration, while state-to-playback selection rules remain owned by the controller. PlaybackCommand.Play.placementStart may be negative so playback windows such as PING_PONG can continue from a committed intermediate time; it is still advanced by the same RootTimeline without creating a second clock.

Data-driven proxy_model_be uses the same Proxy path. A single model can still declare model; when loading multiple sub-parts simultaneously, declare model_groups, where each part uses a stable id, model resource, and optional local transforms. Registration builds an immutable CompiledModelGroup containing only resolved geometry and part identities; handles, ModelInstances, and playback state are created in later runtime phases. model_by_state selects a whole group ID, and every group must keep the same ordered list of part IDs so switching groups preserves kasuga:part_root target addresses and the visual layer atomically swaps the underlying model instances. Gameplay interactions and animation policies remain owned by the content mod's dedicated Block and controller.

docs.title: 3. Make the Block Entity Implement ProxySessionHost
docs.text:
public final class MyBlockEntity extends BlockEntity implements ProxySessionHost {

    private final ProxyAttachToken attachToken = ProxyAttachToken.random();
    @Nullable
    private ProxySession<?, ?, ?, ?, ?> proxySession;

    @Override
    public ProxyAttachToken proxyAttachToken() {
        return attachToken;
    }

    @Override
    public @Nullable ProxySession<?, ?, ?, ?, ?> proxySession() {
        return proxySession;
    }

    @Override
    public void proxySession(@Nullable ProxySession<?, ?, ?, ?, ?> session) {
        if (session != null && proxySession != null && proxySession != session) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("element already has a proxy session");
        }
        proxySession = session;
    }

    @Override
    public void setRemoved() {
        closeProxySession();
        super.setRemoved();
    }

    @Override
    public void onChunkUnloaded() {
        closeProxySession();
        super.onChunkUnloaded();
    }
}

The token must remain stable for the life of one element instance. A rebuilt element should get a new token; never let callbacks from the old visual control the new session.

docs.title: 4. Declare the Definition During Content Registration
docs.text:
Associate the definition with the BlockEntityType in the block/block-entity registration callback:

BlockEntityProxyDefinitions.register(
        type,
        ResourceLocation.fromNamespaceAndPath("examplemod", "my_proxy"),
        MyProxyComposition::create
);

Use BlockEntityProxyDefinitions.unregister(type) when that type is removed. Normal content code should not need to register directly with ProxyRuntime; the type catalog handles it.

docs.title: 5. Attach Automatically From the Block Ticker
docs.text:
When there is no other ticker:

@Override
public <T extends BlockEntity> BlockEntityTicker<T> getTicker(
        Level level,
        BlockState state,
        BlockEntityType<T> type
) {
    return ProxyTickers.forBlockEntity(type);
}

When the block already has a ticker, compose it and let it run first so the proxy observes the current host state:

return ProxyTickers.forBlockEntity(type, super.getTicker(level, state, type));

The first tick attaches the definition, constructs the composition, binds the visual, and enters ACTIVE. Normal ticks do not call activate() manually. A block with authoritative server machine state must not use forClientBlockEntity().

docs.title: 6. Forward Frames, Commands, and Lifecycle Events
docs.text:
Pass render frames without advancing logical time:

session.publishFrame(new MyFrame(frameRoot));

Queue host commands so they are applied at the next logical step:

session.submitCommand(MyCommand.TOGGLE);
Situation Call Element is hidden or frozen but may return session.suspend() A suspended element returns session.resume() Model/resource is not ready session.waitForResource() Resource recovered and visual must rebuild session.rebind() Element is destroyed or its chunk unloads session.close() or host.closeProxySession()

close() is idempotent and terminal. Do not use suspend() as final cleanup or reactivate a closed session.

docs.title: 7. External Host Integration
docs.text:
A Create train has no normal block-entity proxy attachment point. An adapter such as CreateBogeyProxyAdapter can:

  1. Register a temporary definition with a stable external ProxyKey;
  2. Create one attach token;
  3. Call ProxyRuntime.GLOBAL.attach(definition, element, token);
  4. Forward destroy/hide/show events to close, suspend, and resume;
  5. Call onDetach and unregister the definition on every failure path.

The external host also owns frame forwarding. Do not send partialTick through the logical tick, and do not create a session per rendered frame.

docs.title: 8. What to Test
docs.text:
Use the existing boundary tests as templates:

  • ProxyKernelTest: session ticks, frames, commands, revisions, and lifecycle;
  • ProxyKernelBoundaryTest: recovery and port boundaries;
  • ProxyTickersKernelTest: automatic first-tick attachment;
  • CreateBogeyProxyAdapterTest: external host lifecycle.

At minimum, assert that:

  • One tick advances the scope once;
  • One render frame does not increase the revision;
  • Targets in one batch share a revision;
  • The first tick attaches exactly one session;
  • Hide/suspend prevents drawing and logical advancement;
  • A failed visual replacement preserves the old visual and recovery keeps the original scope;
  • Repeated close calls are harmless.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check first Model never appears Definition registered before the first tick; type/id match; visual bound on the client Animation advances twice per tick A host, visual, or legacy ProxyInstance created another scope Frames duplicate logical events publishFrame() accidentally calls tick() or resamples an animation source Model still draws after hide suspend() hides mounted resources instead of only changing session state Host state does not update ProxyControllerPort.output() returns a non-null value; scope/writeback reports no failure Animation restarts after resource reload rebind() reuses the original session instead of rebuilding the scope An old callback controls a new element Attach tokens are not reused across element rebuilds

See Proxy principles for the system boundary and lifecycle diagrams.

docs.title: Build and Verification Entries
docs.text: Run from the repository root. The tasks below are listed with the evidence they provide; this does not mean the current documentation pass re-ran client or GPU acceptance. Model selection, configuration and output paths for a specific topic are in the matching API reference.

docs.title: JVM And Release Checks
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:modelUnitTest
./gradlew :modules:formula:test
./gradlew :modules:shader-graal:check :modules:shader-graal:assemble :modules:shader:test
./gradlew renderingReleaseCheck

modelUnitTest runs the modelling tests on a plain JVM/JUnit setup, avoiding the NeoForge dedicated-server launcher. When CMake is configured for the current platform, the Box3D native tests are included; without native build capability the matching tags are excluded. Local PMX/glTF asset tests also depend on a local fixture, so a skipped result for a missing optional asset cannot count as real-asset verification.

shader-graal:check runs real GraalJS on a plain Java 21 JVM. It compares scripted and Java-built IR, GLSL, JSON, and parameter schemas, and checks diagnostics, access restrictions, statement limits, and context isolation without starting Minecraft.

renderingReleaseCheck covers Gradle plugin tests, shader tests/assemble, shader-graal check/assemble, render-core/render-opengl assemble, the modelling JVM tests, contentTesting compilation and the jar/source/javadoc artifacts, plus library assemble. That task is not the same as running a real Minecraft world or running every standalone GL regression.

docs.title: Standalone OpenGL Harness
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderGlTest
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderPreview
./gradlew :modules:modelling:renderBench

These tasks start a standalone OpenGL context. Shaders, upload, framebuffer, GPU readback and timer queries run on the current platform; they do not by themselves prove the same results on Minecraft, Sodium/Iris or another platform. For cloud-field scene selection see Volumetric clouds API.

docs.title: Development Client
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient -PkasugaTestModel=mmd
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/absolute/path/to/isolated-client \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=world-view-test

A Quick Play save must already exist under saves/ in the isolated directory; use a dedicated test world or a copy. runClientHeadless is still a full client: hidden by default on desktop platforms, EGL by default on Linux; for driver requirements see headless API.

Content Reference MMD/glTF models, native ragdoll model runtime entry points, configuration/deployment Full GUI and pixel-by-pixel checks of the final output Frame Output Cameras, shared timeline and windows Camera Animation, multi-camera Nebula OBJ/PBR, MRT, volumetric smoke, and fixed-frame capture Nebula demo, scripts/nebula-sim.py --test; check report.json in the output directory Alpha/OIT submit order and debug buffers Alpha/OIT World UI free cursor, text, scrolling, and dragging World UI Input GraalJS shader generation, world pixels, and parameter editor Shader DSL, -PkasugaTestGraalShader=true; check debug/graal-shader/report.json Multi-layer sky and a single cloud Volumetric clouds

docs.title: Recording The Verification Scope
docs.text: A verification record should state the compile/JVM, native physics, standalone GL, real-client and platform/renderer combinations separately. Reports, screenshots and logs record the run date, hardware, configuration, task and success marker; historical records keep their original dates, and old JFR samples, a successful build or standalone-scene GPU time must not be read as the current game FPS or as an all-platform compatibility conclusion.

docs.title: Real-Asset Wardrobe Swap and MC Equipment Example
docs.text: Development example class: test.kasuga.modelling.demo.wardrobe.WardrobeExample, in the contentTesting source set. It loads user-supplied assets through the production PMX Reader, then uses only the generic Model, the assembly cache, material instances, Skeleton Anchor and the MC equipment adapters. The example code does not ship in the release package.

docs.title: Local Asset Preparation
docs.text:
Using the already-extracted test directories pack_1 … pack_9, this example picks:

Component Asset Base body pack_7/TDA Morphable Base by Ayuchan513/TDA Base Edit by Ayuchan.pmx Texture-swappable clothing pack_4/RibbonDress/Dress_ShortSleeves.pmx Colorway the asset's original Dress_Sapphire.jpg / Dress_Rose.jpg Replaceable clothing model pack_4/RibbonDress/Dress_LongSleeves.pmx, original Mist colorway Matching-skeleton assembly comparison pack_3/#1 Dress by Ayuchan513/Dress by Ayuchan513.pmx Hair pack_8/VRoid Overall Hair Presets/13.pmx, included in every outfit Held item the vanilla MC Diamond Sword; can also switch to the Iron Pickaxe

Run from the repository root:

python3 scripts/prepare-wardrobe-example.py \
  --fixtures /absolute/path/to/extracted-fixtures \
  --output /tmp/kasuga-wardrobe-client/resourcepacks/kasuga-wardrobe-local \
  --enable

The script needs only the Python standard library; it keeps the original PMX and texture content and generates six .mmd.zip archives, the matching scale=0.1 configuration and model_proxy.json. The Rose archive only swaps the short-sleeve Sapphire texture for the original Rose texture, so that a second atlas sprite is preloaded; at runtime the two copies of the garment are never rendered at the same time. --enable appends that directory's resource pack to the test client's options.txt, keeping the other resource packs; without the flag, enable it by hand in the MC resource pack screen.

Assets, resource packs, saves and reports should live in a local test directory and are not committed to Git.

docs.title: Interactive Run
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClient \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/tmp/kasuga-wardrobe-client \
  -PkasugaWardrobeDemo=true

On entering the test world, the example opens a standalone preview window by itself; the camera looks at the real model 40 blocks above the player. Only one Wardrobe session is allowed per client. You can also pass no property and run /ksglib wardrobe start after entering the world.

Command Behavior /ksglib wardrobe start Recreates the example and the standalone window; reports an error when the source is not ready /ksglib wardrobe texture blue / rose Switches the material frame on the short model, keeping the same mesh and instance /ksglib wardrobe model short / long / ayuchan Replaces the clothing model, keeping the same body and handle /ksglib wardrobe item sword / pickaxe / none Changes the held item without modifying the real player's inventory /ksglib wardrobe capture Automatically captures six stages, written to debug/wardrobe-example/ /ksglib wardrobe status Shows the current model, texture, item and assembly cache counters /ksglib wardrobe stop Releases the window, camera, equipment bindings, instance, assembly and source references

A resource reload or leaving the current world closes the session; a fresh start picks up newly published assets. Material frames do not migrate to another clothing model automatically, so this example explicitly selects blue when switching back to short.

docs.title: Automated Screenshot Acceptance
docs.text:
First create a test save in the test directory above, or copy an existing test save; for example, a save named wardrobe:

./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=/tmp/kasuga-wardrobe-client \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=wardrobe \
  -PkasugaWardrobeDemo=true -PkasugaWardrobeCapture=true

This mode does not create a preview window and captures 960×720 Free Camera output. It produces, in order:

  1. The short-sleeve original Sapphire colorway.
  2. The same short-sleeve model in the Rose colorway.
  3. Swapped to the long-sleeve Mist model.
  4. Swapped back to the already-cached short sleeves, checking that the Model object is identical and the build counter does not increase.
  5. The vanilla MC sword rendered on the real right-wrist anchor.
  6. The same render after rotating the right wrist, verifying that the weapon follows.

Each stage waits 30 frames and then takes a screenshot; the report records the image differences for material, model, equipment and bone rotation. In a new session the automated mode performs two assembly builds in total; an interactive session that has already been exercised may reuse previous cache results. The success log is WARDROBE_EXAMPLE_PASS, together with report.json.passed=true; the failure log is WARDROBE_EXAMPLE_FAIL. A successful Gradle exit does not replace that client-side evidence. The automated mode exits MC when it finishes.

RibbonDress and this base body bind their same-named bones at different positions, so the example deliberately keeps the clothing's own bind skeleton, enables no physics and runs no full-body animation; this is not automatic body fitting or skeleton retargeting. The ayuchan comparison uses the matching long dress and strictly compatible shared bones. See assembly boundaries and Anchor and rigid equipment.

This is the recipe page. The implementation and verification record for this pass, plus the local performance baseline, are in wardrobe example verification record and performance baseline.

docs.title: Blueprints and Nestable World Displays
docs.text:
WorldDisplayTarget is the client-side owner of a display subtree, bundling models, panels, and proxy controllers. ModelDisplayTarget accepts any MinecraftModelSource, including vanilla structures, Litematic, Create, and UML models. WorldDisplayScene is itself a WorldDisplayTarget, so scenes can be nested arbitrarily.

var source = BlueprintImporters.load(client.level, Path.of("building.litematic"));
var building = new ModelDisplayTarget(source).fit(3).autoPanel();
var group = new WorldDisplayScene();
group.add(building);
var root = new WorldDisplayScene();
root.add(group).transform(new Matrix4f().rotateY(.3f));

// World mount takes ownership of root, including all nested model/UI resources.
var world = SceneModels.open(client.level);
world.add(root, new Vec3(10, 80, 10));
building.stacking().secondsPerLayer(.35).play();
// Pause/resume preserve progress. play() restarts; showAll() stops and assembles.
// world.close() closes the whole subtree and removes its world panels.

fit() scales according to the model bounds; autoPanel() places a panel beside the model that moves with it. Pass absolute world coordinates to SceneModels.Entry.position(Vec3) rather than putting large world coordinates into float local matrices. Child target and parent scene matrices apply together to models, panels, and picking. Do not attach one target to two parents; cycles and duplicate ownership are rejected. Hiding a target only suppresses display; its logical clock keeps advancing.

ModelDisplayPanel can be placed in any Screen or UIBackend. It controls the same target directly—supporting replay, pause/resume, speed, stepping through non-empty layers, stack/slice mode, axis switching, and explode separation—and lists block counts below by block registry ID. Counts ignore air and aggregate different block states of the same block. Long lists are scrollable; non-block models display "No block data / 无方块数据". statistics() returns a read-only map keyed by source-local layer coordinate and does not let animated display offsets affect material counts.

client.setScreen(new WorldDisplayScreen(Component.literal("Blueprint"),
    root, building, false, false, returnAction));

WorldDisplayScreen's world parameter selects see-through world inspection or the standalone 3D viewer; ownsTarget controls whether closing the screen closes the target. Use ownsTarget=false for targets already mounted in the world, and true for a standalone viewer. The viewer supports orbit, pan, zoom, reset, and click-to-inspect block info, sizing the panel to the window. The screen only ticks roots that are not yet mounted; world-mounted targets are ticked by SceneModels. At a lower level, GuiModelPreview(target.borrowedSource()) only samples the source, and closing it only releases its own canvas.

Playback reuses ProxySession and ManagedAnimationScope: there is a single advance entry point per logical tick, and rendering never advances the clock. Before the first tick, you can attach additional controllers via target.controller(RuntimeController<Void>), such as the existing ProxyMachineController and a model FSM; controllers must use Scope checkpoints for rollback-safe state. A target exposes the existing proxy commands, lifecycle, and revision APIs via proxySession().

The local import UI is BlueprintImportScreen(WorldMount, returnAction). Open it in the dev client with /kasuga_model_preview import or via "Import blueprint / 导入蓝图" in the preview selector. After entering any local path, choose either the 3D viewer or world + panel; the input file is read-only, and on failure the reason is shown while keeping the previous world display intact.
