The default world placement distance is within UIBackend's 5-block reach, and panels can also be operated via world-UI pointer mode. In the Create factory inspection entry, "Animation + counts / 分层统计" opens the same shared control panel.

Built-in importers detect vanilla/Create structures, Litematic v5–v7, and Sponge/WorldEdit .schem v2–v3 by NBT structure (supporting both gzip and uncompressed NBT) without relying on filename extensions. Unknown formats are explicitly rejected; call BlueprintImporters.register(id, matches, decoder) to add formats. A decoder returns vanilla StructureBlockInfo entries, and layering, statistics, panels, and the viewer work automatically. Legacy numeric-ID .schematic or other formats require their own importer. For the Sponge schema, see the official v2/v3 specification. Existing bounds apply: 64 MiB input NBT, 131,072 blocks, and axis span 4,096; missing modded blocks and newer data versions are never silently replaced with air.

Verification entry points:

./gradlew :modules:modelling:test --tests '*WorldDisplayTest' --tests '*LayeredModelSourceTest'
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=run/disposable-display-test \
  -PkasugaQuickPlayWorld=display-test -PkasugaTestWorldDisplay=true \
  -PkasugaWorldDisplayOutput=build/world-display-client

The real-client smoke test runs in an isolated test save and verifies file import, per-layer statistics, real panel buttons, unchanged RGBA while paused, pixel parity between the completed stack and the assembled blueprint, nested world-panel input, and close cleanup, writing screenshots and report.json.

docs.title: World-Space Lights
docs.text:
WorldLights provides client-side dynamic point lights, rectangular area lights, and spherical volumetric lights. Each light belongs to a specific ClientLevel and uses the existing EffectRenderPipeline for visibility culling, ticking, removal, and cleanup on world switches. No lights are created by default; when no lights are visible, the scene is neither copied nor shaded by the lighting pass.

EffectHandle<WorldLight> lamp = WorldLights.spawn(level,
        LightSource.point(10, 65, 10)
                .temperature(2700)
                .intensity(30)
                .range(14)
                .build());

EffectHandle<WorldLight> panel = WorldLights.spawn(level,
        LightSource.area(10, 69, 10, 4, 2)
                .rotation(0, 90)
                .temperature(4500)
                .intensity(8)
                .range(16)
                .build());

EffectHandle<WorldLight> mist = WorldLights.spawn(level,
        LightSource.volumetric(13, 65, 10)
                .temperature(9000)
                .intensity(120)
                .range(4)
                .medium(0.12f, 0.2f)
                .build());

Import lib.kasuga.rendering.lighting.LightSource, lib.kasuga.rendering.effect.EffectHandle, and WorldLights / WorldLight from lib.kasuga.rendering.effect.builtin.light. Spawn lights after client registration completes; WorldLights.ready() reports whether the resource shader is ready. Rendering and updates are client-only; the server does not load these classes.

docs.title: Placing in a Scene and Moving
docs.text:
WorldLightTarget is a WorldDisplayTarget and can be added alongside models and UI into a nested WorldDisplayScene. Mount the scene to the world with the existing SceneModels; node positions, area light orientations, and dimensions inherit the scene and mount transforms.

WorldDisplayScene scene = new WorldDisplayScene();
WorldLightTarget light = scene.add(new WorldLightTarget(
        LightSource.point(0, 3, 0).temperature(2700).intensity(30).build()));

SceneModels models = SceneModels.open(level);
SceneModels.Entry mount = models.add(scene, new Vec3(10, 64, 10));

light.moveBy(2, 0, 0);                      // Move one light in parent scene coordinates
light.position(new Vec3(0, 4, 0));          // Set one light's local position
scene.transform(new Matrix4f().translation(3, 0, 0).rotateY(0.5f));
mount.position(new Vec3(20, 64, 10));       // Move the whole world mount
scene.visible(false);                       // Hide lights across the subtree
scene.visible(true);
scene.remove(light);                        // Close this node and remove its light
models.close();                             // Close the mount, scene, and all child lights

Call all of these APIs on the client render thread. WorldDisplayScene and WorldLightTarget live in lib.kasuga.rendering.models.mc.scene.display; SceneModels lives in lib.kasuga.scene. mount.follow(host) can reuse a SceneHost to follow moving objects; each camera view only samples the current pose without advancing scene time. When a scene closes, a node is removed, or a host disappears, the mount's lifecycle cleans up the lights. Hiding removes the rendered light instances and re-mounts them when made visible again.

Area lights preserve full rotation (including roll) and panel scale. Under non-uniform scale or shear, the falloff range and spherical medium use a bounding-sphere approximation while the emitting rectangle keeps the full affine transform. Standalone lights spawned via WorldLights.spawn also expose moveTo(x, y, z) / moveBy(x, y, z) on WorldLight (handle.effect()).

Parameter Semantics World coordinates Double-precision block coordinates. The current camera position is subtracted before GPU upload to preserve local precision far from origin temperature(kelvin) Optional approximate color temperature in 1000–40000 K; white when omitted color(new LightColor(r, g, b)) Linear RGB tint directly; overrides or is overridden by temperature (last setter wins) intensity(value) Non-negative relative intensity; 0 disables emission. Not calibrated in lumens or candelas range(blocks) Positive finite radius; smoothly attenuates to 0 at the boundary. Also acts as the medium radius for volumetric lights Area size Rectangle width and height in blocks; intensity represents radiance per unit area, so enlarging the panel increases total output rotation(yaw, pitch) Degrees; zero faces +Z and pitch +90 points downward. The rectangle's width axis rotates with yaw twoSided(true) Emits from both faces of the rectangle (single-sided by default); creates no visible fixture geometry medium(density, anisotropy) Non-negative scattering/extinction coefficient; anisotropy in [-0.9, 0.9]. Used only by volumetric lights

LightSource is immutable; replace it atomically on update so ticking and rendering never observe partially mutated state:

LightSource current = lamp.effect().source();
lamp.effect().source(current.toBuilder().position(12, 65, 10).intensity(40).build());
lamp.remove(); // or lamp.effect().close()
panel.remove();
mist.remove();

Color temperature uses Tanner Helland's approximation fit and converts the result to linear RGB; it is an artistic tint rather than a spectral simulation.

docs.title: Rendering Path and Boundaries
docs.text:
Reuses the existing shader registration, post-process graph, scene color/depth copy, fullscreen draw, and TBOBuffer. Collection and shading run at POST_PROCESS priorities 700 and 701, before the built-in water pass. All three light types are evaluated in a single fullscreen pass, uploading only the actually visible lights with no fixed count cap. Each camera view uses its own matrices, world, position, and output dimensions; rendering never advances light time.

The shader files are at assets/kasuga_lib/shaders/core/lighting/world_lights.{json,vsh,fsh}, loaded from resources and compatible with the standard resource reload flow. No new GLSL is embedded in Java code.

This is screen-depth dynamic lighting: it illuminates vanilla blocks and Kasuga models that write to scene depth, reconstructing surface normals from neighboring depth samples. Scene color approximates surface albedo; there are no separate PBR material channels, shadow maps, offscreen occlusion queries, or indirect light bounces. Consequently, walls do not cast shadows from these lights onto surfaces behind them, and translucent materials without separate depth/normals are not shaded independently. These lights do not change vanilla block lighting values and do not affect mob spawning or game logic. When a shader pack is enabled, its depth and color conventions must be verified separately.

Volumetric lights integrate across 48 steps through a spherical medium with smooth radial density, extinction, and the Henyey–Greenstein phase function; the integration range is clamped to the visible scene depth along each ray and supports the camera being inside the medium. It is not a billboard. Multiple volumes add their scattered light and optical depths without solving multi-scattering between overlapping media. Cost scales with visible light count: area lights take 16 samples per pixel, and each intersected volumetric light takes 48 steps.

docs.title: Demo and Verification
docs.text:
./gradlew :modules:modelling:modelUnitTest :modules:modelling:renderGlTest --offline
./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless \
  -PkasugaTestWorldLights=true \
  -PkasugaClientDirectory=run/world-lights-demo --offline

Each client run automatically creates a disposable world-light-demo-<timestamp> world, builds a test room near spawn, and captures 30 images across two camera views (960×600 and 480×300) covering baseline, warm/cool point lights, intensity, area light, volumetric light, combined lights, single-light movement, parent scene movement, hide, restore, close, and Blockbench exported lights before and after bone rotation and model close. Images and report.json are written to debug/world-lights/ inside the specified client directory, and the client exits automatically upon completion. Use a dedicated run directory; this demo modifies its test world.

The standalone GL regression uses the production shaders and production buffer layout to verify color temperature, attenuation, intensity, panel orientation, two-sided emission, volumetric depth occlusion, insertion order, and removal restoration, saving low-resolution pixel verification images.

docs.title: Model Collision, Chunk Lifecycle, and Distant Rendering
Animated Entity Collision
docs.text:
On the server, call collisionModel(id) on AnimationBlockEntity. For example, with example:models/gate.bbmodel, place the matching geometry at data/example/models/gate.bbmodel while the client loads the visible model from resource packs. The data-pack entry point supports Blockbench and standalone glTF/GLB, or can be loaded directly via ServerCollisionModels.find(level, id). For other formats, wrap a loaded UML Model in ServerCollisionModels.Asset and attach it to a custom block entity via MinecraftModelCollisions.attach; custom hosts call Handle.tick(deltaSeconds) (or publish()) on server ticks and close() on removal.

At load time, vertices associated with each bone are transformed from the bind pose into bone-local space to record their six extrema. Vertices with multiple positive skin weights contribute to each associated bone's bounding box. On each server tick, the server transforms those boxes by the final bone matrices and exposes Minecraft world-axis-aligned collision shapes for entity movement; rotated boxes wrap the bounds of the oriented AABB. Collisions update on game ticks, and the server syncs the shapes to players tracking the chunk for local movement prediction.

docs.title: Player Departure and Return
docs.text:
When a chunk unloads, the host releases its model instance, animation bindings, and collision handles. The client also verifies whether the original host object is still present in the live chunk cache to catch cache evictions caused by shrinking render distance. When approaching again, the client receives the chunk and block entity and mounts the model in onLoad or on the first host tick; if resources are still publishing, subsequent ticks keep retrying. By default, models are culled by the global render pipeline. Models scheduled with VANILLA_RENDERER are marked by the vanilla block entity renderer callback and drawn after the block entity pass of the same frame.

  • JVM unit tests cover host instance release, stale callbacks, first visible frame, and cross-chunk collision sync: ./gradlew :modules:modelling:modelUnitTest.
  • Dedicated-server GameTests use an armor stand to verify bind-pose collision, animated displacement collision, and removal cleanup: ./gradlew :modules:modelling:runGameTestServer.
  • The client test mounts the model and verifies collision in a temporary integrated world, teleports 512 blocks away until both sides unload, then approaches to 112 blocks and 48 blocks to verify client re-creation and restored collision: ./gradlew :modules:modelling:runClientHeadless -PkasugaTestModelLifecycle=true -PkasugaClientDirectory=/tmp/kasuga-model-lifecycle.

docs.title: Voxy and Create
docs.text:
Distant rendering shares the main view's projection and depth with terrain. When Voxy is active, models take an isolated transparency path so Voxy's terrain pass stays intact. In standalone scenes, SceneModels.distantRange(blocks) extends the distant range for statically placed models (passing 0 restores the default range); placements that follow a host still expire with their host's lifecycle.

Combined compatibility tests used Minecraft 1.21.1, NeoForge 21.1.228, Sodium 0.6.13, Voxy NeoForge 0.6.0, and Forgified Fabric API 0.116.7+2.2.0 (which requires NeoForge 21.1.217 or newer).

Every 4 game ticks, the server syncs simplified block meshes for active Create contraptions within 512 blocks of a player (up to 64 per player), following the server's rotation and translation. The client continues using Create's renderer whenever normal entity rendering is available. Distant meshes start downsampling at 2 blocks per cell and step up in powers of two to at most 64 blocks per cell for large structures (capped at 2,048 cells per mesh); block entity rendering, moving-part effects, and contraption interaction remain on the near path. Distant sync never force-loads server chunks, and removes the client's distant mesh once the contraption entity unloads or is removed on the server. This feature can be toggled via the common config enable_contraption_lod (default true).

The Create client regression assembles a real windmill at a 4-chunk render distance, verifying image and depth changes at 320 blocks away, restored entity tracking on approach, and distant mesh removal: ./gradlew :modules:create:runClientHeadless -PkasugaTestContraptionLod=true -PkasugaClientDirectory=/tmp/kasuga-contraption-lod. In a graphics environment with Voxy support, place Voxy and its dependencies in that directory's mods/ folder and add -Pneo_version=21.1.228 -PkasugaTestContraptionLodVoxy=true to assert that the Voxy terrain renderer is active.

docs.title: Carriage Vertical Posture
docs.text: KasugaLibNext's Create integration lets a carriage body move vertically relative to its bogeys: the body can bob up and down while the bogeys stay on the track. The offset is computed authoritatively on the server, sent to clients through the entity's synched data, and eased smoothly on the client. This is a system independent of the multi-bogey feature — a plain two-bogey carriage can use it just as well. For the mechanism see How Carriage Posture Works.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Create is installed and the train is assembled through a Create station;
  • the kasuga_lib common config enable_carriage_y_offset is true;
  • some code subscribes to ModifyCarriagePostureEvent to supply the posture (with no listener the offset stays 0).

docs.title: Config entries
docs.text:
Edit config/kasuga_lib-common.toml:

enable_carriage_y_offset = true
max_carriage_y_offset = 0.5
Key Default Effect enable_carriage_y_offset false Posture switch; when off, no event is posted and the offset is 0. max_carriage_y_offset 0.5 Maximum offset magnitude (in blocks, symmetric up and down); the event result and restored save values are clamped to it.
  • This is a common config: the client and the server each read their own local file; keep them consistent.
  • Defaults can be changed through the API (see "For other mods"); a value explicitly written in the config file always wins.
  • Restart the game (or wait for the config to reload) after changing it.

docs.title: Supplying the posture: ModifyCarriagePostureEvent
docs.text:
With the switch on, the server posts lib.kasuga.create.content.train.event.ModifyCarriagePostureEvent once per carriage per tick. Subscribe and return that tick's vertical offset:

@EventBusSubscriber(modid = "your_mod")
public final class CarriagePosture {
    @SubscribeEvent
    public static void onPosture(ModifyCarriagePostureEvent event) {
        if (event.getLevel().isClientSide())
            return;
        event.setYOffset(computeOffset(event.getCarriage(), event.getLevel()));
    }
}
  • getLevel() / getCarriage() provide the context; getYOffset() starts at 0, and setYOffset(float) is in blocks, positive upwards.
  • After the event returns, the result is clamped to ±max_carriage_y_offset and becomes that tick's authoritative value.
  • The client does not post the event; it eases towards the synced value at 0.5 blocks per tick, and rendering interpolates with the partial tick, so motion stays smooth between syncs.

docs.title: What it looks like in game
docs.text:
• The body (block structure and block entities) moves up and down while the bogeys stay on the rails; on a multi-bogey carriage the interior bogeys are likewise unaffected.
  • The authoritative value feeds the server hitbox and collisions: Entity#position() adds the offset, so the hitbox moves with the body; position() − getPrevPositionVec() still reflects only real movement.
  • Wheel speed is unaffected: wheels turn according to the real track movement with the offset removed.
  • The offset is written to the save with the carriage and restored on load; clients receive it by sync and ease into it.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text: test.kasuga.create.train.CarriagePostureBobDemo in contentTesting is a complete example: a sine of ±0.5 blocks with a 100-tick period.

docs.title: For other mods: changing the default
docs.text:
A mod that depends on the feature can call this from its @Mod constructor or FMLConstructModEvent:

KasugaLibCreateApi.setCarriageYOffsetDefault(true);

The default is evaluated lazily when configs are loaded, after all mods have been constructed, so there is no ordering hazard. It only affects the default: a newly generated config file, or an existing file that lacks the key. An explicit value in the file always wins.

docs.title: Behaviour boundaries
docs.text:
• only the body moves; bogey positions, wheel speed, and track geometry are unchanged;
  • the offset is carriage-level state, shared by every per-dimension entity of that carriage;
  • it is independent of the multi-bogey system; either can be enabled alone or both together (see Multi-Bogey Train Carriages);
  • keep the common config identical on client and server.

docs.title: Verification checklist
docs.text:
• With the switch on and a listener setting a value, the body bobs while the bogeys stay put;
  • a value beyond max_carriage_y_offset is clamped to the limit;
  • save and rejoin the world — the offset is restored, then recomputed by the event every tick;
  • a player joining later sees the posture, easing in smoothly.

docs.title: Multi-Bogey Train Carriages
docs.text: KasugaLibNext's Create integration lets a single carriage be assembled with more than the vanilla two bogeys: the first bogey in the structure becomes the leading bogey, the last one becomes the trailing bogey, and every bogey in between is an interior bogey that moves, renders, persists, and syncs with the carriage, following the real track geometry in curves. For the mechanism see How Multi-Bogey Carriages Work. The carriage body's vertical posture relative to the bogeys is a separate system; see Carriage Vertical Posture.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Create is installed and the train is assembled through a Create station;
  • the carriage structure captures at least 3 bogeys during assembly;
  • those bogeys are contiguous and ordered in the station's bogey list (front to back along the assembly direction), with no foreign structure or missing bogey in between;
  • the kasuga_lib common config enable_multi_bogey_carriage is true.

docs.title: Config entries
docs.text:
Edit config/kasuga_lib-common.toml:

enable_multi_bogey_carriage = true
max_bogey_offset = 1.0
derailed_on_bogey_offset_overflow = false
Key Default Effect enable_multi_bogey_carriage false Master switch: capture, assembly, persistence, sync, rendering, and angle computation. max_bogey_offset 1.0 Maximum lateral curve offset (in blocks) an interior bogey may receive; larger values are clamped. derailed_on_bogey_offset_overflow false When the curve would require more than max_bogey_offset, the server derails the train.
  • These are common configs: the client and the server each read their own local file. Single-player shares one file; a dedicated server needs the server-side file changed, and the client should match (the client owns rendering and interior-bogey angles).
  • Defaults can be changed through the API (see "For other mods"); a value explicitly written in the config file always wins.
  • Restart the game (or wait for the config to reload) after changing them.

Disabling enable_multi_bogey_carriage returns everything to vanilla: assembling more than two bogeys at a station throws train_assembly.too_many_bogeys again, and existing multi-bogey data is no longer rendered or synced and is dropped on the next save. Loading an old save with the feature disabled also treats it as vanilla.

docs.title: Building and assembling
docs.text:
1. Build one complete carriage structure along the track and place at least 3 bogey blocks inside it. Styles may be mixed and bogeys may be upside down.
  2. Build the rest of the carriage as usual; each interior bogey occupies its own part of the structure.
  3. Trigger station assembly.
  4. Result: exactly one carriage, with the first bogey leading and the last bogey trailing, bogeySpacing covering the full length, and the interior bogeys following the carriage.

If the interior bogeys are not contiguous with the ends, are out of order, or the contraption captured a bogey outside the station list, the merge is rejected and vanilla behaviour applies, usually surfacing as train_assembly.not_connected_in_order.

docs.title: Curve tracking and derailing
docs.text:
Interior bogeys are positioned and oriented from the real track geometry (Bezier turns and nodes included), so they receive a lateral offset from the carriage's straight chord that keeps their wheels on the rails:

  • the offset grows with curvature, and the part beyond max_bogey_offset is clamped;
  • with derailed_on_bogey_offset_overflow on, a curve that would need more than the limit derails the train server-side, using Create's high-stress derailment procedure;
  • right after joining, before the client has received the track graph, orientation temporarily falls back to interpolating the end bogeys; it switches to real track sampling once the graph arrives.

docs.title: For other mods: changing the defaults
docs.text:
A mod that depends on the feature can call these from its @Mod constructor or FMLConstructModEvent:

KasugaLibCreateApi.setMultiBogeyCarriageDefault(true);
KasugaLibCreateApi.setDerailedOnBogeyOffsetDefault(true);

The defaults are evaluated lazily when configs are loaded (ModConfigSpec.Builder#define(path, Supplier<Boolean>)), and config loading happens after all mods have been constructed, so there is no ordering hazard. The calls only affect the defaults: a newly generated config file, or an existing file that lacks the keys. An explicit value in the file always wins. The API does not force the feature on against a user's explicit choice.

docs.title: Behaviour boundaries
docs.text:
• Interior bogeys are not coupling points; they participate in movement, rendering, and lighting only;
  • their orientation is sampled from the real track (Bezier turns and nodes), so it stays continuous across S-bends;
  • portal clipping and lighting use the same carriage-local frame as vanilla bogeys;
  • the client receives interior bogeys over a dedicated RPC;
  • the style comes from each bogey's own bogeyData, so mixed styles and upside-down placement are supported.

docs.title: Verification checklist
docs.text:
• With the feature on, assembling a structure with 3+ bogeys yields one carriage instead of several;
  • interior bogeys roll with the carriage and follow the real track on curves and slopes;
  • save and rejoin the world — the interior bogeys are still there;
  • a player joining later sees the interior bogeys;
  • lowering max_bogey_offset with derailed_on_bogey_offset_overflow enabled derails the train on a sharp curve;
  • setting enable_multi_bogey_carriage back to false and assembling the same structure takes the vanilla error path.

docs.title: Path 1: adding content with data-driven files (organization and best practices)
docs.text:
For content authors: add blocks, items, groups, state machines, and animation clips with JSON alone, without writing Java. Applies to: Minecraft 1.21.1 · NeoForge 21.1.203 · Parchment 2024.11.17 · Java 21. Line numbers in this page refer to the current working tree (the uncommitted data-driven reimplementation), baseline commit ec864a1. This page answers "how to organize files" and "why organize them this way". The complete list of fields is not here — see schema.md.

This page is written for someone with a concrete goal in hand: adding the blocks of one carriage, wiring up a fan, setting up a creative tab. Every step gives JSON fragments you can copy as-is and spells out the cost. Anything that takes Java to do (registering the factory behind a type, registering a new top-level field) lives in guide-extension.md and is not repeated here.

docs.title: 0. Separate the three concepts first (about 30 seconds)
docs.text:
The three words each have a clear identity in this system:

  • index manifest: a manifest file of "which files to parse". It lists paths only and contains no object definitions.
  • content file: the single source of truth for definitions of blocks, items, and groups. The top-level field name (blocks, items, registry_groups) decides which handler this set of definitions is handed to.
  • domain: content files are split into two domains by when they are read. Registration phase (register) content is read once during mod construction and written into Minecraft's registries; reload phase (reload) content is read on /reload and written into the reload bucket; state machines and animation clips belong here.

How the three relate:

flowchart LR
    IDX["index manifest<br>kasuga_lib/data_driven/*.json<br>{ on_register: [...], on_reload: [...] }"]
    IDX -->|on_register| REG["registration-phase content file<br>{ blocks, items, registry_groups }"]
    IDX -->|on_reload| REL["reload-phase content file<br>{ state_machines, animation_clips }"]
    GLOB["directory glob<br>data/<ns>/state_machines/*.json"]
    GLOB --> REL

This diagram holds one asymmetry, and it is the easiest pitfall in the whole page: state_machines/ has an extra directory-glob entry point, while animation_clips/ does not — the latter's files can only be listed by the index manifest (see section 6).

The authoritative table of field names, types, requiredness, defaults, and rule IDs D1–D6 is in schema.md. The examples in this page are copied from real fixtures and can be adapted directly.

docs.title: 1. Goal: get a batch of content loaded — how to organize the index manifest
1.1 The index directory is fixed and cannot be moved
docs.text:
Put the manifest into this four-segment path; the spelling must match exactly:

data/<your mod id>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/

The path is locked down by JsonTreeBuilder.indexDirectorySegments(modId) to {"data", modId, "kasuga_lib", "data_driven"} (JsonTreeBuilder.java:745-747). kasuga_lib uses an underscore, and so does data_driven; write kasuga-lib instead, or drop the kasuga_lib level, and the system concludes you have no index directory and then does nothing at all (leaving a single DEBUG line in the log). Every .json file under the directory is treated as a manifest and read in ascending filename order; index.json is only a conventional name, not a requirement (JsonTreeBuilder.listIndexFiles, :762-774).

So do not put content files in this directory — a content file gets parsed as a manifest and reports "missing on_register/on_reload".

docs.title: 1.2 One manifest per mod, or several?
docs.text:
Both work, and you can mix them. All .json manifests under the index directory for the same mod are read in full first and then consumed together; paths are joined in the order "ascending manifest filename → written order of the array inside the manifest" (JsonTreeBuilder.java:92-96, :296-301).

The trade-off:

  • Splitting has the benefit that each feature unit can carry its own manifest fragment. KuaYue has one data/kuayue/kasuga_lib/data_driven/cXX.json per carriage; after compilation these fragments merge into the same jar directory, and the system aggregates them as several manifests of the same mod (see section 9).
  • The cost of splitting is that filenames must be unique. Once several manifests are merged, files with the same name cannot overwrite each other (they are appended side by side, not overwritten), but you have to make sure each manifest lists only its own files, or content is parsed twice (the same path listed in more than one place within one mod is silently deduplicated, with no error, parseSource's parsedSources, :400-402).

docs.title: 1.3 What goes in on_register and on_reload
docs.text:
A manifest has only two top-level fields, each a string array:

Field What it lists When it is read on_register content files that go into Minecraft's registries, such as blocks, items, and groups during mod construction, once on_reload reload-phase content files, such as state machines and animation clips on every /reload

Both fields may be omitted, but at least one must be written; a "pure reload mod" that writes only on_reload is legal (JsonTreeBuilder.java:100-104, :323-326). An empty array [] also counts as "written" (rule D2). Omitting both records one error.

A minimal two-domain manifest:

{
  "on_register": [
    "kasuga_lib_content/groups.json",
    "kasuga_lib_content/blocks.json"
  ],
  "on_reload": [
    "animation_clips/fan_fsm_data_driven.json"
  ]
}

Array elements are paths relative to data/<your mod id>/, must carry the .json suffix, must not start with /, and must not contain an empty segment or a ./.. segment (JsonTreeBuilder.validateSourcePath, :383-392). They are always joined under data/<your mod id>/, so cross-namespace is structurally impossible.

Best practice: write the groups (groups.json) ahead of the block manifest so a human can see the dependency at a glance. But this has nothing to do with "order is semantic" — the group application phase comes before blocks anyway, see section 3.

docs.title: 1.4 Why leaving a file out means it never loads
docs.text:
The registration phase has no directory scan: buildForMod reads only the paths listed in on_register and does not walk your data/ directory (JsonTreeBuilder.java:105-110). A content file that really exists in the jar still never gets read as long as no manifest lists it, and nothing is reported either.

The reload side has different rules: state_machines/ has a directory glob, animation_clips/ does not. The difference is spelled out in section 6.

The cost: the index is a hand-maintained manifest, and "adding a file = editing the index" is what this design pays for "what gets loaded is fully controllable and auditable". Change the directory structure and forget the index, and the symptom is silently loading less, not an error. That is why the first thing in the verification steps of section 8 is counting entries in the log.

docs.title: 2. How to split content files
docs.text: Content files go anywhere under data/<your mod id>/ (they do not have to be squeezed in next to the index directory), and one file may hold several top-level fields at once. Files do not reference one another, so there is no recursion and no need for cycle detection (JsonTreeBuilder.java:372-373).

docs.title: 2.1 Split by type, or split by feature
docs.text:
Both hold up; the choice depends on whether the question you need to answer is "where is everything of this type" or "where is everything of this feature".

Split by type (one big file each for groups and blocks):

data/mymod/kasuga_lib/data_driven/index.json
data/mymod/content/groups.json        # all registry_groups
data/mymod/content/blocks.json        # all blocks
data/mymod/content/items.json         # all standalone items

Split by feature (each feature directory carries its own type files):

data/mymod/kasuga_lib/data_driven/panels.json     # on_register: content/panels/*
data/mymod/kasuga_lib/data_driven/lighting.json   # on_register: content/lighting/*
data/mymod/content/panels/groups.json
data/mymod/content/panels/blocks.json
data/mymod/content/lighting/groups.json
data/mymod/content/lighting/blocks.json

The trade-off:

  • Splitting by type makes reuse and cross-feature lookup convenient (one file is the complete set for one type), but files keep growing, several people editing one file conflict easily, and nothing reminds you not to stuff unrelated things in.
  • Splitting by feature keeps one feature's changes in one place, which suits units that can be delivered on their own, such as "one carriage = one feature"; the cost is that every feature has to list its own files in the index one by one.

Best practice: take "the smallest unit that can be delivered and verified on its own" as the splitting unit. Inside a feature unit, split further by type (groups.json + blocks.json); that keeps reusability and keeps index entries readable. KuaYue's carriages are split that way (section 9).

docs.title: 2.2 More files means listing them one by one in the index
docs.text: After splitting by feature, the manifest grows into one file per line — which is exactly what it is for: the manifest is the explicit declaration of "which files this feature contains". Do not stuff a whole block of content into one file just to keep the manifest short. A longer manifest is a readability cost, a stuffed file is a maintainability cost, and the former is easier to handle.

docs.title: 3. Goal: share properties across blocks — inheritance with registry_groups
docs.text: A group is a container for shared properties: write properties on a group and the blocks in it inherit them automatically.

docs.title: 3.1 Create a group and attach blocks to it
docs.text:
{
  "registry_groups": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:base_panels",
      "properties": {
        "no_occlusion": true,
        "strength": [1.5, 3.0]
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "mymod:detail_panels",
      "parent": "mymod:base_panels",
      "item_properties": {
        "tab": "mymod:main_tab"
      }
    }
  ]
}

A block names the group it attaches to with registry_group:

{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:simple_panel",
      "type": "simple_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:detail_panels",
      "properties": {
        "destroy_time": 2.0
      }
    }
  ]
}

This passage is copied verbatim from the real fixtures modules/data-driven/src/contentTesting/resources/data/kasuga_lib/kasuga_lib_content/groups.json and blocks.json.

docs.title: 3.2 Inheritance chain: block level > child group > parent group > root
docs.text:
Properties are not "merged"; they are applied in turn along the parent chain. The parent group's properties are applied first, then the group's own, so definitions closer to the block take effect later and override what came before (Reg.applyProperties, Reg.java:103-114). Priority in one sentence:

Block level > child group > parent group > root group.

This order holds for both properties and item_properties. The real fixture inheritance_blocks.json shows three cases:

{
  "blocks": [
    { "id": "mymod:inherited_block", "type": "simple_block", "registry_group": "mymod:inherit_group" },
    {
      "id": "mymod:overridden_block",
      "type": "simple_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:inherit_group",
      "properties": { "strength": [5.0, 5.0] }
    },
    {
      "id": "mymod:item_inherit_override",
      "type": "simple_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:inherit_group",
      "item_properties": { "stacks_to": 1, "durability": 100 }
    }
  ]
}
  • inherited_block touches no property at all and inherits the group entirely.
  • overridden_block overrides the group value with a block-level properties.strength.
  • item_inherit_override overrides the group's stacks_to with a block-level item_properties, and adds a durability the group does not have.

One exception is worth noting on its own: the creative tab (tab). The group's item_properties.tab is recorded separately and used only when the block has no tab of its own (RegTypeHandler.java:89-97). So "block-level tab wins" works like most fields here, but the implementation goes through a different channel, and that is worth remembering when troubleshooting tab problems.

docs.title: 3.3 What happens with a missing parent group or a cycle
docs.text:
Both anomalies are caught and neither crashes, but the result may differ from what you expect:

  • The parent group does not exist → the group silently attaches to the root group (RegistryGroupHandler.store, :58-63). Blocks register as usual, they just inherit nothing. With no log message.
  • The ancestor chain contains a cycle → the loader does a topological sort first, and on detecting a cycle emits a WARN: Cycle detected among registry groups: [...]; the groups in the cycle fall back to their original order and end up attached to the root (JsonTreeBuilder.java:823-842).

The real fixture edge_cases_groups.json contains a ready-made cycle:

{
  "registry_groups": [
    { "id": "mymod:orphan_group" },
    { "id": "mymod:circular_a", "parent": "mymod:circular_b" },
    { "id": "mymod:circular_b", "parent": "mymod:circular_a" }
  ]
}

orphan_group explicitly has no parent and attaches to the root; circular_a/circular_b are each other's parent.

The cost and the advice: group inheritance saves a lot of repeated fields, but "silently attaches to the root" means a mistyped group id is not reported. So give group ids a namespace prefix (starting with mymod:), and make "the group definition" and "the block that references the group" appear as a pair in the same manifest, so changing an id changes both together.

docs.title: 4. Goal: know who wins on a duplicate id — last-wins
4.1 What counts as "the same id"
docs.text:
A duplicate is decided only within the same type field (blocks against blocks, items against items, registry_groups against registry_groups, embedded block entities against embedded block entities). The same name in different fields is not a conflict (DuplicateIdResolver's collision key is (typeName, identity), :73-100).

The three types compute identity differently:

Type What identity is Normalization blocks / items the ResourceLocation at registration no namespace or a minecraft: prefix → <your mod id>:<path>; any other namespace is kept as-is (EffectiveId.of, :39-52) registry_groups the entry's literal id, not normalized groups are internal nodes and do not go into a registry, so door and minecraft:door count as two groups (RegistryGroupHandler.resolveIdentity, :50-52) the embedded block entity the identity of the host block only two block_entity keys on the same block count as a duplicate (BlockEntityTypeHandler.resolveIdentity, :66-68)

Normalization is the easiest one to trip over: as blocks, foo and minecraft:foo are the same id and conflict with each other (EffectiveIdTest.explicitMinecraftNamespaceResolvesToTheOwningMod). But foo in blocks and foo in items do not conflict; they are two registration spaces.

docs.title: 4.2 "Later" means load order, not lexicographic order
docs.text:
The rule for duplicates is last-wins (the later definition wins). "Who is later" is decided entirely by load order:

  1. Several manifests of the same mod, by ascending filename;
  2. Inside one manifest's on_register array, by written order;
  3. Inside one content file's type array, by written order.

DuplicateIdResolverTest.lastMeansLastInSequenceNotLexicographicallyLastSource locks this down specifically: even when the later candidate comes from a file whose path sorts earlier lexicographically, it is still the winner. In other words, order is a semantic switch, not a layout preference.

docs.title: 4.3 Conflicting entries: isolated, no crash
docs.text:
When a duplicate is found (DuplicateIdResolver.describe, :109-115):

  • No crash: loading finishes as usual and the game starts normally.
  • The loser does not take effect at all: the earlier definition never reaches registration, so no ghost entry is left in Minecraft's registries.
  • No collateral damage: only the conflicting entry is dropped; other entries in the file and other types proceed as usual.
  • Evidence is kept: one WARN log line (giving the id, the type field, and the winner's and the loser's source files) plus one loading error recorded against that mod.

Best practice: treat order as an "override switch", not as "layout". When you have no intent to override, make sure ids are unique within the type and keep the WARN away; when you do intend an override (a base file plus a variant file), point out which one is the patch file in the manifest with a comment or a name. The cost is that such an override tells you nothing about "who got overridden" beyond that WARN, so override files should be as small and focused as possible.

docs.title: 5. Goal: bind a block entity to a block — how to use an embedded type
5.1 The block entity is embedded, not a top-level field
docs.text:
A block entity (BE) does not get a top-level field of its own; it is written in the block_entity key of the block entry:

{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:be_test_block",
      "type": "be_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:data_driven_group",
      "block_entity": {
        "type": "my_be",
        "params": {
          "tick_interval": 4
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

(from kasuga_lib_content/block_entities.json.) block_entity accepts type (the BE factory) and params; after the host block is registered, the system creates the BE automatically and attaches it as its child node, and the BE id is automatically <block path>_be. So a block can embed at most one BE (BlockEntityTypeHandler.apply, :88-95).

FSM blocks have a common pattern: state_machine is written at the top level of the block entry, and the system forwards it into the BE's params:

{
  "blocks": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:my_fsm_block",
      "type": "fsm_block",
      "registry_group": "mymod:data_driven_group",
      "state_machine": "mymod:my_machine",
      "properties": { "destroy_time": 2.0 },
      "block_entity": {
        "type": "fsm_be",
        "params": { "model": "mymod:models/my_cube.obj" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

(from modelling contentTesting's fsm_blocks.json; the forwarding logic is in BlockEntityTypeHandler.extractEmbedded, :33-44, covered by BlockEntityStateMachineExtractTest.)

docs.title: 5.2 "In the same file" or "in its own file"
docs.text:
The filename block_entities.json is a convention, and its top-level key is still blocks once you open it. So the choice here is file organization, not syntax:

  • Keeping blocks with BEs together with ordinary blocks puts the whole block picture in one place, which is convenient for comparison.
  • Opening a separate file (such as block_entities.json) for blocks with BEs shows "which blocks have entities" at a glance, and lets this kind of block evolve on its own.

Either choice must list the file in the manifest. The trade-off is review cost: a separate file makes the BE set stand out, but seeing "a block's full definition" then takes two files.

docs.title: 5.3 Anti-pattern: writing an embedded type as a top-level field
docs.text:
The following form is illegal:

{
  "block_entities": [ { "type": "my_be" } ],
  "blocks": [ { "id": "mymod:ok", "type": "simple_block" } ]
}

The result: the top-level block_entities is reported as an "unsupported top-level field", with the hint "it should be written in the block_entity key of a blocks entry"; the key point is that blocks in the same file still dispatches as usual (partial-apply), so this one mistake does not throw away the whole file (JsonTreeBuilderEmbeddedTypeDispatchTest.topLevelEmbeddedTypeIsReportedAndTheRestOfTheFileStillDispatches, JsonTreeBuilder.java:475-490).

Likewise, a single BE failing in the apply phase (a missing BE factory, for example) only emits a WARN and is skipped, leaving the other blocks in the same file alone (BlockEntityTypeHandler.apply, :81-100).

Best practice: always write block_entity next to its host block. A BE has no id of its own, so an "orphan BE" does not exist syntactically.

docs.title: 6. Goal: add state machines and animation clips — reload-domain content
docs.text: The reload domain has two kinds of content, and their top-level field names are each the only legal key.

docs.title: 6.1 State machines (state_machines): two entry points
docs.text:
A state machine file looks like this:

{
  "state_machines": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:fan_machine",
      "state_vars": [
        { "name": "cycle", "type": "bool", "default": false, "ephemeral": true, "reference": "mymod:fan/cycle" }
      ],
      "layers": [
        {
          "id": "gear",
          "mode": "base",
          "initial_state": "off",
          "states": [
            { "id": "off", "clip": { "id": "mymod:fan_clip", "loop": true } },
            { "id": "g1", "clip": { "id": "mymod:fan_clip", "loop": true } }
          ],
          "transitions": [
            { "id": "off_to_g1", "from": "off", "to": "g1", "trigger_on": "cycle", "cross_fade_seconds": 0.25 }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

(the full version of the real fixture modules/modelling/src/contentTesting/resources/data/kasuga_lib/state_machines/fan_machine_data_driven.json has 4 states and 4 transitions; a subset is taken here for space, with no field changed.)

A state machine has two entry points; use either one or both:

  1. Directory glob: put the file at data/<your namespace>/state_machines/*.json and it is discovered automatically (StateMachineDefinitionLoader.PATH = "state_machines", :39; the directory is declared by FsmReloadHandler.globDirectories(), :69-71). No need to list it in the index.
  2. The on_reload array: list the path in the manifest and it is read as well.

When both entry points hit the same file, the glob skips the one the index already lists, so the file is read once (ReloadOrchestrator.collectGlob, :348-367). The relative order of the two entry points is glob first, index second, and for the same id the later one still wins (ReloadOrchestrator class documentation, :77-91).

docs.title: 6.2 Animation clips (animation_clips): the index is the only entry point
docs.text:
{
  "animation_clips": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:fan_clip",
      "duration_seconds": 12.0,
      "formula_transforms": [
        {
          "target": { "bone": "fan" },
          "transform": { "rotate": { "y": "11 * query.angle" } }
        },
        {
          "target": { "bone": "cover" },
          "transform": { "rotate": { "z": "sin(rad(2 * query.angle)) * 30" } }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

(from animation_clips/fan_fsm_data_driven.json.)

The same formula_transforms list may also drive a rigid part or a bone inside a part:

{
  "animation_clips": [
    {
      "id": "mymod:mechanism",
      "variables": [
        { "name": "mechanism.angle", "expression": "rad(query.wheel_angle)" }
      ],
      "formula_transforms": [
        {
          "target": { "part": "part_06" },
          "transform": {
            "translate": { "z": "sin(mechanism.angle)" },
            "rotate": { "x": "-query.wheel_angle", "y": "180" }
          }
        },
        {
          "target": { "part": "part_06", "bone": "pin" },
          "transform": { "rotate": { "z": "query.pin_angle" } }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

variables are evaluated in declaration order. target.part drives an entire rigid part, while target.bone drives a bone inside that instance. A host uses FormulaTransformSampler to compile the expressions and bind the resulting FormulaTransformPose to model motion.

animation_clips/ has no directory glob, so clip files can only be read through the manifest's on_reload array (AnimationClipLoader class documentation, :28-29). Put a clip file under data/<ns>/animation_clips/ and forget to list it in the manifest, and it is never loaded, with no hint at all.

Compare the real fixture modelling.json, which lists two entries under on_register and one under on_reload:

{
  "on_register": [
    "kasuga_lib_content/fan_formula_data_driven.json",
    "kasuga_lib_content/fsm_blocks.json"
  ],
  "on_reload": [
    "animation_clips/fan_fsm_data_driven.json"
  ]
}

The state machine file state_machines/fan_machine_data_driven.json is not in this manifest — the glob picks it up. fsm_blocks.json originally belonged to data-driven's contentTesting, and moved to the modelling side because the fsm_block / fsm_be factories live in modelling only (the content is still written with blocks as its top-level key).

docs.title: 6.3 A few rules for reload content
docs.text:
• One file can carry several top-level keys: writing state_machines and animation_clips in the same file is legal, and the two handlers each read their own key and register their own entries (ReloadOrchestrator.dispatch, :429-470). A genuinely unknown key (claimed by no reload type, a mistyped foo for instance) is reported as an unsupported-top-level-field error, but known keys still contribute as usual and do not drag down the whole file.
  • Reload paths go through the pack stack: paths in on_reload are resolved with ResourceManager.getResource, so data packs can override your reload content; on_register goes through the mod's jar (IModFile.findResource), which data packs cannot reach (ReloadOrchestrator.collectIndex, :369).
  • Dangling clip references are checked after the fact: once a reload round finishes, the loader checks whether the id that states[].clip points at exists in every state machine definition just registered, and if it is missing it emits a WARN and records it in the error bucket, while that state degrades to a static pose (FsmReloadHandler.afterReload, :95-116). The check does not block registration.

Best practice: keep state machines in state_machines/ for the glob to discover, which cuts manifest maintenance; clips must be listed in on_reload one by one, so make clip files coarser rather than finer (one file per feature) instead of letting the manifest grow to dozens of lines.

docs.title: 7. Anti-patterns and boundary checklist
docs.text:
What you write Symptom Cause / handling "sources": [...] in a manifest two errors: contains unsupported field 'sources' + declares neither 'on_register' nor 'on_reload', and that manifest contributes no path sources is a deprecated field, not an alias (JsonTreeBuilder.parseIndexManifest, :222-243; JsonTreeBuilderIndexSchemaTest.legacySourcesFieldIsReportedAsUnknown). Change it to on_register listing a state_machines file under on_register error: unsupported top-level field 'state_machines', with the hint "list this file under 'on_reload' instead" the conditional D9 hint; the registration domain does not recognize a reload-domain shape, and the hint points you at the other array (JsonTreeBuilder.java:474-491; JsonTreeBuilderReloadHintTest) listing registration content under on_reload error: unsupported top-level field 'blocks', with the hint to list it under on_register the reverse D9 hint (ReloadOrchestrator.dispatch, :441-446) the same path in both on_register and on_reload error, and that path is consumed by neither domain rule D6's fail-closed (JsonTreeBuilder.resolveIndexManifests, :308-316; JsonTreeBuilderIndexSchemaTest.crossListedPathIsConsumedByNeitherDomain) a top-level block_entities error + the hint to write it in the block_entity key of a blocks entry embedded types do not take a top-level field (section 5.3) a path written as /blocks.json, blocks (no suffix), a/../b.json error: path must be relative / path must include the '.json' suffix / path must not contain '.' or '..' validateSourcePath (:383-392; JsonTreeBuilderSourcePathTest.rejectsMalformedSourcePaths) the manifest points at a file that does not exist error: Source file not found ... the path is relative to data/<mod>/; first confirm the file really made it into the jar a content file placed in the index directory error: the file is parsed as a manifest and reports the two domain fields as missing the index directory holds manifests only a block type with no corresponding factory and no state_properties the block does not appear; log WARN No factory for type '...' log only, not into the error bucket (RegTypeHandler.apply, :70-74). The factory must be registered first, see guide-extension.md a block referencing a registry_group that does not exist the block still appears, but its properties/tab do not match expectations silently attaches to the root group, no log (section 3.3) a misspelled property name (such as sound_type) that property is ignored; log WARN Unknown block property / Unknown sound type log only, not into the error bucket (JsonPropertyParser, :50-57, :87-95) an element's parse throws during the registration phase (malformed fields in that element) error: Content file '<label>' for mod '<mod>': entry <i> in '<key>' failed to parse: <msg>; entry skipped only that element is dropped; sibling entries in the same file register as usual (JsonTreeBuilder.java:530, 592; isomorphic to the reload side's …; element skipped).

Best practice: distinguish "errors that go into the error bucket" from "errors that only emit a WARN". The former (index, path, field, duplicate id, apply failure) can be asserted red through getLoadingErrors; the latter (unknown factory, unknown property, missing group, group cycle) can only be found by reading the log. Lumping the two together will make you miss the second half of the problems.

docs.title: 7.1 Data-driven does not generate assets or localization
docs.text:
Data-driven registers the block / item / block entity itself only (blocks entries have no model / textures field, see schema.md section 2.3). For a block to display properly, its model, texture, and language still have to be provided in the resource pack following vanilla conventions, and the system does not generate them for you:

  • Model / texture: looked up following Minecraft conventions at assets/<namespace>/blockstates/<path>.json and assets/<namespace>/models/block/<path>.json, and you must supply them by hand; leave them out and you get a purple-and-black block.
  • Translation key: derived by convention as block.<namespace>.<path> (item.<namespace>.<path> for items), and you must add it in lang/*.json by hand; leave it out and the raw key name is displayed.

docs.title: 8. Goal: confirm you got it right — verification and troubleshooting
8.1 Count the entries in the log first
docs.text:
After startup the log should contain this line (INFO):

Loaded N JSON entries across M types for mod '<your mod id>'

JsonTreeBuilder.java:114. N is the total number of entries parsed, and M is the number of distinct top-level types with content. Turn DEBUG on and you also see the applied count per type (Applying N entries for type '<type>', :129). An N that is too small usually means a missed index entry or a wrong path. If the line is entirely absent, check the index directory path first (when the directory does not exist there is only one DEBUG line: No data-driven index directory for mod '...', :77).

docs.title: 8.2 Inspect the error bucket with a command
docs.text:
In game (permission level 2 required):

/kasuga_data errors
/kasuga_data errors <your mod id>

With no argument it prints a one-line summary for every non-empty bucket (both dimensions included: the mod dimension and the reload RELOAD_DATA[<namespace>] source dimension); with a mod id it prints that mod's per-entry failures in both dimensions (DataDiagnosticsCommands, :45-92). Registration-phase errors go into the mod dimension; reload-phase errors go into the Domain.RELOAD_DATA source dimension, keyed by namespace (ReloadOrchestrator.reportError, :566-573).

docs.title: 8.3 Assert in a test that the error bucket is empty
docs.text:
An integration test or a debugging tool can assert directly:

JsonTreeBuilder.getLoadingErrors("mymod")   // this mod's list of errors
JsonTreeBuilder.getLoadingErrorsByMod()     // bucketed by mod

Turning "silent errors" into a red light is the least-effort approach. Error buckets are isolated per mod, and one mod's buildForMod clears only its own bucket (JsonTreeBuilderLoadingErrorTest.errorsAreIsolatedPerMod).

docs.title: 8.4 A troubleshooting order table
docs.text: Symptom Look first at no Loaded ... JSON entries at all is the index directory's four-segment path right? is there a .json in the directory? N smaller than expected is the manifest missing an entry? Source file not found? the block does not appear No factory for type? (WARN); are the block item, blockstate, and model assets all present? properties are wrong Unknown block property (WARN); is registry_group written correctly (silent attach to root)? an id takes effect as something other than what you wrote the duplicate-id WARN; look at the winner/loser source files (section 4) the state machine does not take effect is the file in state_machines/? or is it listed in on_reload? the clip does not take effect almost always it is not listed in on_reload — clips have no glob (section 6.2) the state machine runs but the animation is frozen look for the unresolved clip references after reload WARN (section 6.3)

docs.title: 9. Production-scale reference: how KuaYue organizes carriages
docs.text:
This section only observes the KuaYue repository's modules/train-parts/resources/carriages/ read-only; nothing is modified.

KuaYue's 11 carriages (22/25/25b/25g/25k/25t/25z/cr200j/freight/jy30/m1) show what "split by feature, each feature carrying its own manifest fragment" looks like in a real project. Each carriage is an independent resource-compilation module, and its source directory top level holds blockstates/, data/, lang/, loots/, models/, recipes/, tags/, textures/ and module.toml — there is no assets/; only after resource compilation does it merge into the assets//data/ layout in the output. Model assets, localization, loot tables, and data-driven content are delivered together inside the same carriage directory.

scripts/ is a generic passthrough category: scripts/packages/... inside a module is copied unchanged to the resource root at scripts/packages/..., without JSON merging or any other transformation. It is suitable for JavaScript packages delivered with a feature module; modules without scripts do not need this directory.

For the data-driven part there are three files per carriage (exception: jy30 has module.toml but no data-driven content at all, so it does not take part in data-driven):

carriages/22/
├── module.toml                                              # module root marker
└── data/kuayue/
    ├── kasuga_lib/data_driven/c22.json                      # index manifest (one per carriage)
    └── carriages/c22/
        ├── groups.json                                      # this carriage's groups
        └── blocks.json                                      # this carriage's blocks

The manifest content is "groups first, blocks after":

{
  "on_register": [
    "carriages/c22/groups.json",
    "carriages/c22/blocks.json"
  ]
}

The group (c22):

{
  "registry_groups": [
    {
      "id": "kuayue:c22_panels",
      "properties": {
        "no_occlusion": true,
        "strength": [1.5, 3.0],
        "map_color": "blue"
      },
      "item_properties": { "tab": "kuayue:train_panel_tab" }
    }
  ]
}

The blocks (c22, excerpt):

{
  "blocks": [
    { "id": "kuayue:22_floor", "type": "slab", "registry_group": "kuayue:c22_panels" },
    {
      "id": "kuayue:22_large_window",
      "type": "train_openable_window",
      "params": { "wide": 2 },
      "registry_group": "kuayue:c22_panels"
    }
  ]
}

How it is split, and why:

  • The splitting unit is one carriage, because a carriage can be delivered and verified on its own, and the whole carriage's assets (models, language, block definitions) travel together anyway.
  • One manifest per carriage (c22.json, c25.json, …; the filenames all differ). At compile time they merge into the same jar directory, and the framework aggregates them as several manifests of the same mod. This answers exactly the question in section 1.2: "several manifests per mod" in production is split by delivery unit.
  • Inside a carriage, split further into two files by type (groups.json + blocks.json) rather than stuffing groups and blocks into one — that keeps the readability of "split by type" while putting groups before blocks, matching the framework's "groups are applied first" phase order.
  • A block's type is a factory KuaYue registers itself (slab, train_panel, train_openable_window, and so on), not one of the library's built-in test factories — this is exactly the extension point described in guide-extension.md used in production.

A lesson unrelated to data-driven content, but one that makes content "vanish into thin air": the two carriage directories cr200j and freight have no module.toml. The resource compiler only walks directories that contain module.toml (ResourceCompilerMain.java:24-39; ResourceScanner.scanModule, :43-58), so the content in these two directories (index and data-driven files included) never makes it into the jar, and the blocks in them are never registered. Transferring this to your own project: even with the manifest written correctly, confirm that the directory carrying it is really picked up by your resource compilation/packaging pipeline. compileResources clears its generated output before every run, so deleting or moving a source resource also removes its old jar entry.

docs.title: 10. Further reading
docs.text: What you want Where to go the complete list of fields, types, requiredness, defaults, and D1–D6 rules schema.md complete signatures of Java classes and methods, load timing, and the pure-function test surface the data-driven API reference getting the first path working from scratch intro.md registering your own type factory, property compiler, and TypeHandler guide-extension.md a dedicated explanation of the FSM state machine ../../reference/fsm.md

docs.title: Extension guide: what you have to write Java for (How-to)
docs.text:
For mod developers who want to give data-driven new capabilities. Readers need a working path first (see intro.md) and a basic grasp of the JSON format (see schema.md). This page covers only the extension points that have to land in Java, and every section is organized as "goal → code → why": adding a top-level type, an embedded type, registering a factory, extending property parsing, wiring into diagnostics, adding a reload content type, and how to write tests. Boundaries: for per-class and per-method signatures see api-registration.md / api-extension.md / api-diagnostics.md / api-reload.md; for content organization expressible in pure JSON (groups, blocks, items, index writing, the property cheat sheet) see guide-content.md; for field-level JSON rules and D1–D6 see schema.md. This page repeats neither the signature tables nor the JSON field rules.

Version baseline: Minecraft 1.21.1 / NeoForge 21.1.203 / mojmap + Parchment 2024.11.17 / Java 21. Line numbers in the text correspond to the file contents in the current working tree (the uncommitted data-driven reimplementation), baseline commit ec864a1; signatures follow api-registration.md / api-extension.md / api-diagnostics.md / api-reload.md.

docs.title: 0. Decide first: does this need Java?
docs.text:
Data-driven has two extension surfaces: JSON content, and capabilities JSON cannot recognize. Only the latter needs Java. Match your case in the table below:

flowchart TD
    A["What do you want to add?"] -->|"A different block/item/entity under an existing top-level type"| B["Register a factory<br/>FactoryRegistry"]
    A -->|"A new key for properties / item_properties"| C["Register a property compiler<br/>JsonPropertyParser / JsonItemParser"]
    A -->|"A brand-new top-level field in a content file"| D["Add a TypeHandler<br/>TypeHandlerRegistry"]
    A -->|"One more content type at reload time"| E["Implement and register a ReloadHandler"]
    A -->|"None of the above, you just want to write more blocks"| F["No Java needed<br/>see guide-content.md"]
Your goal Extension point Does the result need to go into a Minecraft registry Where in this page "type": "my_door" produces a block FactoryRegistry.register Yes §3 "type": "my_material" produces an item FactoryRegistry.registerItem Yes §3 "type": "my_be" attaches a block entity FactoryRegistry.registerBlockEntity Yes §3 A custom non-MC-registry object (effect, definition, ...) FactoryRegistry.registerGeneric + a custom TypeHandler No §1, §3 mymod:my_key appears in properties JsonPropertyParser.registerCompiler — §4 "my_things": [...] appears at the top level of a content file Implement and register a TypeHandler Depends on the definition §1 A block embeds "my_attach": {...} Embedded TypeHandler — §2 One more "xxx": [...] file is read after reload Implement and register a ReloadHandler — §6 Expose an extension's failures to ops/tests Diagnostics / JsonTreeBuilder.addLoadingError — §5

The factory classes used as examples, DataDrivenTestFactories and FanDataDrivenFactories, both live in their modules' contentTesting source set. Such content loads as a mod at test runtime but does not go into the published jar; a real mod puts its factories in its own src/main/java. See §8.

docs.title: 1.1 Goal
docs.text: Let a new top-level field appear in a content file, for example "my_definitions": [ {...}, {...} ], interpreted by your Java code. The system dispatches arrays to the matching TypeHandler by top-level field name: in the registration phase this happens in JsonTreeBuilder.dispatchContent, which walks TypeHandlerRegistry.all() (JsonTreeBuilder.java:492-513), and the field name is getTypeName().

docs.title: 1.2 Pick a shape first
docs.text:
Two shapes; decide which one you are taking:

  • It produces a Reg (goes into an MC registry): extend RegTypeHandler<T> (handler/RegTypeHandler.java:15). It bakes in the template "split the id → look up the factory → attach namespace/group/creative tab → store into the context" (RegTypeHandler.apply:63-112), so you implement only two abstract methods. blocks / items are written this way.
  • It produces no Reg (a pure data definition, or an object obtained through FactoryRegistry.registerGeneric): implement TypeHandler<T> directly (TypeHandler.java:8) and handle things yourself in apply. TestGenericFactory in the tests takes this route (TestGenericFactory.java:51-73).

docs.title: 1.3 Skeleton (Reg-shaped, lifted from the RegTypeHandler template)
docs.text:
The class below compiles as-is (EffectDef is only a placeholder definition). It is shaped after BlockTypeHandler (handler/BlockTypeHandler.java:16-64), with just the factory lookup step swapped for a Generic factory. To save space, code blocks from here on omit imports, and every symbol involved is given a source:

package com.example.mymod.data;

import com.google.gson.JsonObject;
import lib.kasuga.registration.Reg;
import lib.kasuga.registration.data_driven.handler.RegTypeHandler;
import lib.kasuga.registration.factory.FactoryRegistry;

public final class EffectTypeHandler extends RegTypeHandler<EffectTypeHandler.EffectDef> {

    /** The product of parse: an immutable definition object. Fields come from JSON, no side effects. */
    public record EffectDef(String id, String type, JsonObject params) {}

    @Override
    public String getTypeName() { return "effects"; }   // the top-level field name this handler claims

    @Override
    public int getPhase() { return PHASE_CONTENT; }     // see 1.5

    @Override
    public EffectDef parse(JsonObject json) {
        return new EffectDef(
                json.get("id").getAsString(),
                json.get("type").getAsString(),
                json.has("params") ? json.getAsJsonObject("params") : null);
    }

    @Override
    protected String resolveRawId(EffectDef definition) { return definition.id(); }

    /** Diagnostics show the JSON `type` value (such as my_effect), not the top-level field name effects. */
    @Override
    protected String resolveType(EffectDef definition) { return definition.type(); }

    @Override
    protected Reg<?, ?> createRegistration(EffectDef definition, String path) {
        FactoryRegistry.GenericFactory factory = FactoryRegistry.getGeneric(definition.type());
        if (factory == null) return null;    // returning null means "no factory"; the framework warns and skips (see §3.4)
        return factory.create(path, definition.params());
    }
}

path has already been stripped out of the id by the template and carries no namespace (RegTypeHandler.resolvePath:43-46); do not prepend a namespace again in the factory.

The pure-data shape can be shorter. It stores the definition in the BuildContext metadata slot for other handlers to look up (BuildContext.putMeta:22):

public final class MyDefinitionHandler implements TypeHandler<MyDefinition> {

    @Override public String getTypeName() { return "my_definitions"; }
    @Override public int getPhase() { return PHASE_GROUPS; }   // referenced by other content, so apply it first

    @Override public MyDefinition parse(JsonObject json) {
        return new MyDefinition(json.get("id").getAsString());
    }

    @Override public void apply(MyDefinition definition, BuildContext context) {
        context.putMeta(getTypeName(), definition.id(), definition);
    }

    /** Only a non-null result takes part in duplicate-id deduplication; the default null opts out. */
    @Override public String resolveIdentity(String modId, MyDefinition definition) {
        return definition.id();
    }
}

docs.title: 1.4 How parse and apply divide the work
docs.text:
• parse(JsonObject) takes one JSON object from the array and returns your definition object. It should be a pure function: no registration, no mutation of global state, no dependence on call order.
  • apply(T, BuildContext) is what performs registration. It is batched by getPhase() and called after every file has been parsed (JsonTreeBuilder.buildForMod:61).

Splitting it this way has two concrete reasons:

  1. Duplicate ids are decided before apply. All entries are parsed first, resolveDuplicates uses resolveIdentity to find duplicates, and only the winner enters apply (JsonTreeBuilder:119, 652). The losing entries have also been parsed. So if parse has side effects, the losing entries take effect with their side effects.
  2. The same data may be referenced by several files/manifests; parse is the collection stage, apply the execution stage. Separating them lets deduplication and diagnostics happen inside one "side-effect-free window".

docs.title: 1.5 Choosing a phase
docs.text:
apply does not follow file order; it is batched in ascending getPhase() order (JsonTreeBuilder:119-121). The three constants are defined in TypeHandler.java:11-17:

Constant Value Use Reference implementation PHASE_GROUPS 0 Objects created first and referenced later RegistryGroupHandler (getPhase:23) PHASE_CONTENT 1 Regular content (blocks, items) BlockTypeHandler (:22) / ItemTypeHandler (:19) PHASE_EMBEDDED 2 Embedded types attached to a parent object BlockEntityTypeHandler (:24)

Almost every new type uses PHASE_CONTENT. If it gets looked up by id from later content, the way a group does, use PHASE_GROUPS; if it has to land after a parent object, the way a block entity does, use PHASE_EMBEDDED, together with §2.

Within the same phase the order is registration order (a stable Comparator sort); across phases the value order always holds. So do not guess "who comes first" from file order — guarantee it through getPhase or through lookups in BuildContext.

docs.title: 1.6 Registering the handler
docs.text:
TypeHandlerRegistry is a global static table, written with register and indexed by getTypeName() (TypeHandlerRegistry.java:11-17). The four built-in handlers are lazily registered once by JsonTreeBuilder.ensureHandlersRegistered() (JsonTreeBuilder:49-56); your handler must register itself, and it has to do so before the index is read:

@Context                                        // Micronaut eagerly initializes this
public class MyModDataDriven {

    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        TypeHandlerRegistry.register(new EffectTypeHandler());
    }
}

The @Context + @PostConstruct timing is safe: the JsonTreeIntegration that reads the index calls buildForMod only during startup dispatch, through a lazy RegisterContextRegistry callback, which is later than the construction of every @Context bean (see FanDataDrivenFactories.java:39-43 for a note on the same timing). If you register too late, the framework finds no handler for the field and reports that field as an "unknown top-level field" (JsonTreeBuilder:475-490).

docs.title: 1.7 The matching JSON and index
docs.text:
The field name is getTypeName(), the value must be an array, and each element must be an object (JsonTreeBuilder:500-506 enforces both):

{
  "effects": [
    { "id": "mymod:burn", "type": "my_effect", "params": { "duration": 600 } }
  ]
}

For this content file to be read, an index manifest has to list it. The manifest has only two array fields, on_register and on_reload; the old sources field is retired, and writing it is recorded as a loading error since it counts as an unknown field (schema.md §1.3). Registration-phase content goes under on_register:

{ "on_register": [ "mymod_content/effects.json" ] }

For manifest and content-file paths, syntax, and the D1–D6 rules see schema.md §1 and §2; for how to organize several content files see guide-content.md. The manifest location is fixed at data/<mod_id>/kasuga_lib/data_driven/ (JsonTreeBuilder.indexDirectorySegments:745-747).

docs.title: 1.8 Deduplication identity (optional)
docs.text:
resolveIdentity(modId, definition) (TypeHandler.java:64) returns a string meaning "the identity of this definition within the same type field". Two definitions with equal identities count as duplicates, and the later write wins (last-wins). The default returns null, meaning this type never takes part in deduplication.

  • When you extend RegTypeHandler this is already implemented: EffectiveId normalizes the id into its actual namespace so that "foo" and "minecraft:foo" correctly collide (RegTypeHandler:58-60).
  • When you implement TypeHandler directly, override it yourself. If your definition has no registration id (a pure effect list, say), just keep the default null; do not invent a fake id.
  • An exception thrown while resolving the identity degrades to "no identity": the entry is not deduplicated, and loading does not crash (JsonTreeBuilder.identityOf:691).

docs.title: 1.9 Why it is designed this way
docs.text: The reason for the three phases is plain: one content file can declare both groups and blocks, and a block has to attach to a group that already exists; applying in file order would fail when the block is written first. The phase encodes "who must precede whom" as a declaration instead of leaving it to the author's file ordering. Splitting parse and apply lets deduplication and diagnostics finish before registration, so a duplicate id never actually reaches the registry (the DuplicateIdResolver class comment explains why the registrar layer cannot be the backstop).

docs.title: 2. Embedded types: types that hang off a parent entry
2.1 Goal
docs.text: Some content hangs off a parent object instead of standing as its own entry, for example block_entity written inside a block (the block_entity.type in modelling contentTesting's fsm_blocks.json). Such a type takes no top-level field and can only be pulled out of the parent object.

docs.title: 2.2 How the three methods work together
docs.text:
Override getParentTypeName, getEmbeddedKeyName, and extractEmbedded (TypeHandler.java:38-50). The implementation below is taken from BlockEntityTypeHandler (handler/BlockEntityTypeHandler.java:27-53), with block_entity swapped for the key you want to use:

public final class AttachmentTypeHandler implements TypeHandler<AttachmentTypeHandler.AttachmentDef> {

    public record AttachmentDef(String type, String parentBlockId) {}

    @Override public String getTypeName() { return "attachments"; }  // for the registry index only
    @Override public int getPhase() { return PHASE_EMBEDDED; }       // apply after the parent object
    @Override public String getParentTypeName() { return "blocks"; } // lives inside blocks entries
    @Override public String getEmbeddedKeyName() { return "attachment"; } // the key name inside the parent entry

    @Override
    public List<JsonObject> extractEmbedded(JsonObject blockJson) {
        if (!blockJson.has("attachment")) return null;      // no embedded data
        JsonObject attachment = blockJson.getAsJsonObject("attachment").deepCopy();
        attachment.addProperty("_parent_block", blockJson.get("id").getAsString());
        return List.of(attachment);
    }

    @Override
    public AttachmentDef parse(JsonObject json) {
        return new AttachmentDef(
                json.get("type").getAsString(),
                json.get("_parent_block").getAsString());
    }

    @Override
    public void apply(AttachmentDef definition, BuildContext baseContext) {
        RegBuildContext context = (RegBuildContext) baseContext;
        Reg<?, Block> blockReg = context.getBlockReg(definition.parentBlockId());
        if (blockReg == null) return;                        // parent block does not exist; skip (a warn is optional)
        // ... build your embedded object from blockReg and attach it
    }
}

The contracts of the three methods:

  • A non-null getParentTypeName() declares "I am an embedded type", and its value is the parent type's getTypeName().
  • getEmbeddedKeyName() is used for diagnostics only. When an author writes an embedded type as a top-level field by mistake, the error message names "should be written in the <this key> of a <parent type> entry" (JsonTreeBuilder.dispatchContent:475-490). Without the override you lose that hint (it returns null).
  • extractEmbedded(JsonObject parentJson) receives one parent entry and returns a list of embedded objects (null for zero). _parent_block is not a field name the framework enforces; it is the convention this repository's BlockEntityTypeHandler uses. You can define your own, as long as your parse recognizes the key.

docs.title: 2.3 Differences from top-level types
docs.text:
• An embedded type takes no part in top-level field dispatch. dispatchContent filters the embedded handlers out first (JsonTreeBuilder:461-467) and checks root.has(getTypeName()) only for top-level handlers (:500-506); embedded data is extracted separately inside the parent loop (:528-535).
